question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the current law, a card surcharge on rent is likely prohibited, and it makes no difference whether the app company or the agent keeps it. The documents don't cover one possible exception, so I can't rule it out completely.

**Which law applies:** Today (5 November 2026), the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026), is the governing Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) also apply [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Fees for rent payment are restricted.** Under s 51A, a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations list "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The exception is for surcharges permitted under *another* Act. The documents I retrieved don't identify any such Act, so I can't confirm whether one applies.
- **Electronic payment facility charges are restricted.** A person must not demand or receive a charge for the use of any electronic payment facility for paying rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A no-cost option must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank or account fees on the renter's own account) is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bank transfer is a protected method.** Electronic funds transfer is the prescribed payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The provider or agent must permit the renter to pay by any prescribed payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed.** Before the renter consents to a payment method, the provider or agent must give information about costs, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who gets the fee?

Not under the current text. The s 51A prohibition applies to "a person, other than an ADI" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't exempt the app company or the agent. An earlier version (No. 111, in force 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) carved out residential rental providers and agents from s 51A(1) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That carve-out does not appear in the current text I retrieved [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Note that the documents I have are extracts, so I haven't seen the full text of s 51A.

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** to confirm the cost of each payment method, as the agent must disclose costs before you agree to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask that bank transfer be made available** as a no-cost option. The agent must ensure one is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Question the card fee** by pointing to s 51A and the electronic payment facility rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ignore the "slower" point for legal purposes.** The law doesn't address how fast each method is, so speed is a practical issue to raise with the agent.

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether any other Act permits a payment surcharge (which would fall under the Regulations' exception [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)).
- How to make a complaint or enforce these rules, such as through VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria.
- Your rent payment due dates or whether bank transfer timing affects late-payment rules.

This is general information, not legal advice. If the app or agent refuses to change its fees, a tenancy advisory service would be the right next step.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered. The answer says a no-cost payment method must be 'reasonably available'. For the hardest point, it quotes s 51A ('a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee'), cites the Regulations' 'other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act' exception and answers 'Does it matter who gets the fee? Not under the current text.' It also gives next steps such as asking for bank transfer and questioning the card fee.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the fee is allowed because a fee-free option exists; it says "a card surcharge on rent is likely prohibited." It raises the agent exemption only to reject it for the current law: the version 111 carve-out "does not appear in the current text" and s 51A "doesn't exempt the app company or the agent."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026)' and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026)', and applies rules only from those versions. It mentions Version No. 111 only to note that the law was different earlier, which is not relying on it.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

**Short answer:** You don't automatically have to pay. The agent can only require a professional clean if the carpets genuinely need one to return to their starting condition.

- **Current regulations:** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021), Authorised Version 009, are in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Under that version, the rental provider "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless either (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your situation:** Your lease clause (a pet clause requiring professional cleaning) doesn't override this. The regulations also say that where professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises, the renter must have it done or pay for it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So the cost obligation only applies if professional cleaning is actually required under that test.
- **General duty:** At the end of a tenancy, a renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and "in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession of the premises, taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check the start-of-tenancy condition report.** The regulations say the condition report "will help to resolve disputes over cleaning" and that photos should be taken at the beginning and end of the tenancy [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The version I retrieved is the 2022 form, so check it against the current form.
2. **Compare your end-of-tenancy photos** with any move-in photos. Photos should be dated and labelled by location [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask the agent in writing** what condition they say the carpets are in, and whether they say professional cleaning is required to restore them to their move-in condition. This puts the question on record.
4. **Check whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in** and whether you were told. If not, the first exception in reg 12(1) doesn't apply [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Attend the final inspection if you can.** Under the 2022 form, the landlord must complete the final inspection and condition report within 10 days of the end date and give you a chance to attend [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Seek help if they insist.** The Form 4 materials point renters to VCAT and to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **A receipt requirement:** The documents I found don't say that you must provide a professional cleaner's receipt, or that a DIY clean can't count. They also don't define "professional standard."
- **Evidence standards:** They don't say what evidence would be enough to show the carpets were restored.
- **Carpet-specific rules:** I found nothing specific to carpets.

## Important caveat about the Act

The Act text I retrieved (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 110) shows an end date of 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I couldn't find the currently in force version of the Act, so the Act references above should be checked against the current Act. The Regulations version 009 is the one I identified as in force today [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information, not legal advice. If the agent insists on payment, a free tenancy advice service such as Victoria Legal Aid or VCAT can review your specific lease and photos.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. Point 1: it quotes reg 12's two exceptions, prior professional cleaning with the renter told, or cleaning 'required to restore the rented premises to the same condition... taking into account fair wear and tear'. Point 2: it states the duty to leave the premises 'reasonably clean and in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession... taking into account fair wear and tear'. Point 3, the hardest: it tells the renter to 'Check the start-of-tenancy condition report', notes it 'will help to resolve disputes over cleaning', and says to compare end photos 'with any move-in photos'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay because of the clause or the pet; it says the opposite: "You don't automatically have to pay" and "Your lease clause (a pet clause requiring professional cleaning) doesn't override this," with cost applying "only... if professional cleaning is actually required under that test."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer relies on 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 110' for the general end-of-tenancy duty instead of the in-force Authorised Version No. 115, and it presents steps such as the 10-day final inspection from the 2022 Regulations version (21-3sra002) as actions the user can take, even with a caveat.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction also commits you to pay a separate invoice. They do set out what a landlord or agent can claim from a bond and what the renter can do, so the points below are the most relevant.

**Which law applies:** The current version is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- A provider may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- At the end of a tenancy, a renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Before a provider makes a bond claim to the bond authority, "at least 3 days before" the claim, the provider "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Bond claim evidence includes "an invoice," "a receipt," "a quote," or "a photograph" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- That evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A provider must not ask you to sign a claim form unless the form specifies "the amount of bond to be refunded" and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Your situation**

- **Do you have to pay the invoice?** The documents don't answer this directly. The Act's bond-claim provisions govern how the provider recovers cleaning costs from the bond [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since your full bond was returned, the documents don't say whether a further invoice for the same cleaning can be enforced against you.
- **Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?** The documents don't address this. Whether your earlier agreement covers a separate invoice depends on its exact wording, which I don't have.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the bond claim evidence.** If the agent wanted the cleaning cost from your bond, they had to provide supporting evidence (such as an invoice, quote, or photos) at least 3 days before claiming [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Ask whether this was done.
2. **Check the condition report.** Compare the cleaning claim with your move-in condition report, because bond claim evidence must not conflict with it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for the amount and basis.** Ask the agent to show that the cost is "reasonable" and that the premises were not left reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Seek dispute resolution if needed.** The Act allows an application to the Tribunal, and for a provider's application for repayment of a bond, the time limit is "within 14 days after the residential rental agreement has terminated" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check the timing against your tenancy end date.

The documents I retrieved don't cover whether a provider can pursue a renter for costs after the full bond has been released, so you may want to get specific advice on that point.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer misses the point that agreeing to a bond deduction is agreement to a claim on the bond, not to pay a separate invoice. It hedges with 'The documents don't address this. Whether your earlier agreement covers a separate invoice depends on its exact wording,' so a reader cannot tell which way it falls. The reasonably-clean test against the condition at the start of the tenancy is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither forbidden claim: it says "The documents don't answer this directly" on whether the invoice must be paid, and "The documents I retrieved don't cover whether a provider can pursue a renter for costs after the full bond has been released."

The answer names the required document with its in-force version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026", and every rule it applies is cited to that version via the link 97-109aa115-authorised.pdf, with no reliance on any other version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't necessarily have to wait. Under the Act, if the owner can't or won't get an urgent repair done, you can arrange it yourself and seek reimbursement. Whether a broken tap that cut off the water supply counts as an "urgent repair" is a question I can't fully answer from these documents.

**Version used:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version (reprint) No. 115, which took effect on 13 October 2026 and is the version in force today [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026, is the current version of the Regulations [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **You must tell the owner first.** You must give the owner written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of a breakdown of facilities or equipment they provided [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **You can arrange urgent repairs if two conditions are met.** You may do so if (a) you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner or their agent to immediately carry out the repairs, and (b) you are unable to get them to do it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **You must give written notice afterwards.** You must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner must pay you back.** The owner must reimburse the reasonable cost of the repairs, or the prescribed amount if it is less, within 7 days of receiving your written notice of the repairs and cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary says reimbursement is available for repairs "up to $2500" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Only suitably qualified people may do repairs.** The Regulations state that "only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This means any plumber you use should be properly qualified.

## What you can ask for

- **Tribunal order:** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out the urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or the owner refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days after it is made [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't answer

- **Whether a broken tap or loss of water is an "urgent repair":** The Act defines urgent repairs in section 3(1), but that definition isn't in the documents I retrieved. The Regulations list "failure or breakdown of any essential service or appliance provided for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering" as urgent repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Water supply to the whole house is not listed in that extract.
- **Whether the owner's "own tradespeople only" rule is enforceable:** The documents don't address this clause.
- **How long you must wait:** The documents don't say how long is "immediate" or what counts as reasonable steps.

## Suggested next steps

1. Put the problem in writing to the owner or emergency contact now, describing the leak and loss of water. The emergency contact form says that for an urgent repair, the resident should notify the operator in writing [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. Keep a record of every attempt to get the owner or their agent to act.
3. If they still can't or won't act, arrange a qualified plumber and keep all invoices.
4. Give written notice of the repair and its cost within 7 days, and ask for reimbursement.
5. If the owner refuses to pay or the cost is high, consider applying to VCAT. For the definition of urgent repairs and advice on your specific situation, check Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs), which the Regulations refer you to [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

It also misses the third point: instead of saying that a term requiring the landlord's nominated tradesperson is prohibited (reg 11(e)), it says "the documents don't address this clause." The second point (reasonable steps, then reimbursement within 7 days of written notice) is covered.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents show that the rental provider must fix these problems, and they set out a repair process. They do not contain a right to cancel the lease or to a rent reduction for this situation, so I can't confirm either option from them.

**Documents relied on**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 and the current version in the retrieved material [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

I've taken the version numbers from the document metadata. The retrieved text doesn't use the phrase "Authorised Version number."

**What the law says**
- Rented premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof," and "each room... must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- "Urgent repairs" include "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" and "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A renter must give the provider written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Before you move in, the provider must complete a condition report. You should note anything that needs repair, and you have 5 business days after moving in to complete your part [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you find something later that was not visible when you filled it in, you can apply to VCAT to correct the report within 30 days of the start date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Your options**

1. **Ask for repairs (non-urgent).** Give written notice. If the provider doesn't carry out the repairs within 14 days of receiving notice, you can apply to the Director to investigate or to VCAT for an order [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

2. **Urgent repairs.** You may arrange repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't. You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to the lesser of the actual cost or any prescribed amount [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An earlier version of the Regulations stated a $2,500 limit [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), but the retrieved current version doesn't confirm that figure, so please check it before relying on it.

3. **Apply to VCAT.** VCAT can order the provider to carry out urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) or non-urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the Tribunal finds a breach of the duty to maintain the premises in good repair, it can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

4. **Pay rent into the Rent Special Account.** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT for an order to pay rent into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal must make that order if the provider has failed to carry out the repairs and has not shown financial hardship [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This holds the rent until repairs are made. It is not a rent reduction.

**What the documents don't cover**
- **Cancelling the lease:** The retrieved documents don't include termination rights for unfit or defective premises. I can't say whether you could cancel.
- **Lowering the rent:** The retrieved documents don't include a power to reduce rent for defects. The only rent-related option is the Rent Special Account in option 4.
- **Compensation amounts** and the specific provision for defects found before the tenancy starts were not in the retrieved text.

**Next steps:** Put your concerns in writing now, list the defects, and attach photos to your condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). For advice on cancelling or on rent, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting) or a tenants' legal service. This is general information, not legal advice.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** The break-in damage should be reported to your landlord in writing now, not at the end of the lease. If the plumbing or wiring problem is urgent, you may be able to arrange repairs yourselves and claim the cost back, subject to conditions. The documents don't say whether burglary damage counts as your responsibility, so get that confirmed for your case.

**Which law applies today:** As of 5 November 2026, the current documents are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Duty to report:** As soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage, a renter must give written notice to the landlord stating that the damage occurred and its nature [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations also require written notice of damage and of breakdowns of facilities [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your cleaning duty:** A renter must keep the premises reasonably clean. At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave them, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Damage liability:** A renter and visitor must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, and fair wear and tear is excluded [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpt I found doesn't address damage by burglars who are not your visitors.
- **Landlord's duties:** The landlord must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation, and must only use suitably qualified people for repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning:** The landlord cannot require professional cleaning unless it was done before you moved in, or it is required to restore the premises to their starting condition, with regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice now.** Tell the landlord in writing about the break-in, the plumbing and wiring damage, and the resulting cleaning problem [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for urgent repairs if they qualify.** The Regulations say the landlord must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. If you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to act immediately and they haven't, you may arrange repairs yourselves. The landlord must then reimburse the reasonable cost, up to $2,500 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do the repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2,500, or the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Under the earlier Act text, VCAT must hear urgent repair applications within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** If an issue isn't urgent, you may apply to VCAT if the landlord has not carried out the repairs within 14 days of receiving notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Locks.** The landlord must provide locks as required. You need the landlord's consent to change a lock in the master key system, and the landlord must not unreasonably refuse [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **Document everything.** Take dated photos showing the damage and its location, and keep copies of notices and receipts [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Before the end of the lease, the landlord must inspect and complete the condition report within 10 days after the end date, and you should be given the chance to attend [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
7. **Cleaning.** Make reasonable efforts to clean what you can now, and tell the landlord in writing what you could not clean because of the damage [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the landlord says professional cleaning is needed, check whether it is required to restore the premises, as described above [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Whether the plumbing or wiring damage is "urgent."** The current urgent repairs list is not in the retrieved text. The 2019 version of the Act lists items such as a burst water service and a dangerous electrical fault [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but that version is outdated.
- **Full current repair procedures.** The sections on urgent and non-urgent repairs (ss 72–75) appear in the earlier Version 111 of the Act, which ended on 29 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The current Version 115 excerpt I found does not include them, so confirm the current wording.
- **Whether you must pay for burglary damage**, or whether rent can be reduced while the property is unusable.
- **Police reports, insurance, or security upgrades** beyond the lock rules above.

For advice on your specific situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the current Act, a rent payment fee is generally prohibited, and it doesn't matter whether the app company or the agent keeps it. One exception may apply, but the documents I found don't show that it does here.

**Governing document:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), reprint **version 115**, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations I found (*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021) are version 005, which the metadata shows as in force only until 9 February 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I could not find a current Regulations version, so I can't confirm the current Regulations.

### What the law says

- **Fees for paying rent are prohibited.** A person, other than an ADI (authorised deposit-taking institution), must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 penalty units for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The prescribed matters include "rent payment"**, but the list excludes "payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't identify any Act that permits a payment surcharge for your app, so I can't confirm the exception applies.
- **Electronic payment charges are separately prohibited.** A person must not demand or receive a charge for the establishment or use of direct debit or any other electronic payment facility for rent. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The provider or agent must offer a no-extra-cost method.** They must ensure a payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than your own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed before you choose a method.** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, before you consent to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who gets the fee?

The prohibition in s 51A applies to "a person" who demands or receives the fee, with the exception of ADIs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't carve out the app company. The documents don't say whether your app is the agent or a third party. The obligations to offer a free method and to disclose costs fall on the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whoever receives the fee, the card fee is still a fee for paying rent.

### What you can do or ask

- **Ask the provider or agent** to confirm in writing which payment methods are fee-free and to explain any card fee, as they must disclose costs before you use a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Use the bank transfer.** It is the kind of no-extra-cost method the provider or agent must make reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say anything about how fast it must be processed, so the slower speed is a practical issue they don't address.
- **Ask for a receipt.** If you pay by a method other than in person and request a receipt at the time of payment, the recipient must give a written receipt within 5 business days (penalty: 25 penalty units) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Not covered:** The documents don't set out how to get a refund of a card fee already paid, or which body handles complaints about it.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer says a no-extra-cost method must be 'reasonably available to you'. It says the fee is banned for anyone other than an ADI and states 'it doesn't matter whether the app company or the agent keeps it', noting the exception for 'payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act'. It also gives next steps, such as using the bank transfer and asking the agent in writing about fee-free methods.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the fee is allowed because a fee-free option exists, and it does not exempt the landlord or agent; it states the fee is 'generally prohibited, and it doesn't matter whether the app company or the agent keeps it' and that the ban applies to 'a person' other than an ADI.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer correctly cites the Act as 'version 115' but relies on the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 'version 005' (21-3sra005) for the rule that prescribed matters include 'rent payment' and exclude permitted surcharge fees, rather than the in-force Authorised Version No. 009, and deleting that rule would change the substance of the answer.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if the carpets are back to their move-in condition. The rules turn on whether professional cleaning is *required* to restore the premises, not on whether the lease clause mentions it. The documents don't say the agent can insist on a professional's receipt.

**Which document applies:** The current document is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), Authorised Version **009**, which has effect from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act itself ([Residential Tenancies Act 1997](#)) has no current version in these results. The latest Act text I found, version 110, was in force only until 24 November 2025 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm the current Act wording.

### What the law says

- **Landlord's limit:** The landlord "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless either (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter's obligation:** The renter must pay for or arrange professional cleaning only "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The standard-form wording (Form 1, item 11) says the same [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter's general duty:** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, taking into account fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). This is from a 2021 version of the Act, so check it against the current text.
- **Clause validity:** The Act says a landlord must not include a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy "unless that term is contained in the standard form" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A term that is not in the standard form may be invalid, and a renter can apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring a term invalid or varying it [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Compare the carpets to the condition report.** The cleaning test refers to the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the agent's report describes the carpets as clean at move-in, your evidence that they are now in that state matters most.
2. **Ask the agent to say why professional cleaning is required.** Under the regulation, the requirement must be one needed to restore the original condition, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Ask them to identify what is still not restored.
3. **Gather your own evidence.** The documents don't list what evidence is acceptable. Practical options (my suggestions, not from the documents) include dated photos and video of each room, your cleaning receipts for products, and the move-in condition report.
4. **Consider the Tribunal if it stays unresolved.** If the agent insists and you disagree, the Act allows an application to the Tribunal [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't give the process or costs, so check with the Tribunal or Consumer Affairs Victoria.

**Not covered by the documents:** whether a professional receipt is required as proof, what counts as acceptable evidence, and how the bond process handles disputed cleaning. The regulations don't address these points.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The hardest one, the condition report as evidence of starting condition, is covered by 'Compare the carpets to the condition report. The cleaning test refers to the condition report... having regard to the condition report.' The other two points are also stated: the reg 12 exceptions (prior professional cleaning with notice, or cleaning needed to restore pre-tenancy condition allowing for fair wear and tear), and the s 63 duty to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition, fair wear and tear excepted.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay because of the clause or the pet; it says the opposite: "Probably not, if the carpets are back to their move-in condition. The rules turn on whether professional cleaning is *required* to restore the premises, not on whether the lease clause mentions it."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Regulations correctly as 'Authorised Version 009', but it never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Authorised Version No. 115. Instead it applies rules from Act versions that were not in force on that date: the clause-validity and Tribunal rules come from 'version 110' (97-109aa110), and the renter's general cleaning duty comes from the 2021 version 098 (97-109aa098). Deleting that material would change the substance of the answer.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't settle whether you must pay the separate invoice. They show that cleaning costs are normally claimed from the bond, not billed separately after the bond is returned. They don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction also binds you to pay an invoice.

**Governing version:** Today is 5 November 2026, and the Act version in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Cleaning can be claimed from the bond.** A landlord may claim "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence must be provided first.** At least 3 days before a claim to the provider is made, the provider or their agent "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Bond claim evidence means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph, or other prescribed evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The evidence must match the condition report.** Bond claim evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty to leave the premises clean.** At the end of a tenancy, a renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The text I retrieved for this section is from Version 110, which is no longer in force, so I could not confirm the current wording in Version 115.

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the bond claim evidence.** Ask whether the agent gave you an invoice, receipt, quote or photographs at least 3 days before the claim, and check whether it conflicts with your condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check what the claim was for.** Cleaning is only claimable if the premises were not left reasonably clean, judged against their condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask the Authority about any other party's claim.** If a claim is made without everyone's consent, the Authority must notify the other parties, who have 14 days to say the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Apply to the Tribunal if you dispute it.** An application for a bond repayment order "must be made within 14 days after the residential rental agreement has terminated" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether agreeing to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay an invoice. The retrieved sections don't address this.
- Whether an agent can send a separate invoice after the bond has been fully refunded.
- Whether your earlier agreement was valid or binding, or what effect it had.

For these points, you'd need the residential tenancy agreement, any written deduction agreement, and advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Tribunal (VCAT).

---

**Sources:**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026).
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110 (in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025; superseded).

It says the documents 'don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction also binds you to pay an invoice', so a reader cannot tell which way it falls. It never states that agreeing to a bond deduction is agreement to a claim on the bond, not to pay a separate invoice. The reasonably-clean test is covered ('judged against their condition at the start of the tenancy').

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely. If you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do the repair immediately and they cannot, the law lets you arrange urgent repairs yourself. The owner's restriction to their own tradespeople doesn't settle the question, and the documents don't say whether it does.

**Which documents I relied on:** The current Regulations are *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act text I found is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 111, which is in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Nothing I retrieved covers the Act from 30 June 2026 onward, so I can't confirm that version is still the current one. Section 72 has the same wording in version 110 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and I'm relying on version 111.

**What the law says**

- A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to carry them out immediately, and they are unable to get the landlord or agent to do them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- A burst water service is given as an example of an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So any plumber you engage should be properly qualified.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Report it in writing now.** Give the landlord or agent written notice as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The emergency contact on the form is the person to use for urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Keep a record of every attempt** to get the repair done immediately, including the time, who you contacted, and their response. This evidence supports the "reasonable steps" and "unable to get" requirements [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **If they still can't attend, arrange a suitably qualified person** to fix it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give written notice afterwards.** Within 7 days you must give the landlord written notice of the repairs and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask for reimbursement.** The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if that is less, and must pay within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations state that you may be reimbursed directly for the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **If the landlord refuses to pay or the cost is too high, go to VCAT.** You can apply if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). They also don't address the effect of shutting off the water to the whole house. If you're unsure, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs), which the Regulations refer to for the full list of urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The current law gives you a clear right to repairs, but the retrieved documents don't cover cancelling the lease or reducing the rent for defects found before you move in.

**Which law applies today (5 November 2026):** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The excerpts I retrieved are partial.

---

## What the law says

- **Mould and damp:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure." The premises must also be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes a failure to comply with the rental minimum standards, and "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber may fall under "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure," but the documents don't say this directly, so get advice on your specific defects.
- **Duty to repair:** The landlord (residential rental provider) must maintain the premises in good repair [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Before you move in:** An older version of the Act (2020) said a tenant is not required to move in if the premises don't comply with the landlord's duty to be vacant and reasonably clean, and no rent is payable until the tenant actually moves in [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). The current excerpts I retrieved don't include this provision, so please check it in the current Act before relying on it.

## What you can do or ask

**1. Ask for repairs in writing (required first step).** You must give the provider written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Urgent repairs.** If the problem is urgent, you may arrange repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't. You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A 2025 version of the standard form summarised the cap as $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That is not the current figure, so verify it. If you can't afford the repairs, or the provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear an urgent repair application within 2 business days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Non-urgent repairs.** If you give written notice and the provider doesn't carry out the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) or apply to VCAT [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear a non-urgent repair application within 7 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**4. Rent.** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay your rent into the Rent Special Account [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This holds the rent rather than reducing it. VCAT can order the rent paid to you if the required repairs are not done by the deadline in its order [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). **The documents do not contain a power to reduce rent.**

**5. Cancelling the lease.** **The retrieved documents do not cover this.** I can't say whether you can cancel based on these defects.

**6. Condition report.** Your condition report is a record of the premises' state at the start. A 2025 version of the regulations' Form 4 said that if you later find something not working or in poor repair, you may apply to VCAT to correct the report within 30 days after the start date of the agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The current Form 4 is not in the retrieved excerpts, so check it.

---

**Next steps:** Document everything with dated photos, put your complaint in writing, and check the current Act and regulations on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or get advice from a tenants' legal service before deciding whether to end the lease.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current Act, you should notify your landlord in writing now, and you may be able to arrange urgent repairs yourselves and get the cost reimbursed. The retrieved documents don't settle whether you must clean the place before the lease ends, or whether burglary damage counts as damage you're responsible for.

**Document relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), **Authorised Version No. 115**, which the metadata shows in force from 13 October 2026 with no end date [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is the version in force today (5 November 2026).

## What the law says

- **Reporting damage:** A renter must give written notice to the landlord "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the premises, or of a breakdown of facilities. The notice must state the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice may be given electronically [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and the landlord is unable or fails to do so [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The renter must then give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice, up to the prescribed amount [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved current text doesn't state the prescribed amount.
- **What counts as urgent:** The retrieved definition is from the 2019 version, not the current one. It includes "a dangerous electrical fault", "a burst water service", "a blocked or broken lavatory system", and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises unsafe or insecure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The current definition wasn't in the retrieved text, so please confirm it before relying on it.
- **Cleaning at the end:** A renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The "as far as practicable" wording may matter here, but the documents don't address damage that prevents cleaning.
- **Renter's damage duty:** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises, and fair wear and tear is excluded [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether burglars count as "visitors." The definition of visitor refers to a person on the premises "with the permission of the tenant" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf), which suggests they would not, but this is my inference, not something the documents state.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice now** to the landlord describing the break-ins and the damaged plumbing and wiring [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the landlord to repair urgently.** Electrical and plumbing faults may qualify as urgent under the 2019 definition [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf), but confirm under the current Act.
3. **If the landlord doesn't act,** you may arrange urgent repairs yourselves, provided you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to act first [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep receipts. Send the 7-day written notice of the repairs and cost [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **If the landlord refuses to pay or you can't meet the cost,** you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask the landlord about cleaning** in writing, noting that the damage prevents cleaning.

## Gaps in the documents

- The current text of the landlord's duty to maintain the premises in good repair wasn't retrieved. The 2020 version appears in the search results [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf), but it isn't the current law.
- The current rules for non-urgent repairs and rent payment into the Rent Special Account appear only in older versions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm them as current.
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 version retrieved (S.R. No. 3/2021, version 005) expired on 9 February 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Its $2,500 urgent-repair reimbursement figure therefore may not apply today.
- The documents don't address insurance, police reports, or changing locks after a break-in.

Because the lease is ongoing and the damage is serious, consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria, which the regulations list as a source for urgent repairs information [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least for a card fee charged to you as rent. Victorian law restricts charges for electronic rent payments, but the documents don't expressly say whether a card payment through an app is covered. Whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent affects which provision applies, but the restrictions reach both.

**Governing document:** The current law is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Today's date is 5 November 2026, so this is the version that applies. The regulations in force are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- The provider or agent must ensure that a rent payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to the renter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 penalty units for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A person must not demand or receive a charge from a renter in relation to the use of any other electronic payment facility for paying rent. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the provision most likely to cover a card fee, though the documents don't say expressly that a card payment is an "electronic payment facility."
- A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to paying rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't list the prescribed matters, so I can't confirm whether a card fee is one of them.
- Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations' standard terms say the rental provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

The charging prohibition applies to "a person," not only to the provider or agent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The duty to offer a no-additional-cost method applies to the provider or agent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether the app company is the agent, so I can't say which duties apply to it. A fee taken by the app company is still caught by the charging prohibition if it is a charge for paying rent electronically.

**What you can do or ask**

- Ask the provider or agent to confirm in writing whether the card fee is a charge for an electronic payment facility, and to identify the fee-free option.
- Use the fee-free bank transfer. The law requires that a no-additional-cost method be "reasonably available," but the documents don't define that term or say anything about how quickly payments must clear, so the slower speed is not addressed.
- Ask for a written receipt. If you pay other than in person and request a receipt at the time, it must be given within 5 business days, with a penalty of 25 penalty units [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Agree with the provider in writing to change the payment method, since the parties may change the manner of payment by agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Don't consent to the card option until you have received the cost information the law requires [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover how to make a complaint or what remedies are available if the fee is unlawful, so I can't advise on those steps from these sources.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Not automatically. Under the current regulations, the clause can only require professional cleaning if it is needed to restore the carpets to their move-in condition, and fair wear and tear is taken into account. Your own cleaning may be enough to meet that test, but the documents don't say how a dispute over it would be decided.

## What the law says

- The governing instrument is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version version 009** (in force from 30 June 2026). It is the most recent version I found [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act version I retrieved, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* version 110, shows an end date of 24 November 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so I could not confirm the current Act version.
- Regulation 12(1) says the landlord **must not require** you to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy **unless** either:
  - (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and you were told so; or
  - (b) professional cleaning **is required to restore the premises to the same condition** they were in immediately before the tenancy started, **having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Regulation 12(2) is the prescribed term that lets the renter be made to pay for professional cleaning, but only "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises" to that move-in condition, again having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Under the Act, a clause requiring professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 27C allows the standard form to include this kind of term [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A renter may apply to VCAT for an order declaring invalid or varying a term that is harsh or unconscionable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check the two conditions.** Look at your condition report from move-in. Did it record carpets as clean? Was professional cleaning done before you moved in, and were you told? If the answer to the second is no, the landlord's requirement is weaker.
2. **Ask the agent in writing** which of the two conditions they say applies, and what they say is required to restore the carpets to the move-in condition. Note that the regulation requires the assessment to take account of fair wear and tear.
3. **Gather evidence of the carpets' condition:**
   - The move-in condition report and any photos or videos from move-in.
   - Your own photos or video of the carpets at move-out, dated and showing the whole room.
   - Your cleaning receipts, the method and products used, and the date.
   - Any agent inspection report or correspondence.
4. **If the dispute continues,** you can apply to VCAT under the harsh or unconscionable terms provision [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents I found don't say how VCAT would weigh your evidence, so check VCAT's guidance.

## What the documents don't cover

- They don't say what evidence VCAT would accept as proof of carpet condition.
- They don't say whether the agent can deduct cleaning costs from your bond, or how a bond claim is handled.
- I could not check whether your lease is in the standard form, which affects whether the clause is valid.
