question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction also commits you to pay a separate invoice. What they do say is how a landlord can recover cleaning costs, and that process runs through the bond.

I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is the version in force today, November 5, 2026.

## What the law says

- **Cleaning costs are a bond claim matter.** A landlord is entitled to claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The renter's duty.** At the end of a tenancy, the renter must leave the premises, as far as practicable, "reasonably clean" and in the same condition as when they moved in, taking fair wear and tear into account. This comes from section 63 as it appears in Authorised Version No. 98 (dated 29 March 2021), so I could not confirm the current wording from Version 115 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence before a claim.** At least 3 days before a bond claim is made to the landlord, the landlord or their agent "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim." Bond claim evidence includes "an invoice," "a receipt," "a quote," or "a photograph" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Claim form.** A landlord must not get a renter's signature on a claim form unless it specifies the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice of claims.** If a claim is made without the consent of all parties, the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority must notify the other parties. The notice must state that the Authority will pay the claim unless, within 14 days, a party gives written notice that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether agreeing to a bond deduction counts as agreeing to pay an invoice. None of the retrieved documents addresses this.
- Whether a landlord or agent can send a separate invoice for cleaning after the full bond has been refunded, or whether they can pursue you for more than the bond. The provisions I found describe claims against the bond, and I found nothing on other recovery routes.
- Whether the cleaning charge is reasonable in your case. That depends on facts I don't have, such as the condition report and the invoice.

## What you can do

1. **Ask for the bond claim evidence.** Request the invoice, quote, receipts, or photographs supporting the charge. Under [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), a claim against the bond should be backed by this evidence.
2. **Compare it with the condition report.** Check whether the evidence conflicts with the condition report. Under [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), it must not.
3. **Check the amount.** Ask whether the cost is reasonable and whether the premises were actually left unclean beyond fair wear and tear.
4. **Check the bond status.** Since your full bond was returned, no bond claim for cleaning appears to have succeeded. If the agent later makes a claim, you'd get notice and a 14-day window to object [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Get advice before paying.** If you dispute the invoice, the Tribunal is the forum the Act refers to. The 14-day window for a bond-related Tribunal application under section 419A(2) runs from when the tenancy ended, so check your dates [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I haven't confirmed how that applies to a separate invoice, so consider getting legal advice or a Victorian tenancy service.

I also retrieved a 2021 Residential Tenancies Regulations document, but its version ran only to 30 November 2024 [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), so I didn't rely on it for current law.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait for the owner's tradespeople. The law lets you arrange urgent repairs yourself in some circumstances, but the repairer must be suitably qualified, and you must give written notice and keep the costs reasonable.

**Which version applies:** The most recent Regulations text I retrieved is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **009**, which has an in-force date of 30 June 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Its urgent-repairs section wasn't in the excerpt I could retrieve, so I've relied on the previous version, Authorised Version 005 (in force 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The latest *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* I retrieved is Authorised Version 110, which ended on 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't include the Act version in force today, so please check the current text before relying on this.

**What the law says**

- **Urgent repairs:** Water supply failure counts. The definition covers "a failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" and "a burst water service" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). This definition comes from the 2021 Act text [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm it is unchanged. The documents don't say whether a broken tap alone qualifies, or whether turning off the whole house's water makes it urgent.
- **Your right to arrange repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and you are unable to get them to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Qualified repairers only:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost limit:** The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost of the repairs, up to $2,500 under the 2025 Regulations [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The Act says the landlord is liable for the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Notify in writing now.** Renters must give written notice to the landlord as soon as practicable after becoming aware of a breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Send this to the emergency contact, and keep a copy.
2. **Document your attempts.** Keep a record of your attempts to reach the owner or their tradespeople, since you must show reasonable steps and that you could not get the repairs done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Arrange a suitably qualified plumber.** Get a quote and keep the invoice.
4. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The landlord must reimburse you within 7 days after receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the owner refuses to pay or the cost is too high,** you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the landlord to carry out the urgent repairs, if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't say whether an owner's requirement to use only their own tradespeople overrides your right to arrange urgent repairs. They also don't confirm whether a broken tap, as opposed to a burst pipe or a whole-house supply failure, is urgent. For a definite answer, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs) or VCAT.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The law requires your landlord to fix these problems. It gives you a repair route and a VCAT route. The documents don't give you a right to reduce your rent, and they don't contain enough detail to confirm when you can cancel.

Documents used: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Older versions appear in the search results but are superseded.

## What the law says

- **Mould and damp:** Each room must be free from "mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Structure:** The premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't mention rotting timber specifically, so I can't say whether it falls under this standard.
- **Condition at move-in:** The rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the minimum standards and are "vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in," and must maintain them "in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" and "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That text comes from version 111, which was superseded on 29 June 2026. The current version 115 excerpt I retrieved stops before this part, so I can't confirm its current wording.

## Your options

**1. Put it in writing (do this first).**
- A condition report that lists something needing repair gives the landlord written notice of the issue [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You must fill in and return the condition report within 5 business days after moving in. Note anything that seems unsafe or needs repair, and take dated photos [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If you find problems later, you can apply to VCAT to correct the report within 30 days after the start date of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Tell the landlord about any defect that could threaten safety [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for repairs.**
- **Urgent repairs:** The landlord must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. If you have taken reasonable steps to get them done immediately and the landlord hasn't acted, you may arrange them yourself and be reimbursed for the reasonable cost of up to $2,500. You can apply to VCAT if you can't afford the repairs, the cost is over $2,500, or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** You must notify the landlord in writing as soon as practicable. The landlord must carry out repairs within a reasonable time, and you can apply to VCAT for an order if repairs aren't done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**3. Cancel (leave the lease).**
- The documents refer to a notice to vacate under section 91ZD of the Act "on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation," with no rent foregone for the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The text of section 91ZD is not in the retrieved documents, so I can't confirm its conditions, notice period, or whether it applies before you have moved in.
- You can also apply to VCAT under section 91U to reduce the agreement term on the basis of severe hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This reduces the term, not the rent.

**4. Ask for lower rent.**
- The documents don't contain a rent-reduction right for these defects, so I can't answer this from them. Your options above are the ones the documents support.

## Next steps
- Write to the landlord or agent now, describe each problem, and attach dated photos.
- Consumer Affairs Victoria can be reached on 1300 55 81 81 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Before relying on section 91ZD or a VCAT application, check the full current Act, since the retrieved excerpts don't include it. This isn't formal legal advice, so consider speaking to a tenancy lawyer or Victoria Legal Aid.

Deleting it would remove the basis for treating the user's mould and damp as an urgent repair, so the answer's substance would change.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Governing document:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (title "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026), is the version in force today [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (dated 30 June 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Duty to report:** A renter must give written notice to the provider "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the premises or a breakdown of facilities [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under the Regulations, the notice must be in writing [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Damage by others:** A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises, and this applies to the renter and visitors [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say how this applies to damage by burglars.
- **Cleaning:** A renter must keep the premises reasonably clean, but at the end of the agreement must leave them "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because the lease has not ended, this end-of-tenancy duty does not yet apply.
- **Provider's duty:** The provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do urgent or non-urgent repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Notify the provider in writing now.** Describe the break-in, the damage to the plumbing and wiring, and the fact that you cannot clean properly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy.
2. **Request urgent repairs.** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to carry them out immediately and you cannot get them done [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must then give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations state that reimbursement can be up to $2500 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for urgent repairs.** You can apply if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **For non-urgent repairs,** you can apply to the Director if the provider has not acted within 14 days of your written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT for an order if the provider has not carried out the repairs within 14 days of receiving notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep evidence.** The Regulations suggest keeping a condition report and dated photos [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says the renter's documentary evidence of repairs is a matter VCAT must consider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Gaps in the documents

- **Whether the damage is "urgent":** The Regulations refer to the Consumer Affairs Victoria website for the full list of urgent repairs. The documents only list failure of hot water, cooking, heating or laundering services as examples [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They do not say whether plumbing or wiring damage from a break-in qualifies.
- **Security and locks:** The documents say the provider must provide locks to secure windows and external doors, but they do not address replacing locks after a break-in [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Insurance, police reports, and compensation for stolen items:** The documents do not cover these.
- **Rent reduction or the Rent Special Account:** An earlier version of the Act includes a process for paying rent into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That version is no longer in force, and the current excerpt I retrieved does not confirm it, so I have not relied on it.

For advice on your specific situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009** (in force from **30 June 2026**; Author **Lavina Mandy**). It says that, from **31 March 2026**, “rent payment” fees are prohibited **except for payment surcharge fees permitted under another Act**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

That document does **not** say whether a card fee charged through a rent app is permitted, nor whether the result differs depending on whether the fee is received by the app company or the agent. **The retrieved documents therefore do not contain enough information to answer those questions for the law in force today.**

The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111** (Author **Barbara Hargreaves**) contains relevant rules about fee-free payment methods and disclosure of electronic-payment fees, but it was in force only until **29 June 2026**, so I cannot treat it as the law today. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

You can ask the agent or rental provider:

- what legal authority permits the card “payment surcharge fee”;
- who receives the fee—the app company, agent, or someone else; and
- whether the fee is a surcharge for the payment method rather than a separate rent-payment fee.

You can also use the no-fee bank-transfer option if acceptable. **The retrieved documents do not establish whether the app may lawfully charge the card fee today or whether the recipient changes that result.**

must-mention.reason: No. The output never states that a fee-free payment method must be reasonably available; it says only that the Act 'contains relevant rules about fee-free payment methods' and declines to treat them as current law. It also leaves open whether the recipient matters ('The retrieved documents do not establish whether the app may lawfully charge the card fee today or whether the recipient changes that result'), so the point that the ban applies to anyone other than a bank, whoever collects the fee, is hedged too far. Only the next-step point (use the no-fee bank transfer, ask the agent) is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the fee is allowed because a fee-free option exists, and never says the landlord or agent is exempt from the ban. It mentions the version 111 fee-free-payment rules only to say "I cannot treat it as the law today," and concludes that "the retrieved documents do not establish whether the app may lawfully charge the card fee today or whether the recipient changes that result."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009' correctly, but it never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Authorised Version No. 115. question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (in force 13 October 2026)**, a lease term requiring professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy is prohibited **unless it is in the standard form**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard-form cleaning term only permits requiring professional cleaning—or payment for it—when it is needed to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy, taking account of the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if you have cleaned the carpets so they are back to their starting condition, the documents do **not** say that you must pay for professional cleaning merely to obtain a receipt. They also do not state that a professional-cleaner receipt is required. If the clause is an additional blanket requirement rather than the standard-form condition-based term, it is invalid. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Send the agent the **signed condition report**, pointing to the carpets’ condition at the start and now. The prescribed condition report is intended to help resolve disputes about cleaning and damage. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- Provide dated, labelled photographs of the carpets from the beginning and end of the tenancy, identifying the room or location. The form specifically recommends photographs at both times and says they may help in a dispute. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to identify, in writing, what condition allegedly requires professional restoration and how it differs from the starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. The relevant test is restoration to the pre-tenancy condition, not simply production of a receipt. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Keep evidence of your cleaning, such as photographs, messages, receipts for cleaning products or equipment, and a brief written description of what you did. **The retrieved documents do not state that these particular items are legally required**, but they may help demonstrate the carpets’ condition.

The current documents are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115**, and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer omits the reg 12 alternative that professional cleaning can be required if it was done before the tenancy and the renter was told; it says the term 'only permits' it when restoration is needed, which materially narrows the rule. It also never states the renter's s 63 duty to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition, fair wear and tear excepted. The condition report point is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes — the answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet; it says the documents "do **not** say that you must pay for professional cleaning merely to obtain a receipt" and that a blanket clause beyond the standard-form condition-based term "is invalid."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009', but its condition-report and photograph advice rests on citation [1], a link to 21-3sra005 (Regulations version 005), which was not in force on that date; deleting that material would remove much of the 'what would help' guidance.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved version is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter must leave the premises reasonably clean, considering their condition when the tenancy began. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A rental provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved Act does **not** say whether:

- agreeing that cleaning could be deducted from the bond is also an agreement to pay a separate invoice; or
- returning the full bond prevents the agent from later pursuing the cleaning cost separately.

So, based only on these documents, **I cannot say that you definitely have to pay the invoice, or that you definitely do not**. The documents do not answer that specific question. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act treats a bond claim as a claim to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority for repayment of all or part of the bond, including an apportionment between renter and rental provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) It also requires a rental provider seeking a bond claim to give supporting evidence at least **3 days before** making the claim. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Those provisions do not expressly resolve a separate invoice issued after the full bond was repaid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent to identify:

1. the legal or contractual basis for the separate invoice;
2. why the full bond was returned if they say cleaning costs were still owing;
3. the cleaning report, photos, condition report and itemised invoice; and
4. whether the amount claimed is limited to the **reasonable cost** of cleaning. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can state that you agreed only to a proposed **bond deduction**, not necessarily to a separate debt, and ask them to explain why they say the agreement has that wider effect. The retrieved documents do not establish whether that argument succeeds. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the matter becomes a dispute, the documents indicate that the Tribunal can determine applications concerning repayment of bond, but the retrieved material does not provide a rule deciding the separate-invoice issue. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing because it is hedged too far: the answer says the Act does "not say whether agreeing that cleaning could be deducted from the bond is also an agreement to pay a separate invoice" and that the documents "do not establish whether that argument succeeds," so a reader cannot tell that a bond-deduction agreement is only agreement to a bond claim. The reasonably-clean test judged against the starting condition is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither prohibited claim is made. The output explicitly says "I cannot say that you definitely have to pay the invoice, or that you definitely do not," and notes the Act does not say whether "returning the full bond prevents the agent from later pursuing the cleaning cost separately."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the only required document with its in-force version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026'. Every rule it applies is cited to that version (link 97-109aa115), and it relies on no other version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
### What the law says

Under **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 115** (in force from 13 October 2026), a renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to carry them out immediately, but cannot get them to do so. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not expressly state whether a **broken tap that requires the whole house’s water to be turned off** meets the current Act’s definition of “urgent repairs.” They do state that only a **suitably qualified person** may carry out urgent or non-urgent repairs. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, you do **not necessarily have to wait for the owner’s preferred tradespeople** if the repair is urgent and they cannot arrange it immediately. You may arrange a suitably qualified tradesperson yourself, but the documents do not say that the owner can nominate an exclusive tradesperson for this purpose. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

- Keep records showing that you contacted the emergency repair contact, what they said, and when the owner’s tradespeople could attend. This helps show you took “reasonable steps” to arrange immediate repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Arrange a **suitably qualified** tradesperson to repair the tap. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Give the rental provider **7 days’ written notice** of the repair and its cost. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable repair cost, or the prescribed amount if lower, within **7 days** after receiving that written notice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The current prescribed reimbursement limit stated in the retrieved regulations is **$2,500**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you cannot pay, the repair costs more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the rental provider or agent to carry out the urgent repair; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The relevant current documents are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing: instead of stating that no water supply or a burst water service is an urgent repair, the answer says 'The documents do not expressly state whether a broken tap that requires the whole house's water to be turned off meets the current Act's definition of "urgent repairs."' That hedge leaves the reader unable to tell whether the repair is urgent, which the other conclusions depend on, even though the reimbursement point (s 72) and the preferred-tradesperson point are roughly covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden claim: it states "you do **not necessarily have to wait for the owner's preferred tradespeople**" and "The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable repair cost," so it never says the renter must wait or cannot recover costs.

version-cited.reason: Yes — the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009' (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version for any rule it applies.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

Today’s applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf**, **Authorised Version 115**, author **Barbara Hargreaves**, in force from 13 October 2026. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf**, **Authorised Version 009**, author **Lavina Mandy**, in force from 30 June 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Mould or damp caused by the building structure is expressly an **urgent repair**; a failure to comply with rental minimum standards is also an urgent repair. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Rotting timber may also indicate that the premises are not structurally sound, but the documents do not classify every instance of rotting timber automatically as an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

### 1. Cancel the agreement

If you **have not entered into possession**, section 91L allows you to give the rental provider a **notice of termination** because the premises:

- are not in good repair;
- are unfit for human habitation;
- do not meet rental minimum standards; or
- are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not define whether merely collecting the keys constitutes “entering into possession”. Therefore, they do not establish conclusively whether section 91L applies to your exact facts. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You can also ask the rental provider to agree to end the agreement; an agreement may be terminated by mutual agreement. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

### 2. Ask for repairs

Give the rental provider or agent **written notice**, with dated photographs and a detailed list of the damp, mould and rotting timber. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Because structural mould or damp and non-compliance with minimum standards are urgent repairs, you can request that they be dealt with urgently. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the provider does not act, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring urgent repairs; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

For non-urgent repairs, after written notice you may apply to the Director if repairs have not been completed within **14 days**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You may then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs, and the Tribunal must hear that application within **7 days**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Tribunal may order specified repairs, require a suitably qualified person to perform them, and order compensation under section 212(2). [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### 3. Ask for lower rent or stop paying rent

You may ask the rental provider to agree to a lower rent, but the retrieved documents do **not** state a general statutory right to demand a rent reduction merely because repairs are needed.

You should not unilaterally stop paying rent. If the premises do not comply with the requirement to be vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day, you are not required to enter into occupation and are not required to pay rent for the period before you actually enter occupation. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If you have entered into occupation and the provider fails to carry out required repairs, you may apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account** rather than directly to the provider. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the Tribunal has ordered that rent be paid into that account because of a breach of the rental minimum standards and the repairs are still not done by the specified deadline, you may apply for all or part of that rent to be paid to you. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Practical course:** do not move in, do not treat the keys as accepting the condition, and immediately send written notice seeking either (a) termination under section 91L, or (b) urgent repairs and a written rent arrangement. The documents do not say that collecting the keys alone prevents termination, so that specific issue cannot be answered from them.

It only says the premises 'must be structurally sound and weatherproof' and mentions the separate 'vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day' requirement.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not require the renter to move in and pay rent first (it advises "do not move in" and says that before taking possession "section 91L allows you to give the rental provider a notice of termination"), and it does not claim a legal right to lower rent, stating "the retrieved documents do not state a general statutory right to demand a rent reduction merely because repairs are needed" and tying any rent relief to agreement or Tribunal orders.

However, its main cancellation option, the section 91L notice of termination and termination by mutual agreement, is sourced only from the link 97-109aa110, which is Authorised Version 110 of the Act and was not in force on that date. That rule is presented as a step the user can take, and deleting it would remove the cancellation advice and change the answer's substance.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, dated 30 June 2026**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

It says the rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and fit for occupation. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Damage to the premises must be reported to the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Plumbing or wiring problems may require urgent repairs, but the retrieved document does not classify these particular burglary-related problems definitively. It says urgent-repair obligations apply after the renter gives notice. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The renter must keep the premises reasonably clean and, at the end of the agreement, leave them as far as practicable reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The document does not expressly say who bears responsibility for cleaning that has been prevented by burglary damage.

## What you can do or ask

- **Immediately notify the rental provider or agent in writing** about each break-in and list the damaged plumbing, wiring, doors, locks and any safety risks. Keep copies, photographs, police reports and repair reports. The retrieved document specifically requires written notice of damage. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- **Request urgent repairs immediately**, particularly where the damage affects essential services or safety. Only a suitably qualified person may perform repairs. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the rental provider does not arrange urgent repairs after reasonable steps by you, you may arrange them yourself; the current retrieved document states reimbursement may be available for reasonable urgent-repair costs up to **$2,500**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you cannot afford the repairs, the cost exceeds **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses reimbursement, you may apply to **VCAT** for an order requiring the repairs. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- **Ask in writing for agreement about cleaning and handover**, explaining that the premises cannot reasonably be cleaned until the plumbing and wiring are repaired. The documents do not provide a specific automatic exemption from cleaning or a specific rule excusing rent because of burglary damage.
- The retrieved documents do **not** state that burglary by itself lets you end a fixed-term lease early, nor do they provide a specific early-termination process for this situation. The only retrieved Act version, **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, dated 25 November 2025**, was in force only until **29 June 2026**, so it cannot be treated as the law in force today. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer omits point 3, the s 91ZD right to end the lease with an immediate notice of intention to vacate if the home is unfit or unsafe, and instead says the documents 'do not provide a specific early-termination process for this situation'. It also hedges point 2 by saying the document 'does not classify these particular burglary-related problems definitively' as urgent repairs.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not make either claim: it says "the rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair" and presents self-arranged repairs only as a reimbursable fallback ("you may arrange them yourself... reimbursement may be available"). On early termination it says only that the retrieved documents "do not state that burglary by itself lets you end a fixed-term lease early", which is not a claim that the renter must stay regardless of the home's condition.

It names the Regulations correctly as 'Authorised Version No. 009, dated 30 June 2026', but leaving out version 115 of the Act is enough to fail.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The current regulations document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026**, authored by **Lavina Mandy**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent **must make reasonably available at least one rent-payment method with no additional cost**, except bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A person must not charge the renter for the **establishment or use of a direct-debit facility or any other electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Before the renter agrees to use a payment method, the rental provider or agent must provide information about costs the renter may incur, including **third-party transaction fees and other electronic-payment-facility fees**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The prescribed rental-agreement form also says the rental provider must permit a **fee-free** payment method and allow payment by Centrepay or another electronic-funds-transfer method. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

**On the documents provided, the app cannot make the only available rent-payment method a fee-charging card method.** The no-fee manual bank-transfer option appears capable of satisfying the requirement if it is reasonably available, although the documents do not say how speed or processing delays affect that assessment. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** expressly answer whether a particular card surcharge is lawful in every circumstance, or define which “prescribed matter” is covered by section 51A. They also do not state a different rule depending on whether the fee is received by the app company or the agent. Section 51A instead refers generally to **“a person”**, subject to an exception for an authorised deposit-taking institution. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or rental provider:

1. **Which fee-free payment method is available** and how it can be used. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. For a written breakdown of every card, third-party transaction or electronic-payment-facility fee **before consenting to use the card option**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. **Who receives the fee**—the app company, agent, rental provider or an authorised deposit-taking institution—and the legal basis they rely on for charging it. The documents do not indicate that directing the fee to the app company rather than the agent avoids the restrictions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. Whether the manual transfer option is the required fee-free option and whether payment is treated as made when you initiate the transfer or when it clears; the retrieved documents do not answer that timing question.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

Under **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009 (in force 30 June 2026)**, the rental provider cannot require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless:

- professional cleaning was carried out immediately before you moved in and you were told this; **or**
- professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If you have cleaned the carpets yourself and restored them to their starting condition, the retrieved documents do **not** say that you must pay for professional cleaning merely to obtain a receipt. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) They also do not state that an agent may insist on a professional cleaner’s receipt where professional cleaning is not needed to restore the carpets. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Send the agent:

- the original condition report, showing the carpets’ condition when you moved in; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- dated, labelled photographs or video from the start and end of the tenancy, showing the carpets and identifying each room; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- any written explanation of the cleaning you carried out; and [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- a request that they identify the specific difference between the starting and ending condition that allegedly requires professional cleaning, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed condition-report information says that photos should be taken at the beginning and end of the tenancy and may help resolve disputes about cleaning; it also says the renter may attach additional information and photos to the report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider or agent must complete the final inspection and condition report within **10 days after the end date**, and must give you an opportunity to attend if possible. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

**Document relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* — **Authorised Version v009**, Author **Lavina Mandy**, in force from **30 June 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, **Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**; its listed Author is **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Under section 411AB, a residential rental provider may claim **an amount of bond** for the reasonable cost of cleaning if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A bond claim is made to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority and must specify the amount and any apportionment of the bond. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the **full bond has been repaid to you**, the documents do not say that a later cleaning invoice is automatically enforceable, and they do not say that agreeing to a bond deduction is automatically the same as agreeing to pay a separate invoice. **The documents therefore do not provide a definitive answer to whether you must pay this invoice.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to explain in writing:

- why the agreed bond deduction was not made;
- whether the invoice is intended to replace, or is additional to, the agreed deduction;
- the cleaning evidence and condition-report comparison supporting the charge; and
- the actual reasonable cost of the cleaning.

Do not assume that the invoice is valid merely because you previously agreed to a bond deduction: the retrieved document does not establish that legal equivalence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the agent seeks a bond order, a renter or other interested person may apply to the Tribunal about repayment of the bond, but the documents state that such an application must be made within **14 days after the residential rental agreement ended**, and any Tribunal order cannot exceed the amount of bond held by the Authority. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the cleaning test ('not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the agreement' under s 411AB) but never says that agreeing to a deduction is agreeing to a claim on the bond rather than to a separate invoice; it says only that 'the documents do not say' they are the same and that they 'do not provide a definitive answer', which leaves the reader unable to tell which way the first point falls.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
### What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A failure or breakdown of the **water supply to rented premises** is an “urgent repair”. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) On the facts you gave—water turned off to the whole house—the repair is therefore urgent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You do **not** have to wait indefinitely for the owner’s preferred tradespeople. You may arrange the urgent repair yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to arrange it immediately, but are unable to get them to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that the owner can require you to use only their tradespeople in those circumstances.  

### What you can do

- Arrange the repair **now**, using a **suitably qualified person**; the current prescribed agreement says only a suitably qualified person may do urgent repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
- Keep the messages or call records showing that you notified the emergency contact and that the owner’s tradespeople could not attend.  
- Give the rental provider **written notice within 7 days** stating what repair was done and its cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
- The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days** after receiving that notice, and the prescribed agreement states that direct reimbursement is available up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If you cannot afford the repair, it costs more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay if you arrange it, you may apply to the Tribunal for an urgent-repairs order; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are stated: water supply failure is an urgent repair; after reasonable steps the renter can arrange the repair and be reimbursed the reasonable cost (up to $2,500) within 7 days of written notice; and the hardest point is covered by "You do not have to wait indefinitely for the owner's preferred tradespeople... Arrange the repair now," which tells the reader the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop the urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. Neither failure condition is asserted: the answer says "You do **not** have to wait indefinitely for the owner's preferred tradespeople" and "The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days** after receiving that notice," so it neither requires waiting for the landlord's tradespeople nor denies cost recovery.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** (in force from 13 October 2026) and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009** (in force from 30 June 2026). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Structural mould or damp is expressly classified as an **urgent repair**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Rotting timber may also indicate a structural or safety defect, but the retrieved documents do not determine whether particular timber damage meets that threshold. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents provided do **not** state whether signing the lease and collecting the keys gives you a right to cancel or terminate in these circumstances. They also do not state a right to an automatic rent reduction because of the defects.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing immediately.** Describe the damp, mould and rotting timber, attach dated photographs, and state that you consider the mould/damp and any resulting safety issue to be urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs.** The rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) If the issue is treated as a non-urgent repair, the provider must complete it within a reasonable time, and you may apply to VCAT for a repair order if it has not been done within **14 days** after notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. **If urgent repairs are not done**, you may arrange them yourself after taking reasonable steps to have the provider do them immediately. The provider may have to reimburse reasonable costs up to **$2,500**; you may apply to VCAT for an order if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask for a lower rent**, but the retrieved documents do not give a specific right or process for a rent reduction based on these defects. Any reduction would therefore need to be agreed with the rental provider, or supported by a legal mechanism not contained in the retrieved documents.

5. **Do not simply stop paying rent or assume the lease is cancelled.** The retrieved documents do not authorise either step on these facts. They also do not contain the cancellation/termination rule you asked about, so I cannot say from these documents that you can cancel without possible liability.

It also omits that the minimum standards must be met by the day the renter moves in (s 65A), though it does cover the repair route.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- You must notify the rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable** about damage and breakdowns. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Urgent repairs must be carried out after notification. The regulations specifically include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance supplied by the rental provider for **hot water, cooking, heating or laundering**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- You must keep the premises reasonably clean. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The retrieved current regulation does not say that burglary damage automatically ends the lease, suspends rent, excuses all cleaning, or gives you an automatic right to terminate before the agreed end date. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110** contains related provisions about notifying damage and leaving premises reasonably clean, but its stated in-force period ended on **24 November 2025**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do **not** contain the current Act version for today, **5 November 2026**, so I cannot give a current statutory answer about early termination, rent reduction, compensation, or liability for the burglary damage.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider or agent in writing immediately.** Describe each break-in and the plumbing and wiring damage, attach dated photographs or videos, and state that you cannot safely or properly clean until the damage is repaired. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

2. **Request immediate inspection and qualified repairs.** The regulations state that only a suitably qualified person may perform urgent or non-urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Ask the provider to arrange an electrician and plumber, and identify any loss of essential services as an urgent-repair request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask in writing for agreement on cleaning and the lease end.** You can ask the provider to confirm that cleaning will wait until repairs are completed, agree to waive or reduce any cleaning requirement affected by the burglary, and agree to an earlier end date. The retrieved documents do not state that the provider must agree to those requests.

4. **Preserve evidence.** Keep police reports, repair requests, photographs, receipts and correspondence. The current condition-report form says photographs can help resolve disputes about cleaning, damage and missing items. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

5. **If repairs are not done:** for non-urgent repairs, the retrieved regulation summary says you may apply to VCAT if repairs have not been carried out within **14 days** after notice; for urgent repairs, you may apply to VCAT for an order if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds **$2,500**, or the provider refuses to pay. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish whether your particular plumbing or wiring damage qualifies as an urgent repair.

Do **not** assume you can stop paying rent or leave before the lease ends without further current legal authority or an agreed termination; the retrieved documents do not provide that answer for today.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The relevant regulations are **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent **must make reasonably available a rent-payment method with no additional cost**, except the renter’s own bank or account fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- They must also tell you about costs—including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees—**before you consent to use that payment method**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Therefore, if the manual bank transfer is genuinely available and carries no additional cost apart from your own bank/account fees, the app cannot make card payment the only fee-free option. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also says that a person **other than an ADI** must not demand or receive a fee for a prescribed matter relating to payment of rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The regulations prescribe rent-payment fees, but exclude “payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act.” [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

So, **the documents do not conclusively establish that this particular card fee is lawful**. They do establish that a fee-free payment method must be reasonably available and that the fee must be disclosed beforehand. Whether the card charge is a permitted payment surcharge under another Act is not explained in the retrieved documents. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

It **may matter who receives the fee**: the Act’s prohibition applies to a “person other than an ADI,” so the documents do not support treating a fee as lawful merely because it goes to the app company rather than the agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) But the documents do not say whether this app company or agent is an ADI, nor do they identify the “other Act” that might permit a surcharge. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or rental provider, in writing:

1. **Which fee-free payment method is being provided** under section 42(4). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
2. **Who receives the card fee**—the app company, agent, or another entity.  
3. Whether the recipient is an **ADI**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
4. The legal basis for claiming the card fee is a **payment surcharge permitted under another Act**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)  
5. For the fee and all other payment-method costs to be disclosed before you consent to that method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

On the documents available, you can insist on using the available fee-free bank-transfer option, subject to complying with the tenancy agreement’s payment requirements and payment deadlines. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

(1) The answer says the provider "must make reasonably available a rent-payment method with no additional cost" apart from the renter's own bank fees.
