question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, dated 30 June 2026** (Author: Lavina Mandy). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A lease cannot require professional cleaning merely because it contains a pet or cleaning clause. Professional cleaning may be required only if:

1. the premises were professionally cleaned immediately before you moved in **and you were told that they were**; or  
2. professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition, based on the condition report and allowing for fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If your self-cleaning has returned the carpets to their original condition, professional cleaning would generally not be required on the second ground. The retrieved documents do **not** say that you must provide a receipt from a professional cleaner, so they do not establish that the agent can demand a receipt simply because the clause says so. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Send the agent the entry condition report and explain that the carpets are in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Provide dated, labelled photographs taken at the end, including both close-up detail and wider room views; the prescribed condition-report form says photographs should be taken at the beginning and end and may help in a dispute. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask to attend the final inspection. The agent must complete the end condition report within **10 days** after the agreement ends and give you a reasonable opportunity to be present. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to identify the specific carpet condition that allegedly requires professional cleaning and to compare it with the entry condition report. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Keep your cleaning records, photographs and all messages. If professional cleaning genuinely is required to restore the original condition, the prescribed term says you must arrange it or pay its cost; otherwise, the retrieved documents do not show that you must pay for a professional receipt. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A residential rental provider may claim from a bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also allows claims for rent or other charges owing under the agreement or the Act. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A bond claim is a claim to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority for repayment of all or part of the bond. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The current Act requires the provider or agent, at least **3 days before making a claim for repayment of bond to the provider**, to give the renter bond-claim evidence supporting that claim. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved documents **do not say whether agreeing to a proposed bond deduction is legally the same as agreeing to pay a later, separate invoice**. They also do not state that returning the full bond either automatically extinguishes, or automatically preserves, a separate cleaning claim. Therefore, the documents do not establish that you must pay this invoice merely because you agreed to a deduction, or that you do not have to pay it merely because the full bond was returned. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to identify the legal basis for the invoice and provide:

- evidence of the cleaning cost and why it is reasonable; [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- evidence that the premises were not left reasonably clean compared with their condition at the start; [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- an explanation of why the agreed bond deduction was not processed and why a separate invoice is now being issued; and
- the exact wording of anything you signed or agreed to, including whether it referred only to a bond apportionment or also said you personally owed the cleaning cost.

You can dispute the invoice in writing and state that your agreement was to an amount being deducted from the bond, not necessarily to a separate payment. The retrieved documents do not provide a specific procedure or deadline for disputing a separate cleaning invoice.

It says the documents 'do not say whether agreeing to a proposed bond deduction is legally the same as agreeing to pay a later, separate invoice', and suggests the agreement was 'not necessarily' to a separate payment. That hedges too far for a reader to tell that agreeing to a deduction is agreement to a bond claim and not to a separate invoice. The second point is covered by 'not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither prohibited thing; it states that 'the documents do not establish that you must pay this invoice merely because you agreed to a deduction, or that you do not have to pay it merely because the full bond was returned,' and that the documents 'do not state that returning the full bond either automatically extinguishes, or automatically preserves, a separate cleaning claim.'

version-cited.reason: Yes — the answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on that date, and every rule it applies is sourced only from that version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**. It says that only a **suitably qualified person** may carry out urgent or non-urgent repairs. It also says a renter may arrange an urgent repair after taking reasonable steps to have the rental provider immediately do it, where the provider has not done so. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The regulation’s examples include a **burst water service**, but the retrieved documents do not expressly say whether every broken tap requiring the water to be shut off is an urgent repair. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The regulation does **not** say that you must wait for the owner’s preferred tradespeople. If the repair is urgent and you have reasonably tried to get the owner or agent to arrange it immediately, the stated condition is that they have not carried out the repair—not that you must use their nominated tradesperson. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Tell the owner or agent **in writing** that the water is shut off and that you are arranging an urgent repair because their tradespeople are unavailable. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you proceed, use a **suitably qualified person**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Keep the written communications, invoice and evidence that the water had to be shut off.
- The current regulation says you may be reimbursed for the reasonable cost **up to $2,500**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you cannot pay, the repair will cost more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay, you may apply to **VCAT** for an order requiring the rental provider to carry out the urgent repair. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111** contains similar urgent-repair provisions, but its metadata says it was in force only until **29 June 2026**; the documents retrieved do not contain the current Act version for today. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The second point is incomplete. The answer says only that the renter "may be reimbursed for the reasonable cost up to $2,500." It never says the rental provider must reimburse, and it omits the requirement to do so within 7 days of written notice under s 72. The other two points are adequately covered: a burst water service is given as an urgent-repair example, and the answer says the law does not require using the owner's nominated tradesperson.

It cites only "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111", so a required document version is missing.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (in force 13 October 2026), Author: Barbara Hargreaves** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009 (in force 30 June 2026), Author: Lavina Mandy** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must ensure the premises are in **good repair** and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation, even if the renter knew about disrepair before moving in. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Mould or damp related to the building structure, failure to meet rental minimum standards, and faults or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure are classified as **urgent repairs**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must ensure the premises meet the rental minimum standards **on or before the day you enter into occupation**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The Act does **not expressly provide an automatic right to cancel merely because you signed the lease, collected the keys, and then discovered these defects**. The documents do, however, provide the termination options below. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

### 1. Ask for urgent repairs

Give the rental provider or agent **written notice immediately**, describing the damp, mould and rotting timber, attaching dated photographs, and asking for suitably qualified contractors to investigate and remedy the underlying cause. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because structural mould or damp and unsafe damage are urgent repairs, the provider must arrange the repairs after being notified. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If they do not act, you may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to have the provider do them immediately; reimbursement may be available for reasonable costs up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds $2,500, or the provider refuses to reimburse you, you may apply to **VCAT** for an order requiring the urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### 2. Ask for non-urgent repairs or a VCAT order

The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Give written notice and, if the repairs are not completed within **14 days**, you may apply to VCAT for a repairs order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### 3. Do not move in if the premises are not fit

If the premises are not vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day, you are not required to enter into occupation and are not required to pay rent for the period before you actually enter. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not state that collecting the keys itself removes this protection, but they also do not clearly decide how key collection affects “occupation”; that may depend on the facts.

### 4. Ask for a rent reduction or compensation

You can ask the provider to agree to a temporary rent reduction while the premises are unusable or partly unusable. The documents do not state an automatic percentage reduction or an automatic right to reduce the rent unilaterally. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You may apply to VCAT for compensation where the provider failed to comply with the residential rental agreement or statutory duties, or where you paid more than required. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT may order compensation, including a **refund or reduction of rent**. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Do not simply stop paying rent without an agreement or VCAT order.

### 5. End the lease

- If the house is **unfit for human habitation** or has been rendered unsafe, section 91ZD allows you to give a written notice of intention to vacate effective immediately or on a later date. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If the provider fails to comply with a VCAT order, you may give at least **14 days’ notice** under section 91ZE. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- For a fixed-term agreement, successive breaches can support termination after the provider has breached the same duty on two previous occasions and the required breach notices have been given; the notice must specify a termination date at least **14 days** after it is given. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not establish that damp, mould and rotting timber automatically make every property “unfit for human habitation.” That will depend on the seriousness and safety impact of the defects.

**Practical next step:** do not move in or pay further rent without first sending written notice, preserving photographs and other evidence, and clearly stating whether you seek immediate repairs, an agreed termination, or a rent reduction. If the provider disputes the condition or refuses to act, apply to VCAT for urgent repairs, compensation, or—if justified—orders supporting termination.

Instead it states that 'The Act does not expressly provide an automatic right to cancel merely because you signed the lease, collected the keys, and then discovered these defects' and lists only ss 91ZD, 91ZE and successive-breach termination. The s 65A minimum-standards timing point and the repair route are covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states the renter is 'not required to enter into occupation' and need not pay rent before entering if the premises are not vacant and reasonably clean, and on rent it says 'The documents do not state... an automatic right to reduce the rent unilaterally' and 'Do not simply stop paying rent without an agreement or VCAT order.'

The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (in force 13 October 2026)' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009 (in force 30 June 2026)', and every citation links only to 97-109aa115 or 21-3sra009, so it relies on no other version.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved version is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The current retrieved regulations are the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**, authored by **Lavina Mandy** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- You must give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of damage to the premises or a breakdown of facilities, fixtures or equipment supplied by the rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair; the regulations’ rental-agreement form says urgent repairs may include a **burst water service, gas leak or flood damage** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents do not expressly classify damaged wiring or plumbing from a burglary as urgent in every case.
- If urgent repairs are needed, you may arrange them only after taking reasonable steps to have the rental provider or agent carry them out immediately and being unable to get them to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Only a **suitably qualified person** may do urgent or non-urgent repairs [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If you arrange urgent repairs, you must give **7 days’ written notice** of the repairs and their cost; the rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days** after receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the rental provider refuses to pay; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The rental-agreement form identifies the prescribed amount as **$2,500** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- For non-urgent repairs, after written notice, you may apply to the Tribunal if the rental provider has not carried them out within **14 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises **as far as practicable reasonably clean** and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations say professional cleaning cannot be required merely because the tenancy ends unless the stated pre-tenancy or restoration conditions apply [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The Act prohibits a renter or visitor from intentionally or negligently causing damage; the retrieved provision does not say that a renter is responsible for damage caused by unrelated burglars [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask now

1. **Write immediately** to the rental provider or agent, describing each break-in and the plumbing and wiring damage, and request immediate inspection and repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. State that you cannot safely or properly clean until the damaged services are repaired, and ask them to confirm in writing how they will address cleaning before the lease ends. The documents require cleaning only **as far as practicable**, but do not state a specific cleaning exemption for burglary damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If the damage is urgent and they do not act, arrange only the necessary work through a suitably qualified person, keep invoices and evidence, and follow the Act’s **7-day written notice** and reimbursement procedure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. If you cannot pay, the repairs exceed **$2,500**, or the provider refuses to reimburse you, apply to the Tribunal for urgent-repair orders; the application must be heard within **2 business days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. If the repairs are non-urgent and remain undone for **14 days after written notice**, apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. Preserve police reports, photographs, videos, the condition report, correspondence and repair quotations. The retrieved documents support the importance of condition reports and dated photographs in resolving end-of-tenancy damage and cleaning disputes [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents mention early termination where premises are “destroyed or unfit for habitation” under section 91ZD, but they do **not** provide that section’s test or procedure. Therefore, they do not contain enough information to confirm whether you can end this particular lease early without liability. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

It says the documents "do not contain enough information to confirm whether you can end this particular lease early," so it never states that a renter can give a notice of intention to vacate with an immediate termination date when the home is unfit or unsafe. It also says the documents "do not expressly classify damaged wiring or plumbing from a burglary as urgent," so a reader cannot tell whether these are urgent repairs the landlord must fix immediately. The written-notice point (s 72AA) is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer places repair duties on the provider ("The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair"), says renter-arranged urgent repairs are reimbursed ("the rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days"), states "the retrieved provision does not say that a renter is responsible for damage caused by unrelated burglars," and on early termination says only that the documents "do not contain enough information to confirm whether you can end this particular lease early," so it never claims the renter is liable for the burglary damage or must stay until the lease ends regardless of the home's condition.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 111) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 009), here is how Victorian tenancy law applies to your situation:

### **The Law**
Your rental provider or agent has strict legal obligations regarding how you pay rent:
- They must ensure that a payment method with **no additional costs** (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard tenancy agreement also explicitly notes that the provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method and allow Centrepay or electronic funds transfer [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- They must inform you of any costs you might incur before you agree to use a payment method, which explicitly includes **"third party transaction fees"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### **Can the app charge me a card fee?**
The legislation does not explicitly ban third-party apps from charging their own processing fees. However, it strictly requires your provider/agent to offer you a fee-free alternative (like the manual bank transfer option you found) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Because the law specifically calls out "third party transaction fees" as costs that must be disclosed, the app is permitted to charge a fee *provided* your agent has clearly told you about this cost before you agreed to use that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### **Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?**
No, the law does not distinguish based on who receives the fee. As long as your agent provides a free alternative and discloses the card fee upfront, the legal requirements are met regardless of whether the fee is kept by the app company or passed on to the agent.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version No. rt-regs-2021-v009), which is in force today, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says about professional cleaning
A rental provider cannot legally require you to arrange or pay for professional carpet cleaning unless one of two conditions is met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
1. Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before you moved in, and you were explicitly advised that it had been done; **or**
2. Professional cleaning is genuinely required to restore the carpets to the same condition they were in when you moved in, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to pay for a professional cleaner?
**No.** Since you have cleaned the carpets yourself and they are back to their original condition (accounting for normal wear and tear), professional cleaning is not required. The law only mandates paying for or arranging professional cleaning if it becomes necessary to restore the premises to their starting condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A blanket clause in your lease demanding a receipt regardless of the actual state of the carpets is unenforceable under these regulations.

### What helps prove the carpets' condition?
To protect yourself from an unfair bond claim, rely on the **Condition Report** and photographic evidence:
* **Your signed Condition Report:** You should have received this at the start of your tenancy and were required to fill it out within 5 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Your copy serves as the baseline record of the carpets' original state. If you noted any disagreements or added comments about the carpet condition, keep that document safe [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Dated Photos:** Take clear, close-up photos of the carpets now (at move-out) that show they are clean and match their condition at the start of your tenancy. Ensure the photos are dated and clearly identify the location [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **The Final Inspection:** When you leave, the rental provider must complete a final inspection and fill out the end-of-tenancy section of the condition report within 10 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). They are legally required to allow for fair wear and tear, which does not count as damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

If the agent still demands a receipt, politely decline and provide your signed initial condition report alongside your dated move-out photos. If they attempt to deduct money from your bond based on this, you can dispute it with Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT, where these documents will be the primary evidence used to determine liability [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 110** (the most recent version provided in the retrieved documents):

**What the law says about cleaning costs**
Under section 411AB, a residential rental provider (or their agent) is legally entitled to claim money from your bond for cleaning, but only if specific conditions are met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Act states they can claim "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This means they cannot charge you for standard wear and tear or for cleaning that was already required when you moved in.

**Agreeing to a bond deduction vs. agreeing to pay an invoice**
The retrieved documents **do not contain provisions** that explicitly address whether agreeing to a bond deduction is legally the same as agreeing to pay a separate invoice, nor do they specifically prohibit an agent from issuing a post-bond-return invoice for cleaning. The Act's bond provisions focus on what can be claimed *from* the bond and how those claims must be processed through the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (Homes Victoria), rather than regulating private invoicing after a bond refund [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Therefore, I cannot confirm whether you are legally required to pay the invoice based solely on these texts.

**What you can do or ask**
Because the retrieved documents do not cover the specific scenario of receiving a separate invoice after a full bond refund, I cannot provide a definitive legal answer on your obligation to pay it. However, under the Act:
* Bond claims for cleaning must be made through the Authority using an approved claim form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* If you believe the agent acted improperly by returning your full bond and then issuing a separate invoice, or if they are disputing the cleanliness of the property, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for a bond repayment order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* You may wish to ask the agent to clarify whether this invoice is being issued under the tenancy agreement rather than as a bond claim, and request itemised proof of the cleaning costs if they insist on payment.

*(Note: For disputes involving separate invoices after a bond refund, you may need to consult additional legislation or guidance from Consumer Affairs Victoria or Tenants Victoria, as these specific contractual/invoicing rules are not detailed in the provided bond provisions.)*

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v009)**, which is in force today, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
A broken tap that cuts off your water supply is classified as an urgent repair [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The rental provider (owner) is legally required to carry out urgent repairs immediately after being notified [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

You do **not** have to wait for them if they are unresponsive or unable to attend. You are permitted to arrange for the repairs yourself, provided you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to do it and they have not [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). However, the regulations explicitly state that "only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This means you cannot fix it yourself; you must hire a licensed tradesperson.

### What You Can Do or Ask
1. **Hire a qualified professional:** Contact a licensed plumber to fix the tap immediately [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Ask for reimbursement:** You can ask the owner to reimburse you directly for the reasonable cost of these repairs, up to $2,500 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
3. **Escalate if necessary:** If the repair costs more than $2,500, or if the owner refuses to pay you back, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

However, it misses the 7-day written-notice reimbursement obligation and softens 'must be reimbursed' to 'ask the owner to reimburse you'. It also never states that the owner's own-tradespeople policy is a prohibited term or cannot stop an urgent repair.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the documents currently in force today (5 November 2026), the relevant laws are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (**Authorised Version No. 115**) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (**Authorised Version No. 009**) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the Law Says About Damp, Mould, and Rotting Timber
* **Rental Minimum Standards:** The law requires that rented premises be structurally sound and weatherproof [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Additionally, each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Urgent Repairs:** Under the current Act, "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" is explicitly classified as an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Your Options
* **Asking for Repairs:** Because structural rotting timber and building-related mould/damp breach the rental minimum standards and qualify as urgent repairs, your landlord is legally obligated to address them. You should formally notify the rental provider of the issue in writing. If they fail to carry out the urgent repairs, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do so.
* **Cancelling the Lease:** The provided documents do not contain information about your right to cancel a lease before moving in due to these conditions.
* **Asking for Lower Rent:** The provided documents do not contain information about your right to request a rent reduction for these issues.

It also never says the minimum standards must be met by the day the renter moves in (s 65A). Only the repair route is covered.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
Based on today's date (5 November 2026), the applicable law is the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021***, **v005** (Authorised Version in force from 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says about your situation
*   **Provider's Duty:** Your rental provider is legally required to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). They are also responsible for all safety-related maintenance and repair activities outlined in your agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   **Your Duty:** You must notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable when damage occurs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). However, you are not liable for damage caused by burglars; at the end of the tenancy, you only need to leave the property reasonably clean and in the same condition it was in when you moved in (excluding fair wear and tear) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   **Quiet Enjoyment:** You are entitled to "quiet enjoyment" of the premises, meaning the provider cannot enter your home unless they follow strict legal procedures [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask right now
1.  **Notify the Provider in Writing:** Send a written notice (email is legally acceptable) detailing the break-ins and the specific damage to the plumbing and wiring [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
2.  **Request Urgent Repairs:** The failure or breakdown of essential services like plumbing and electrical wiring qualifies as an "urgent repair" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Once notified, your provider must carry out these repairs immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
3.  **Arrange Repairs Yourself (if necessary):** If the provider does not act immediately after you've asked them to, you can arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix the urgent issues yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can then ask the provider to reimburse you directly for the reasonable costs, up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
4.  **Apply to VCAT:** If the cost of repairs exceeds $2,500, or if the provider refuses to pay or carry out the work, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring them to do the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). For any non-urgent damage, if the provider does not fix it within 14 days of your written notice, you can also apply to VCAT for those repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
5.  **Protect Your Quiet Enjoyment:** You can demand that the provider respects your right to quiet enjoyment and only enters the property with proper legal notice or consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Regarding Cleaning & Moving Out
Because you cannot clean properly due to the damage, remember that the rental provider is responsible for maintaining the premises in a fit condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You are not required to arrange professional cleaning at the end of your tenancy unless it was specifically done before you moved in and you were advised of this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The damage caused by the burglars does not count against you as "damage" you must fix or pay for.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)** (version 111, in force from 25 November 2025) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Vic)** (version 005, in force from 25 November 2025), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Can the app charge you a card fee?
Third-party apps are generally permitted to charge processing fees for card payments, which the law classifies as **"third party transaction fees"** or **"electronic payment facility fees"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the rental provider or their agent **cannot force you to use a paid method** if a free alternative exists. They must ensure that a rent payment method with **no additional costs** (other than your own bank's account/transaction fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

### Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No, it does not matter.** The law focuses entirely on the cost *to you, the renter*. 
* The rental provider or agent is legally required to permit at least one **fee-free payment method** (such as direct debit or bank deposit) regardless of who collects the fee for the paid option [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* Whether the card fee is retained by the app company or passed through to the agent does not change the provider's legal duty to offer you a free alternative [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
1. **Use the free option:** You are fully entitled to use the manual bank transfer (or other fee-free methods like Centrepay) without penalty [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Verify disclosure:** The provider or agent must explicitly inform you of any costs you might incur before you consent to use a specific payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If they haven't, they have breached their legal duty.
3. **Demand a free alternative:** If the app makes the card fee mandatory because no other payment methods are offered, the rental provider or agent is breaking the law by failing to ensure a fee-free method is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: These rules apply to standard residential tenancies in Victoria. Different provisions may apply if your landlord is Homes Victoria [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).)*

The other two points are covered: a fee-free method must be 'reasonably available' apart from the renter's own bank fees, and 'Use the free option' is a next step.

The versions in force on the relevant date are Authorised Version No. 115 and No. 009, so every rule it applies comes from versions that were not in force then.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
Based on the current law in force today (5 November 2026), here is how your situation is handled:

**Document & Version Applied:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009 (rt-regs-2021-v009), effective 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the Law Says
Under the current regulations, a rental provider **cannot** simply demand professional cleaning or a receipt from a professional cleaner just because it is written in your lease [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The law explicitly states that a provider may only require professional cleaning if:
* Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before your tenancy started and you were advised of this; OR
* Professional cleaning is strictly necessary to restore the premises to the same condition they were in at the start of your tenancy, taking into account the condition report and **fair wear and tear** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Because you have cleaned the carpets yourself and returned them to their original state (accounting for fair wear and tear), you are **not legally required to pay for a professional cleaner**. The legal obligation is to restore the premises to their original condition, not to use a specific service provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do or Ask For
To protect yourself from unfair demands or bond claims, take these steps:
* **Reference the Condition Report:** Use the official condition report you signed at the start of your tenancy as your primary evidence for the state of the "floor coverings" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Provide Dated Photos:** Submit dated photos you took when you moved in alongside new photos showing the carpets are clean and undamaged (beyond fair wear and tear) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Request a Final Inspection:** Ask to attend the final inspection so you can verify the condition of the premises yourself before the agent completes their section of the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Cite "Fair Wear and Tear":** Remind the agent that regulations explicitly state they must allow for fair wear and tear, which does not count as damage caused by the renter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

If the agent continues to demand a professional receipt despite your evidence, you can formally dispute the claim through the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT).

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v009)**, which is in force today, here is how your situation is handled:

### What the law says
A broken tap that cuts off water to the entire house qualifies as an **urgent repair** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The rental provider (owner) has a strict legal duty to carry out urgent repairs immediately after being notified [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They cannot legally force you to wait for their own tradespeople if they are failing to act promptly, nor can they restrict repairs solely to their preferred contractors when they are unavailable. Additionally, the regulations mandate that only a suitably qualified person may perform any repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
You **do not** have to wait. You can take the following steps:
1. **Confirm you've taken reasonable steps:** Ensure you have clearly notified the owner/agent of the urgent repair and given them a chance to arrange it immediately [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Arrange the repair yourself:** If the owner still hasn't fixed it, you are entitled to hire a suitably qualified tradesperson to carry out the urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Claim reimbursement:** The owner is legally required to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of these repairs, up to a maximum of **$2500** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep all invoices and receipts to submit your claim.
4. **Escalate if necessary:** If the repair costs exceed $2500, or if the owner refuses to pay you back, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs or cover the cost [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Next step:** Notify the owner/agent in writing that you are arranging a suitably qualified tradesperson to fix the urgent water issue immediately due to their failure to act, and request reimbursement up to $2500 upon completion.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy law in force today (5 November 2026), here is what the retrieved documents state regarding your situation:

**Applicable Documents & Authorised Versions:**
* `Residential Tenancies Act 1997` (Authorised Version v115) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* `Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021` (Authorised Version v009) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### 1. Can you ask for repairs? **Yes.**
Under the current rental minimum standards, each room in the premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure, and the premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber would likely fall under this structural soundness requirement.

Furthermore, the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure is explicitly classified as an **urgent repair** under the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The rental provider is legally required to carry out urgent repairs after you notify them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You should provide written notice immediately. If they do not act, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Can you cancel the lease before moving in?
The retrieved documents **do not contain information** on your right to cancel or terminate a tenancy agreement before moving in due to damp, mould, or rotting timber. 

*(Note: The regulations do state that a rental provider must ensure the premises comply with rental minimum standards and are in "good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" when you move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), but the specific legal pathway to cancel the lease prior to occupancy is not covered in the provided text.)*

### 3. Can you ask for lower rent?
The retrieved documents **do not contain information** on requesting a rent reduction or lowering your rent due to these issues.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
Based on the current law in force today, here is your guidance:

**Document & Version Applied**
*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 005 (Authorised by the Chief Parliamentary Counsel), in force from 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian tenancy law, your rental provider has a strict duty to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You are also entitled to quiet enjoyment of the property [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Damage caused by third parties (like burglars) does not transfer the repair responsibility to you; however, you do have specific duties to report it promptly.

### Your Options & Next Steps

**1. Notify the Provider in Writing Immediately**
You must notify your rental provider in writing as soon as practicable about the fact that damage has occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can send this via electronic communication (e.g., email) in accordance with the *Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000* [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**2. Pursue Urgent Repairs for Plumbing & Wiring**
If the damaged plumbing or wiring causes a failure of an essential service provided by the landlord (such as hot water, cooking, heating, or laundering facilities), this is legally classified as an **urgent repair** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
*   The provider must carry out these repairs immediately after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   If you take reasonable steps to get them to act and they fail to do so, you may arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix it yourself and claim reimbursement of up to **$2,500** directly from the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   If the repair costs exceed $2,500, or if the provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**3. Pursue Non-Urgent Repairs**
For any other damage that does not affect essential services, it is classified as a **non-urgent repair** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The provider must complete these within a reasonable time. If they do not fix the issue within **14 days** of receiving your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**4. End the Lease Early (If Uninhabitable)**
If the burglary damage is severe enough that the premises are effectively "destroyed or unfit for habitation," you may be entitled to give formal notice to vacate the property early under section 91ZD of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If you end the agreement on this basis, the provider **cannot** claim compensation from you for rent foregone [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**5. Cleaning Obligations**
Regarding your inability to clean: You are generally only required to professionally clean at the end of a tenancy if professional cleaning was done immediately before you moved in, or if it is strictly necessary to restore the property to its original condition accounting for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Because the damage and resulting mess were caused by burglars (not you), you are not liable for restoring that specific damage, and the provider's duty to maintain the premises in good repair covers this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**6. Security & Locks**
Ensure the property meets rental minimum standards for locks. External doors must have functioning deadlocks or a locking device operated by a key from the outside [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If security was compromised during the break-ins, you can request the provider to rectify the locks immediately to restore your right to quiet enjoyment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The law itself lists a burst water service and a dangerous electrical fault as urgent repairs. question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
### What the law says
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a rental provider or their agent **must ensure that a fee-free payment method** (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). They are also legally required to give you clear information about any costs you may incur by using a specific payment method—including **"third party transaction fees"**—before you agree to use it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard tenancy agreement reinforces this by noting that the provider must permit at least one fee-free option and allow you to use Centrepay or another electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No.** The law focuses entirely on whether **you** are charged extra, not who collects the money. Because the legislation explicitly calls out "third party transaction fees," a rental provider cannot force you to pay a card fee simply because it is routed through an app rather than their own bank account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). As long as they provide a genuinely free alternative (like your manual bank transfer option), they are complying with the law, even if the app still charges you for convenience.

### What you can do or ask
* **Use the fee-free method:** Since your app offers a manual bank transfer with no fee, you can simply use that option to avoid the charge entirely.
* **Request written confirmation:** If you are ever unsure whether a payment method is truly free, ask your agent in writing to confirm that the method incurs *"no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on your bank account)"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
* **Check your agreement:** Review your standard tenancy agreement's payment section. It should list your available options and explicitly note that a fee-free method is permitted [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---
**Relevant Documents & Authorised Versions (in force today, 5 November 2026):**
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. **111** (Section 42) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. **009** (Standard Term 8) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The first point (a fee-free method must be reasonably available) and the third (use the fee-free method) are covered.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version v009, in force from 30 June 2026), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you have to pay for a professional cleaner?
No, not if your DIY cleaning has successfully restored the carpets to their original condition. Under Victorian law, a rental provider **must not require** you to arrange professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy unless one of two conditions is met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
1. Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before you moved in, and you were explicitly advised of this; or
2. Professional cleaning is actually required to restore the premises to the same condition they were in at the start of the tenancy, after accounting for **fair wear and tear** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Since you have cleaned the carpets yourself and they are back to how they were when you moved in (minus normal fair wear and tear), professional cleaning is not "required" under the law. You cannot be forced to pay for a service that isn't legally necessary to meet your obligations.

### What helps show the carpets' condition?
To prove you have met your cleaning obligations, you should rely on:
* **The signed Condition Report:** This document records the state of the premises (including floor coverings) at the start of your tenancy and is the primary benchmark used to determine if professional cleaning is actually required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Dated photos:** You should take close-up and wide-angle photos of the carpets at both the start and end of your tenancy. These photos must be dated, labelled with the room/location, and attached to or kept alongside the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). They are explicitly noted as highly useful for resolving disputes over cleaning or damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

If the agent still demands a receipt, you can politely decline by pointing out that the law only mandates professional cleaning if it is necessary to restore the premises to their initial state (accounting for fair wear and tear), which your DIY work has already achieved. If they attempt to deduct this from your bond, you would present your signed condition report and dated before/after photos to VCAT as evidence that no professional service was required.

---

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?

**Law in Force Today**
The applicable law is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version `rt-regs-2021-v009` (in force from 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the Law Says About Your Situation**
A broken tap that cuts off your water supply is classified as an urgent repair (such as a burst water service) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). While the rental provider (owner) has a duty to carry out urgent repairs immediately after being notified, they cannot force you to wait indefinitely if their own tradespeople are unavailable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, under the regulations, any repairs—urgent or otherwise—must be carried out by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What You Can Do or Ask**
1. **Arrange the repair yourself:** If you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to fix it and they have not done so immediately, you are legally allowed to arrange for a suitably qualified tradesperson to complete the urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The owner's internal policy of only using their own staff does not override this right.
2. **Claim reimbursement:** The owner is required to reimburse you directly for the reasonable cost of these repairs, up to a maximum limit of $2,500 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep all receipts and invoices to prove the costs were reasonable.
3. **If the cost exceeds $2,500 or the owner refuses to pay:** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the rental provider to carry out the urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

You do not have to wait. Contact a licensed plumber immediately, inform the owner in writing that you are arranging the repair because they failed to act, and submit your receipts for reimbursement up to the $2,500 cap.

Point 2 is incomplete: it covers self-arranging the repair and reimbursement up to $2,500, but never states that reimbursement must be made within 7 days of written notice (s 72).

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force as of today (November 5, 2026), specifically the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 009)**, here is what you can do:

**1. Can you ask for repairs? (Yes, and they are classified as urgent)**
* **Minimum Standards:** Under the current regulations, every room in a rental property must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your landlord is legally required to ensure the premises meet these rental minimum standards [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Urgent Repair Classification:** Under the current Act, the presence of mould or damp caused by the building structure is explicitly classified as an **urgent repair** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber would also likely fall under damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure, which is also listed as an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Your Rights to Repairs:** Once you notify your rental provider, they must carry out these urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If you cannot afford the repairs yourself and the cost exceeds $2,500, or if the landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Self-Arranged Repairs:** If you take reasonable steps to get the landlord to fix it immediately and they fail to do so, you may arrange the repairs yourself and be reimbursed up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**2. Can you ask for lower rent?**
* The provided documents do not explicitly grant renters a direct right to unilaterally demand a rent reduction. 
* However, if your landlord fails to carry out the required repairs after you have given notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a "Rent Special Account" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). 

**3. Can you cancel the lease?**
* The provided documents do not contain specific provisions regarding cancelling a tenancy agreement or terminating the lease before moving in due to these conditions.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer omits the s 91L right of a renter who has not taken possession to end the agreement by notice; it says instead that 'The provided documents do not contain specific provisions regarding cancelling a tenancy agreement... before moving in.' It also never says the minimum standards must be met by the day the renter moves in (s 65A).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must move in and pay rent before acting, and it states "The provided documents do not explicitly grant renters a direct right to unilaterally demand a rent reduction," referring only to a VCAT order for a Rent Special Account rather than asserting a legal right to lower rent.
