Deleting that material would remove the answer's only early-termination option, so it relies on a version not in force on that date.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Source:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the version in force today (6 November 2026). The excerpt doesn't print the words "Authorised Version", so the number 115 comes from the file's version metadata [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **A free option must be available (s 42(4)).** The provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Bank fees or account fees on your own bank account don't count as additional costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your free bank transfer seems to meet this. The document doesn't say whether a *slower* method is still "reasonably available".
- **You must be told about costs first (s 42(7)).** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using a particular payment method, including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees. They must do this before you consent to that method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **There is a separate ban on certain charges (s 51(3)).** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent payment fees (s 51A).** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any *prescribed matter* relating to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Can the app charge you the card fee?

The documents don't give a clear yes or no.

- Section 42(7) assumes some payment methods carry fees, as long as you are told first [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Section 51(3)(b) bans charges for using "any other electronic payment facility" for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A card payment through an app could fall within those words, but the documents don't say whether a card surcharge counts.
- Section 51A depends on what is "prescribed". The prescribed matters are in the regulations, which I didn't retrieve, so I can't say whether a card fee is caught [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **The duties in s 42(4) and (7) bind the provider or their agent** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The app company is not named, so those duties apply to it only if it acts as the agent.
- **The bans in s 51(3) and s 51A apply to "a person"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They are not limited to the provider or agent. On the wording, a fee going to the app company is not automatically outside them.
- **The only exception in the text I have is for an ADI under s 51A** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpt doesn't define "ADI", so I can't say whether the app company qualifies.

## What you can do

- Use the free bank transfer. The agent must keep a no-cost method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask the agent or provider, before you agree to card payment, to state in writing every cost of that method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask who receives the fee and what the agent says it is for.
- If you've already paid a card fee, raise s 51(3)(b) and s 51A with the agent in writing.
- You and the provider can agree to change how rent is paid (s 42(6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents don't cover complaint or enforcement steps, or the regulations that define "prescribed" fees. For a firm answer on your app's card fee, check those or get advice from a tenancy advice service.

It says only that 'the prescribed matters are in the regulations, which I didn't retrieve, so I can't say whether a card fee is caught' and that a fee to the app company 'is not automatically outside them.' That is hedged so far that a reader cannot tell whether the fee is banned regardless of who collects it. The other two points are covered: a no-cost method must be reasonably available, and the next steps include using the free bank transfer.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current law, the agent can't require a professional cleaning receipt just because the lease says so. A professional clean can only be required if one is actually needed to restore the carpets to their starting condition. The documents don't mention pets, so I can't say whether a pet clause is treated differently.

**Documents used (in force today, 6 Nov 2026)**
- *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

I'm taking the version numbers from the documents' metadata, not from text in the documents.

## What the law says

- **Extra cleaning clauses are generally prohibited.** A lease must not include a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 27B(1)(d)–(e)). A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 26A(2)).
- **The standard-form term is conditional.** A lease may include a term for professional cleaning only if it becomes required to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy started, taking into account fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 27C(1)).
- **The Regulations set the same test.** The rental provider must not require professional cleaning, or cleaning to a professional standard, unless:
  - (a) it was carried out immediately before the tenancy started and you were told so; or
  - (b) it is required to restore the premises to the same condition they were in at the start, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (reg 12(1)).
- **Your duty to pay is also conditional.** You must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if cleaning becomes required to restore them to their starting condition, again having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (reg 12(2)).

**Applied to you:** If the carpets are back to their move-in condition (allowing for fair wear and tear), professional cleaning isn't "required". On that basis a receipt shouldn't be demanded. The one exception to check is (a). If the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told, the agent has a stronger argument.

## What you can do or ask

- **Rely on the condition report.** The test is judged "having regard to the condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You should have been given 2 copies (or one emailed copy) on or before move-in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Compare it with the carpets' current state.
- **Ask the agent to identify the problem.** Ask them to point to what in the carpets needs professional cleaning to match the condition report, and to confirm whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before your tenancy.
- **Apply to the Tribunal if needed.** A renter can apply to have a lease term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 28).

**Not covered:** The documents don't say what other evidence helps, such as dated photos or videos, or whether a receipt is ever required. The condition report is the only evidence they name. Photos of the carpets at move-out are a sensible extra, but that suggestion is mine, not from the documents.

must-mention.reason: No. The s 63 point is missing: the answer never says the renter's general duty is to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, fair wear and tear excepted. It covers only the conditional professional-cleaning duty under reg 12(2). The reg 12 test and the condition-report point are both covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay because of the clause or the pet. It states the opposite: "the agent can't require a professional cleaning receipt just because the lease says so. A professional clean can only be required if one is actually needed to restore the carpets to their starting condition." It also says it cannot determine whether a pet clause is treated differently.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Document relied on:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the version in force today (6 Nov 2026). I also checked *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, dated 30 June 2026 [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The excerpt I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version" number for the regulations. The version number "009" comes from the file name and metadata.

## What the law says

- **Cleaning can be claimed from the bond.** A provider may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" of the agreement (s 411AB(1)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). In Part 10, "residential rental provider" includes the provider's agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claims have safeguards.**
  - At least 3 days before a claim to have the bond repaid to the provider, the provider or agent must give each renter "bond claim evidence" supporting it (s 411(1A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph or other prescribed evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" (s 411(1B)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - A provider must not ask for or obtain your signature on a claim form that doesn't state the amount of bond to be refunded and how it is apportioned. The penalty is 60 penalty units (s 411(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning.** The prescribed terms say a renter must pay for professional cleaning only if it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition. That is judged by the condition report, allowing for fair wear and tear. A provider can't require professional cleaning unless it was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told, or it is needed to restore that starting condition (reg 12) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?

**The documents don't say.** I found nothing in them that turns an agreement to a bond deduction into a separate personal debt. I also found nothing on what happens when the bond has already been refunded in full and the agent then bills separately. The bond provisions I retrieved deal with claims against the bond, not with a later invoice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The statement in reg 12 that a renter must "pay the cost" of professional cleaning applies only where cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't say more than that from these documents.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the supporting evidence.** Request the invoice, photos or quote the agent relies on, which the Act calls "bond claim evidence" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Compare it with the condition report.** Evidence that conflicts with the condition report doesn't meet s 411(1B) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Test the amount.** The Act allows only the "reasonable cost" of cleaning, and only if the premises weren't left reasonably clean compared with how they started [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check whether professional cleaning was actually required under reg 12 [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check what you signed.** If you signed a bond claim form, see whether it stated the amount and apportionment, as s 411(5) requires [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Don't assume you must pay.** The retrieved documents don't establish that the invoice is payable. If you dispute it, put that in writing.

I can't tell you from these documents whether the agent can recover the invoice outside the bond, or which body decides that. Those provisions weren't in what I retrieved.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the first, the answer says "The bond provisions I retrieved deal with claims against the bond, not with a later invoice" and that it found "nothing in them that turns an agreement to a bond deduction into a separate personal debt"; under the rubric, saying the documents do not establish something counts as covering it. On the second, it states the s 411AB(1)(c) test: whether the premises were "left reasonably clean... having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement", though it does not name VCAT or s 63.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither prohibited claim: it says "Don't assume you must pay. The retrieved documents don't establish that the invoice is payable," and it leaves open whether more can be claimed, saying "I can't tell you from these documents whether the agent can recover the invoice outside the bond."

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026", and the only other document it relies on is the in-force Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 version 009 ("rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", link 21-3sra009), with no rule drawn from any version not in force on that date.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say you must wait for the owner's tradespeople. They also don't say you can hire anyone you like. Whether you can arrange the repair yourself depends on the steps below, and on whether a broken tap counts as an "urgent repair". I couldn't confirm that last point.

## Which documents I relied on
- **Current document:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version 009 (file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30), in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It is the version in force today (6 November 2026), and it is the only current document I retrieved.
- **Not current:** The only copy of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* I retrieved is Authorised Version 110, in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It has been superseded, so I can't confirm the Act's current wording. I'm using it only to show how section 72 read in that version.

## What the law says
- **Renter's right:** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and they are unable to get the provider or agent to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The current regulations' summary says the same thing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who does the work:** The current regulations' rights summary says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I found nothing in the retrieved documents that lets a rental provider limit repairs to their own tradespeople.
- **Reimbursement:** Under the current regulations' summary, a renter who arranges urgent repairs may be reimbursed by the rental provider for the reasonable cost, up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Applying to VCAT:** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the rental provider to carry out urgent repairs if [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  - you can't meet the cost;
  - the cost is more than $2500; or
  - the rental provider refuses to pay.

## What you can do
1. **Press the urgent request.** Tell the emergency contact and the rental provider or agent, ideally in writing, that the repair is urgent and that you can't wait for their tradespeople. Keep a record. Your own steps to get them to act immediately count as "reasonable steps" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **If they still can't act immediately,** you may arrange the repair yourself, using a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't say how long you must wait before doing this.
3. **Get written notice and costs to the rental provider.** In Version 110 of the Act (superseded), the renter had to give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The rental provider then had to reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm these periods apply today.
4. **If they refuse or you can't pay,** apply to VCAT. In Version 110, VCAT had to hear an urgent repairs application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm that is still the rule.

## What the documents don't answer
- **Is a broken tap an "urgent repair"?** The regulations point to the definition in section 3(1) of the Act, which I didn't retrieve [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The only plumbing example in the documents is a "burst water service" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Don't assume a tap qualifies. A tap that has forced you to shut off water to the whole house may well qualify, but check the definition.
- **Whether the owner's own-tradespeople rule is allowed.** The documents are silent on it.
- **Which form applies to you.** The rights summary I could read in full in the current regulations comes from Form 2, for agreements of more than 5 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your agreement may use a different form.

I'd confirm the current Act text and the section 3(1) definition with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT before paying for a repair.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**The documents I retrieved do not include the version of the law in force today (6 November 2026), so I can't name its Authorised Version number.**

- The most recent Act I found is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" (version 110, dated 6 August 2025). Its metadata says it was in force from 2025-08-06 to 2025-11-24 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The most recent regulations I found are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* in "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf" (version 005, dated 25 November 2025). They were in force from 2025-11-25 to 2026-02-09 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Both ended before today, so what follows describes the law as it stood in those versions. Check it against the current version before relying on it.

My second search failed, so I did not retrieve the text of the section on ending a lease for unfit premises (s 91ZD) or the rental minimum standards themselves.

## What the law says

- **Condition on moving in.** The provider must make sure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed move-in day. If they aren't, you don't have to move in. You also don't pay rent from the agreed day until you actually move in (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That section covers vacancy and cleanliness only. It doesn't mention damp or rot.
- **Rental minimum standards.** The provider must make sure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in (s 65A(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The standards are prescribed elsewhere, and I did not retrieve them.
- **Good repair.** The Act also refers to the provider's duty to keep the premises in good repair (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and the standard-form agreement says the provider must keep them in a fit condition for occupation [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp as urgent repairs.** The 2018 amending text in an older version (v088, dated 2 July 2019) added "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" to the urgent repairs definition in s 3(1) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I did not see the current definition, so confirm it.

## What you can do

**1. Ask for repairs**
- If the premises don't meet the minimum standards on or immediately after move-in day, you can send the provider a request for urgent repairs (s 65A(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- For other repairs, give written notice. If the provider hasn't done them within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) or go to the Tribunal (s 75). The Tribunal must hear a non-urgent application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- For urgent repairs, you can arrange them yourself if you took reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and couldn't. Give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to the prescribed amount, within 7 days of that notice (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations form puts the reimbursement cap at $2500 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- You can apply to the Tribunal for an urgent repairs order if you can't meet the cost, the cost is above the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. It must hear this within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, with a deadline, and can order compensation under s 212(2) (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve s 212.
- A condition report that lists defects counts as notice of them to the provider (s 36(1A)). You can fill one in yourself if you weren't given one, and you have 5 business days after moving in to return it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Putting the mould and rot in writing now helps either way.

**2. Ask for lower rent**
- The retrieved text has no provision letting you simply reduce the rent.
- What it does provide is that, after giving repair notice, you can ask the Tribunal to let you pay rent into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal must make the order if the provider failed to do the repairs and hasn't shown financial hardship (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Rent is not waived under that order. It is held, and paid to the provider at the end of the period. You can apply to have it paid to you if the provider still hasn't done required repairs for a breach of s 68 or the minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The compensation power in s 76(1)(c) may also be relevant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**3. Cancel**
- Section 65(2) lets you refuse to move in only for vacancy or cleanliness problems [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations' standard form refers to a renter giving notice of intention to vacate under s 91ZD "on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation". In that case the provider can't claim rent foregone [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve s 91ZD itself, so I can't say whether damp, mould and rotting timber qualify or what the notice requires.
- The form also says nothing stops you applying to VCAT for a compensation order if the other party breaches the agreement (cl 16.4(c)) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Next step.** Because I couldn't retrieve the current version or s 91ZD, check the in-force Act on legislation.vic.gov.au. You could also contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT before deciding whether to cancel.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## Which law applies

The Act in force today (6 November 2026) is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file **rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf**, labelled **version 115**, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so I'm relying on the version number in the file's metadata. For the $ figures and standard-form wording I used **rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf** (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Tell the provider in writing.** You must give written notice "as soon as practicable" after you become aware of damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email counts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The provider's repair duty.** The standard agreement terms say the rental provider "must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your cleaning duty is limited.** At the end of the agreement you must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That wording is relevant because the damage is stopping you from cleaning properly.
- **Burglar damage is not automatically your fault.** A repair notice to a renter is only available where the damage was caused by the renter's failure to comply with s 61(1). That section covers damage a renter or visitor causes intentionally or negligently [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Give written notice of the break-ins and damage now**, and keep documentary evidence. The Tribunal considers whether the provider was notified and whether you provided documentary evidence of the repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.**
   - You may arrange urgent repairs yourself only if you first took reasonable steps to get the provider or agent to do them immediately and couldn't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - You must then give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The reimbursement is capped at the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), which the regulations' standard terms give as $2500 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT (the Tribunal) for an urgent repairs order** if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount ($2500 per [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)), or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear it within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **For non-urgent repairs:**
   - Give written notice. If the provider hasn't done the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) or to the Tribunal for an order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The Tribunal must hear that application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - It can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, with a deadline, and compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Pay rent into the Rent Special Account.** After you've given repair notice, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay rent into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal must make the order if the provider hasn't complied with the duty and hasn't shown financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Ending the lease early.** The standard terms for agreements of more than 5 years say the provider can't claim "rent foregone" if you give notice to vacate under s 91ZD because the premises are "destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The text of s 91ZD itself wasn't retrieved, so I can't confirm whether your damage meets that test or whether the same wording is in your lease.

## What the documents don't answer

- Whether plumbing or wiring damage from a burglary counts as "urgent repairs". The s 3(1) definition wasn't retrieved. The regulations only point to it and give examples such as a burst water service, a gas leak or flood damage [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Who bears the cost of burglary damage, and anything about insurance, police reports or your bond.

My two follow-up searches for the s 3(1) definition and s 91ZD failed with a tool error. Checking those sections, or asking Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT, would close the gaps.

It also does not say the renter must stay until the lease ends, since it raises "Ending the lease early" via a s 91ZD notice to vacate if the premises are "destroyed or unfit for habitation."

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, unless the surcharge is permitted under another Act. The documents don't say whether the app's card fee is permitted under another Act, so I can't confirm that.

**What the law says**

- Under the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026), a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) prescribe "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a matter covered by that prohibition. This applies from 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The Act also requires the provider or agent to ensure that a rent payment method incurring no additional costs, other than bank or account fees payable on the renter's own account, is reasonably available to the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Before the renter consents to a particular payment method, the provider or agent must tell the renter about any costs they may incur, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

The prohibition in s 51A applies to "a person" (other than an ADI), not only to the agent or provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So the text doesn't suggest that routing the fee to an app company avoids the rule. However, the documents don't address whether a third-party app's fee is attributable to the provider or agent, or how liability would apply in that situation.

**What you can do or ask**

- **Ask for the fee's legal basis.** Ask whether the card fee is a "payment surcharge fee permitted under any other Act." The documents don't identify any such Act, so you can check this with the provider or agent.
- **Ask for the cost information.** The provider or agent must disclose these costs before you agree to use the card method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you haven't been told the fee before choosing card, you can ask for that disclosure.
- **Ask for a no-fee method.** The provider or agent must make a fee-free method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations' prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how "slower" affects whether a method is "reasonably available," so that is a question for the provider or agent or for further research.
- **Ask to change the method by agreement.** The rent payment manner can be changed by agreement between you and the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Complaints or enforcement.** The documents don't cover how to raise a complaint or what remedy is available if the fee is unlawful, so I can't advise on that from these sources.

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. If the fee is significant, consider speaking to a tenancy advice service.

---

**Sources**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026), ss 42 and 51A.
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version No. 009 (in force from 30 June 2026), regs 19 and 21C.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer says the provider or agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than the renter's own bank fees, is reasonably available. (2) It says a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for rent payment unless it is a surcharge permitted under another Act, and that because s 51A applies to 'a person', 'the text doesn't suggest that routing the fee to an app company avoids the rule'. That is the hardest point, and despite some hedging its direction is clear. (3) It gives next steps, such as asking for a no-fee method and consulting a tenancy advice service.

The answer never says the fee is allowed because a fee-free option exists, and never says the landlord or agent is exempt; it states the card fee is 'Probably not' allowed 'unless the surcharge is permitted under another Act,' and that the s 51A prohibition applies to 'a person' (other than an ADI), 'not only to the agent or provider.'

The answer names both required documents with versions in force on the date: 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026)' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version No. 009 (in force from 30 June 2026)', and it relies on no other versions.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say you must pay for a professional cleaner's receipt. Under the law, a professional clean can only be required if it's needed to restore the carpets to their move-in condition, so your own cleaning and photos are relevant evidence.

**Version used:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the versions identified in the retrieved metadata.

### What the law says

- **Professional cleaning clauses are limited.** The prescribed wording says the provider "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless either the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The renter's obligation is conditional.** The renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only "if professional cleaning becomes required" under that same test [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-standard terms can be invalid.** A residential rental agreement must not include a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy "unless that term is contained in the standard form" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An invalid term is void [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the Tribunal can declare a term invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The end-of-lease standard.** At the end, a renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and "in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession... taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond deductions.** A landlord may claim the reasonable cost of cleaning only "if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask whether professional cleaning is actually required.** Under the test above, the question is whether carpets that you've cleaned are back to their move-in condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. If they are, the clause's condition for a professional clean isn't met [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the clause wording against the standard form.** If your lease's cleaning term differs from the prescribed wording, it may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Gather evidence of the carpets' condition:**
   - **Your move-in condition report.** The renter should fill in the report within 5 business days after moving in, and it "may help the renter verify the condition... if there is a later dispute about the renter's responsibility for damage or cleaning" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Note any carpet issues you disagreed with.
   - **Dated photos.** The condition report guidance says photos "should be taken at the beginning and at the end of the tenancy," and should be dated and labelled by location [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - **The end-of-lease condition report.** The provider must complete it "within 10 days after the end date" and give the renter an opportunity to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Check that it describes the carpets accurately, and if not, record your disagreement and attach your photos [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Respond in writing.** If you disagree with any statement, you can record that disagreement on your copy of the report. A signed condition report is conclusive evidence of the premises' state of repair or general condition on the stated day, subject to exceptions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Note that this covers repair or general condition, not necessarily cleaning.
5. **Watch for a bond claim.** Before the provider claims cleaning costs from your bond, they must give you "bond claim evidence" at least 3 days before the claim is made, and that evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- **The receipt requirement.** The documents don't say a renter must provide a professional cleaner's receipt, or that a self-clean is insufficient as proof.
- **What counts as "required."** The documents don't define when a professional clean is "required" beyond the restore-to-move-in-condition test.
- **Your specific lease.** I don't have your lease, so I can't tell whether its clause uses the standard-form wording.

If the agent insists and you can't resolve it, the documents mention VCAT as the forum for disputes over bond claims and condition reports [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but they don't set out the full process here. For specific advice, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction also means agreeing to pay a separate invoice. Whether you must pay depends on whether the cleaning cost was a valid claim, and the documents set out the rules for that.

## What the law says

- **Landlord's right to claim cleaning costs:** A landlord can claim from the bond for "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter's duty:** At the end of a tenancy, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean, and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning:** The landlord cannot require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless it was done before the tenancy started and you were told so, or it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear . Where it is needed, the renter must pay for it .
- **Process for bond claims:** The landlord must give you "bond claim evidence" at least 3 days before claiming bond money, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Claims must be in a form approved by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the evidence.** Request the cleaning invoice, the basis for the charge, and any photos or reports. Check whether the cost is reasonable and whether the premises really were not left reasonably clean, compared with your condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the condition report.** Compare the agent's claim against the condition report and your own photos. Under the rules, a claim cannot conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check for professional cleaning.** If the invoice is for professional cleaning, check whether one of the exceptions in  applies .
4. **Dispute it.** Any bond claim disputed through the Authority goes to the Tribunal (VCAT). An application for a bond repayment order must generally be made within 14 days after the agreement ends [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Where a claim is made without the consent of all parties, the Authority must notify the other parties, and the claim is paid unless, within 14 days of that notice, a party gives written notice that it is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your question: is agreeing to a deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?

The documents do not answer this. They do not say what effect a renter's agreement to a bond deduction has on a separate invoice, or whether that agreement is treated as consent to pay. They also do not explain why the full bond was refunded while a separate invoice was sent. The relevant rules are that the landlord may claim cleaning costs from the bond [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and that a renter must leave the premises reasonably clean [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Whether your agreement covers a further charge is a question the documents don't address.

## Limits of this answer

- The documents I retrieved don't include the terms of your agreement, your bond claim, the invoice, or your condition report, so I can't say whether this specific cleaning charge is valid.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely, but the law doesn't let you repair it yourself. You can arrange urgent repairs through a suitably qualified person, provided you meet certain conditions.

**What the law says**

- The current Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version (version) 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The current Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A renter may arrange urgent repairs only if (a) they have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and (b) they are unable to get the landlord or agent to do them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- "Urgent repairs" includes a failure or breakdown of the water supply to rented premises, and a failure or breakdown of an essential water service or fitting provided by the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether a broken tap alone qualifies is a judgement call. The documents don't say, but a whole-house water shut-off is a strong case for urgency. Consumer Affairs Victoria's urgent repairs guidance is referred to in the Regulations [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act defines a suitably qualified person to include a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires licensing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So you can't do the plumbing yourself. You can engage a suitably qualified person.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Notify the owner in writing now.** Renters should notify the landlord in writing as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Use the emergency contact details in your agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Record that the owner's tradespeople can't attend yet.
2. **Arrange a suitably qualified person** if the owner still can't act promptly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep records of the steps you took to reach the owner.
3. **Give written notice of the repairs and their cost within 7 days** of the work being done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for reimbursement.** The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if that is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations state that a renter may be reimbursed for reasonable repair costs up to $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The owner must reimburse within 7 days after receiving your written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the owner refuses to pay or you can't meet the cost,** you may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT). The Tribunal must hear an urgent repair application within 2 business days of it being made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Gaps in the documents:** They don't say how a court or VCAT would treat a broken tap specifically, and they don't set out a fixed time for "immediately" beyond the reasonable-steps test. Check with Consumer Affairs Victoria before acting.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents clearly support asking for repairs, and in some cases arranging urgent repairs yourself and claiming the cost back. They do not contain a right to a rent reduction. On cancelling, they mention a notice-to-vacate provision but not its terms, so I can't confirm you can cancel.

**Which law applies today (5 November 2026):** The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **115** (metadata "version 115", in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version **009** (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The text doesn't print the words "Authorised Version," so the version numbers come from the document metadata.

## What the law says about your situation

- **Mould and damp:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The premises must also be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Provider's duties:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the minimum standards and are "vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in," and must maintain them "in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The Act's definition includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure," and "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** Before you move in, the provider must give you 2 copies of a signed condition report on the state of repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you aren't given one, you may complete one yourself and give it to the provider before 5 business days after you move in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A condition report you give the provider is taken as notice of any defects it states [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Put it in writing now.** You must give written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). List the damp, mould and rotting timber, and record them on the condition report.
2. **Ask for repairs.** For urgent repairs, you may arrange them yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary says this is directly reimbursable "up to $2500" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Non-urgent repairs:** If repairs are not urgent, you must give written notice, and you can apply to the Director if the provider hasn't repaired within 14 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear a non-urgent repair application within 7 days of it being made [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Urgent-repair applications:** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear these within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Pay rent into the Rent Special Account:** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you may apply to VCAT for an order to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must make that order if the provider has failed to carry out the repairs and has not shown financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Amend the condition report:** Within 30 days after the agreement starts, you may apply to VCAT to amend a statement in the condition report that is inaccurate or incomplete [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Cancelling and lower rent

- **Cancelling:** The Regulations' standard form refers to a renter giving notice of intention to vacate under "section 91ZD" where premises are "destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't include the text of section 91ZD, so I can't tell you its requirements or whether your situation qualifies. A VCAT application for an order is referenced in the Act but also isn't set out in these documents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Lower rent:** The documents don't contain a right to reduce rent for defective premises. The only reduction mentioned is an order reducing the agreement's *term* for severe hardship under section 91U [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), which is not a rent reduction.

## Gaps and next steps

- The documents don't cover what happens if the lease hasn't started yet. Since you have keys but haven't moved in, check the agreement's start date.
- For advice on cancelling, get the text of section 91ZD and related provisions, or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting, cited in the Regulations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)) or VCAT.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** Tell the landlord in writing now, and ask for urgent repairs. The Act lets you arrange urgent repairs yourself and claim the cost back if the landlord doesn't act. The documents don't say who pays for damage caused by burglars, so get advice on that point.

**Which law applies:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026) is the current version as of today [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also relied on the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Duty to report:** A renter must give the landlord written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the premises or a breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice can be given electronically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Landlord's repair duty:** The landlord must keep the premises "in good repair" and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The definition includes "a burst water service," "a dangerous electrical fault," and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Plumbing and wiring damage may fall within these categories, depending on the facts.
- **Renter's damage duty:** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether burglars count as "visitors" or how this applies to a break-in.
- **Cleaning:** The renter must keep the premises reasonably clean, and at the end must leave them "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in their original condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning:** The landlord can't require professional cleaning at the end unless it was done at the start of the tenancy, or it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice now.** Describe the break-in, the plumbing and wiring damage, and the security issue [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** You may arrange them yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to repair immediately and the landlord cannot be reached or does not act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If you pay for urgent repairs,** give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary says the renter may be reimbursed directly up to $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **If the landlord refuses to repair or pay,** you can apply to VCAT for an order. VCAT must hear an urgent repair application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **For non-urgent repairs,** give written notice. If the landlord hasn't acted within 14 days, you can apply to the Director (Consumer Affairs Victoria) or VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **If repairs are not done,** you can ask VCAT to order that rent be paid into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
7. **Security:** Landlords must provide deadlocks and window locks [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You need the landlord's consent to change a master-key lock, and they must not unreasonably refuse it. If they refuse, you can apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
8. **Cleaning:** Ask the landlord in writing to make the premises safe and repaired before you are expected to clean. Your cleaning duty is qualified by "as far as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether the break-in damage is your responsibility or the landlord's, or whether insurance applies.
- Whether you can withhold rent because the premises are damaged. The documents only cover rent-related rules for the period before occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Police reporting requirements.

For these points, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), or get legal advice.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the current law, a rent-payment fee is prohibited unless another Act permits a payment surcharge, and the documents I found don't identify any such Act.

**What the law says**

- The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) says a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) apply from 31 March 2026. They list "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A card fee is therefore covered unless another Act permits it. The documents don't name any Act that does.
- The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs, other than the renter's own bank or account fees, is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Bank transfer appears to be that kind of method.
- Before you agree to use a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about costs such as third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

The prohibition applies to "a person" who demands or receives the fee, so the wording isn't limited to the agent. The only exception in these extracts is for ADIs. The documents don't address how the rule applies to a third-party app company's own arrangements, so I can't confirm that point from them.

**What you can do**

- Ask the agent in writing which payment methods are free and what each one costs. The agent must give you this information before you use a particular method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Use the free bank transfer. The law requires a no-extra-cost method to be reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say anything about processing times, so I can't say whether a slow transfer would be treated as unreasonable.
- Ask for a written receipt. If you request one when paying by a method other than in person, the person receiving the payment must provide it within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Gaps:** The documents don't say how to make a complaint or apply to the Tribunal over a prohibited fee, and they don't cover any surcharge rules in other Acts.

---

**Sources**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026), ss 42, 43, 51A.
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026), reg 21C and reg 19.

(2) It states the s 51A/reg 21C ban and the 'payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act' exception, and says 'the prohibition applies to "a person"... so the wording isn't limited to the agent. The only exception... is for ADIs.' A later caveat about the app company's own arrangements adds some hedging, but a reader can still tell the ban applies whoever collects the fee.
