question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Possibly not. Under Victorian law, you must pay for professional cleaning only if it is actually needed to restore the property to its move-in condition, and your self-cleaning may already have done that. The documents I found don't say that a professional receipt is the only acceptable proof of cleaning.

I used the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents identify versions by these numbers in their metadata, not as "Authorised Version" numbers, so I'm citing those version numbers.

---

### What the law says

- **Professional cleaning terms are limited.** A standard-form agreement may include a term requiring professional cleaning only if it becomes required to restore the premises to their condition before the tenancy started, taking into account fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The prescribed wording.** The landlord must not require you to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless (a) professional cleaning was done before you moved in and you were told so, or (b) it is required to restore the premises to their move-in condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **When you pay.** You must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if professional cleaning "becomes required" to restore them to that condition, again considering the condition report and fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your general duty.** You must leave the premises, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Landlord's bond claim.** The landlord can claim from the bond the reasonable cost of cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, judged against their condition at the start [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Unenforceable terms.** A term that requires professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A renter can ask VCAT to declare a term invalid or vary it if it is harsh or unconscionable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent to show what needs professional cleaning.** Under the law, professional cleaning is required only if the premises are not restored to their move-in condition, so ask what specifically is still dirty or damaged compared with the start condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the wording of your clause.** Compare it to the prescribed wording in regulation 12 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If it requires professional cleaning regardless of the move-in condition, it may go beyond what the law allows [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for a joint end-of-tenancy inspection.** The landlord must complete the end-of-tenancy condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends, in your presence or with a reasonable opportunity for you to attend [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Respond in writing if the landlord disputes the condition.** Renters may add comments and photos to a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Evidence that can show the carpets' condition

- **Your move-in condition report.** It records the state of the premises at the start. Keep it safe, because it helps resolve disputes over cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A signed condition report is conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition on the day specified, subject to some exceptions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Dated photos.** Take photos at the start and end of the tenancy, label them with the room and date, and send copies to the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your own cleaning records.** Receipts for cleaning products or equipment, and dated photos of the carpets after cleaning, may help. I couldn't find a document saying these are legally sufficient, so I can't say how much weight they would carry.
- **Bond claim evidence.** Before the landlord claims bond money, they must give you bond claim evidence at least 3 days in advance, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- The documents don't say that a receipt from a professional cleaner is required to prove the carpets were cleaned.
- They don't define what "professional standard" cleaning means or what counts as fair wear and tear for carpets.
- They don't say whether a pet clause can override the cleaning rules. The cleaning rules appear in the standard form and the prescribed terms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If the agent refuses to return your bond or insists on a professional clean, you can apply to VCAT. Bond repayment applications must be made within 14 days after the agreement has terminated [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The hardest one, reg 12, is covered by: 'The landlord must not require you to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless (a) professional cleaning was done before you moved in and you were told so, or (b) it is required to restore the premises to their move-in condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear'. The s 63 duty is covered by 'leave the premises, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear'. The entry condition report is presented as conclusive evidence of the starting condition.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction also commits you to pay a separate invoice. They do set out the cleaning rules and the bond-claim process, which are relevant to whether the invoice is justified.

**Documents used:** The governing Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021) are also relevant, and the retrieved copy is dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Regulations copy doesn't show an Authorised Version number, so I can't give one for it.

### What the law says about cleaning

- You must leave the premises, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord can claim from the bond the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Professional cleaning can only be required if it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says about the bond claim

- At least 3 days before a claim for repayment to the landlord is made, the landlord must give each renter bond claim evidence supporting it. This can include an invoice, receipt or quote [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Bond claim evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What this means for your situation

The documents don't cover whether a landlord can send a separate invoice for cleaning after the bond has already been fully returned to you, or whether your earlier agreement to a deduction binds you to pay that invoice. I can't say from these sources whether you must pay it.

You can check the following against the documents:

1. **Was the cleaning reasonable and necessary?** Ask whether the cost is "reasonable" and whether the premises were actually left unclean compared with the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check your condition report, since the cleaning must be assessed against it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Was the cleaning professional, and was that permitted?** The landlord can only require professional cleaning in the limited circumstances above [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Was proper evidence provided?** Ask for the invoice or other bond claim evidence, and check whether it was given to you at least 3 days before any claim [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If the landlord disputes your position, the documents refer to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) and to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for more information [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't say whether VCAT would hear a dispute about a separate invoice after bond repayment, so you should confirm that with the relevant authority before relying on it.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely. If the owner or their agent can't get a repair done promptly, the Act lets you arrange urgent repairs yourself, but only after specific steps and with conditions. Whether a broken tap counts as an "urgent repair" is not clear from the documents.

**Documents and versions:** The answer comes from the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both apply today.

---

### What the law says

- **Urgent repairs:** The Act defines urgent repairs to include a "burst water service" and "a failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your situation may fall under one of these, but the documents don't say whether a broken tap alone qualifies.
- **Written notice:** You must give the owner written notice of a breakdown as soon as practicable after you become aware of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **When you can act yourself:** You may arrange urgent repairs only if (a) you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and (b) you are unable to get them to do it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do the work:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act defines this to include a tradesperson who is registered or licensed for the relevant work, where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner's tradespeople:** The documents don't say the owner's tradespeople are the only ones you may use. The standard agreement form says additional terms "must not exclude, restrict or modify any of the rights and duties included in the Act" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

1. **Notify in writing now.** Contact the emergency contact in writing, and keep a copy. The standard form says that if there is a need for an urgent repair, the renter should notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Document your reasonable steps.** Keep records of each attempt to get the repair done immediately, since the Act requires these steps before you can act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If they still can't attend, engage a suitably qualified person.** Be sure they are licensed or registered for the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Reimbursement:** The owner is liable to reimburse the reasonable cost of the repairs, or the prescribed amount if that is less, and must pay within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations summarise the prescribed limit as reimbursement "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't show the prescribed amount in the Act itself, so check the current figure.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents clearly support asking for repairs. They do not contain a rent-reduction provision for this situation. Cancelling is only mentioned in passing, and the operative text isn't in what I retrieved.

**Documents used:**
- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026.
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026.

Both are the versions in force today (5 November 2026).

---

### What the law says

- **Mould and damp:** Each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. The premises must also be structurally sound and weatherproof [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Condition at move-in:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** "Urgent repairs" includes any fault or damage that makes rented premises unsafe or insecure, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. A failure to comply with the rental minimum standards also counts [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't specifically mention rotting timber. It would fall under this definition only if it makes the house unsafe or insecure, or if it breaches the structural-soundness standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** Before you move in, the provider must give you a signed condition report stating the state of repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A report you give the provider is taken as notice of any defects it lists [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can ask VCAT to amend an inaccurate or incomplete report within 30 days after the agreement starts [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can do

**1. Give written notice now.** You must give written notice to the provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). List every defect in writing and note it on the condition report. Photos help, and the regulations recommend dating them and identifying the room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for urgent repairs.** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and the provider can't or doesn't [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you do:
- You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations' summary says reimbursement is available for up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If the provider refuses to pay, or the cost is too high, you can apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for non-urgent repairs.** If the issue isn't urgent, give written notice. If repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can:
- Apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf); or
- Apply to VCAT for an order requiring repairs. VCAT must hear it within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**4. Ask VCAT to direct rent into the Rent Special Account.** If you have given a repair notice and the provider has failed to carry out repairs, VCAT must order rent to be paid into the Rent Special Account if it is satisfied of the listed conditions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This holds rent pending repairs. It is not a reduction in rent, and the documents don't describe a reduction mechanism.

**5. Cancelling the lease.** The documents don't contain the full text of the cancellation rules. The only reference I found says a renter may give notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD "on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set out the conditions, notice period, or process for that. Check section 91ZD of the Act directly before relying on it.

**6. Lower rent.** The documents don't contain a provision that lets you reduce rent because of pre-move-in defects. The rent provisions I found cover rent increases, rent in advance, and payment methods [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act also refers to VCAT reducing a fixed term on grounds of severe hardship under section 91U [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), but that is a reference only, and the documents don't set out how it works.

---

### Other points
- If the house is subject to a Housing Act declaration that it is unfit for habitation, you cannot use the repair applications under sections 72 to 75 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- For practical guidance, the regulations point to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For cancellation or rent-reduction questions, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current Act, you should give the landlord written notice now, and if they don't repair urgent damage promptly, you can arrange the repairs yourself and seek reimbursement or go to VCAT. The documents don't say whether burglary damage is the renter's responsibility, so that point needs further advice.

The documents I searched are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I'm treating these as the current versions as of today, 5 November 2026.

### What the law says

- **Duty to notify:** A renter must give written notice to the landlord "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage to the premises or a breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Section 62 separately requires written notice of the fact and nature of the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** "Urgent repairs" include a burst water service, a blocked or broken lavatory system, a dangerous electrical fault, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who may do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A suitably qualified person includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter's damage duty:** A renter and visitor must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, but fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** A renter must keep the premises reasonably clean during the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The "leave reasonably clean" duty applies at the end of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so it doesn't apply yet.

### What you can do

1. **Give written notice now.** Describe each break-in and each piece of damage (plumbing and wiring), and state that you cannot clean properly. Keep a copy and any evidence of the damage, such as photos. Late notice can count against you: when deciding compensation, the Tribunal must consider whether the renter gave the notice required under section 72AA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** You may arrange urgent repairs yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to carry them out immediately and you cannot get them to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Use a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

3. **Claim reimbursement.** You must give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The landlord is liable for the reasonable cost, capped at the lesser of the actual cost or the prescribed amount, and must reimburse you within 7 days of receiving written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary states that reimbursement is for "the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

4. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you arranged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

5. **Non-urgent repairs.** If an issue isn't urgent, you can apply to VCAT if the landlord hasn't carried out repairs within 14 days of your written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

6. **Locks.** The Regulations say you must get the landlord's consent before changing a lock in the master key system, and the landlord must not unreasonably refuse [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If consent is withheld and you believe that is unreasonable, you can apply to VCAT for a determination that consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

7. **Compensation.** You may apply to VCAT for compensation for loss or damage caused by the landlord's failure to comply with the agreement or the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal considers, among other things, whether the landlord has repaired the damage and whether you took steps to reduce your loss [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- **Whether the burglary damage is your responsibility.** The renter's damage duty covers damage caused by the renter or visitors [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address damage caused by a third-party burglar, so I can't say who must pay for the plumbing and wiring repairs.
- **Police reports and insurance.** The documents don't address reporting the break-ins to police or making an insurance claim.
- **Changing locks, beyond the master key system.** I didn't retrieve the section that governs changing other locks, so I can't say more about that.

**Practical next step:** Give the landlord written notice today, and get a suitably qualified tradesperson to assess the plumbing and wiring. If you can't get the landlord to act promptly, check the urgent repair steps above before paying for repairs yourself.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the current law, the app likely cannot charge you a card fee for paying rent, and it does not matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent. The documents don't say whether any other Act permits a payment surcharge, so I can't rule that out completely.

**Governing documents:** The current Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The current Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I'm reading the version numbers from the document metadata, so please confirm the official Authorised Version label.

**What the law says**

- **Fee-free option:** The provider or agent must ensure that a payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. The only allowed costs are bank or account fees on your own bank account. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 penalty units for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee disclosure:** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Prohibited fees:** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). From 31 March 2026, the prescribed matters include "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Prescribed method:** The prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A bank transfer is likely to fall within this, but the documents don't say so expressly.

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

No, not under the documents. The fee prohibition applies to "a person" who demands or receives the fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so the app company is caught as well as the agent. The fee-free obligation falls on the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Either way, the fee is only allowed if another Act permits a payment surcharge, and the documents don't identify any such Act.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the provider or agent in writing which fee-free methods they accept, and whether the card fee is charged under a payment surcharge permitted by another Act. They must tell you about any costs before you agree to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask for a receipt. If you ask at the time of payment and it isn't made in person, it must be given within 5 business days, and must show your name and the rented premises, the date, the period paid, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If you pay by bank transfer and it is slow, the documents don't say whether a slower method still counts as "reasonably available." They also don't address whether late-payment consequences would apply in that situation.

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't describe how to complain or enforce these rules, or whether the app's fee is in fact a permitted surcharge under another Act. For those points, you would need to check other sources or seek advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advisory service.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't require you to hire a professional cleaner. Your obligation is to restore the carpets if professional cleaning is actually needed, and the documents don't say that a cleaner's receipt is the only proof. Whether your clause is enforceable depends on its wording, which I haven't seen.

**Versions used:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (metadata version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (metadata version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents show these version numbers in their metadata, but they don't label them as "Authorised Version" numbers, so please check that label on the official copies.

---

### What the law says

- **Pet clause validity:** A lease can require professional cleaning or a renter-paid professional clean at the end only if it is in the prescribed standard form. Other such terms are prohibited [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **When the standard-form term applies:** The standard term says the renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Limit on the provider:** The provider must not require professional cleaning at the end unless the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your general duty:** At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claims:** The provider may claim the reasonable cost of cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, "having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Check your lease wording.** Confirm whether the clause matches the standard-form professional-cleaning term. If it's an extra term that goes beyond the standard form, it may be void [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Show the carpets were restored.** Your evidence should show the carpets match their move-in condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set out a required evidence format for residential rentals. The caravan condition report form advises taking dated, labelled photos at the start and end of the residency , but that form applies to caravans, not to your situation.
3. **Ask for the move-in condition report.** The provider must give the renter the condition report before or at move-in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Compare the carpet entry with your photos.
4. **Ask the provider to identify the basis for the request.** If a bond claim is made, the provider must give you bond claim evidence at least 3 days before the claim, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

That evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning:** The provider must not require you to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless the conditions in regulation 12 are met, such as professional cleaning having been done at the start of the tenancy, or being needed to restore the premises to its starting condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Is agreeing to a deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?

4. **Check whether the cleaning was reasonable.** Only the "reasonable cost" of cleaning is claimable, and only if the premises were not left reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Dispute it if needed.** Under the Act, a dispute about a bond claim goes to the Tribunal (VCAT). Applications about bond repayment generally must be made within 14 days after the agreement terminated [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Given the bond has already been returned, get advice quickly on whether that timeframe still matters for you.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely, and the owner's restriction to their own tradespeople doesn't by itself stop you from arranging the repair. But any repair must be done by a suitably qualified person, and you have to follow specific notice and cost rules.

**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I'm assuming you rent under a residential rental agreement from the owner.

**What the law says**

- A burst water service is an urgent repair, and so is a failure or breakdown of the water supply to rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A "suitably qualified person" includes a tradesperson who is registered or licensed for the relevant work, where that work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Notify the owner and give them a chance.** You can arrange urgent repairs only if you have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider to do them immediately, and they have not done so [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep a record of your requests, ideally in writing.
2. **Arrange a suitably qualified tradesperson yourself.** If the owner still hasn't acted, you may arrange the repair. The owner's preference for their own tradespeople is not addressed in these documents, so I can't say whether it changes this right.
3. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** For a claim for reimbursement, you must give the owner written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the owner must reimburse you within 7 days of receiving that notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Reimbursement limit.** You may be reimbursed directly for the reasonable cost of the repairs up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Going to VCAT.** You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the owner refuses to pay for repairs you arranged [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you have arranged repairs and the owner has not reimbursed you within 7 days of written notice, you may apply to VCAT for a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Doing it yourself:** The documents say repairs must be carried out by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So you should not do the plumbing yourself. Use a registered or licensed plumber.

**What the documents don't cover:** The full text of the section that sets out the renter's right to arrange urgent repairs was not in the excerpts I retrieved, so I can't confirm its exact wording. The documents also don't define "reasonable steps" or how quickly the owner must respond. For a definitive answer on those points, check the full Act or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

It never says that a nominated-tradesperson requirement is a prohibited term or cannot stop an urgent repair, so a reader could not tell which way the point falls. question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents support asking for repairs and, in some cases, arranging urgent repairs yourself. They do not clearly support cancelling the lease or getting a rent reduction for damp, mould and rotting timber before you move in. Those parts need legal advice or a VCAT question.

**Version applied:** The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Regulations document is labelled "version 009" in its metadata, but its text does not show an Authorised Version number.

---

### What the law says

- **Standards at move-in:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations require that each room be free from mould and damp "caused by or related to the building structure" and that the premises be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain:** The provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation." This applies even if you knew about the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The definition of urgent repairs includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure," and "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber is not named in that list, so whether it is urgent depends on whether it makes the premises unsafe or insecure.

### What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice.** You must give written notice of damage "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Put the damp, mould and timber in writing to the provider.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** If the premises do not meet the standards when you enter occupation, you may issue a request for urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You may arrange urgent repairs yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and cannot get them done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must then give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days, up to the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' summary gives that limit as "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for urgent repairs.** You can apply if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** If the repairs are not urgent, give written notice. If the provider has not repaired within 14 days, you can apply to the Director (Consumer Affairs Victoria) to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to VCAT for an order requiring repairs within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Record it on the condition report.** You can apply to VCAT within 30 days of the agreement starting to amend an inaccurate or incomplete condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A condition report given to the provider is also taken as notice of defects [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Cancelling the lease

- The documents do not contain the text of the provisions on renter termination before possession (s 91L) or on premises unfit for habitation (s 91ZD). I can only see their headings [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I cannot confirm from these documents whether you can cancel.
- Section 65(2) says a renter is not required to move in if the premises are not "vacant and reasonably clean," and the rent-free period under s 65(3) applies to that situation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not clearly state that failing the rental minimum standards gives you the same right before you move in.

### Lowering the rent

- The documents do not contain a general power to reduce rent for disrepair.
- Under s 65(3), you are not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed move-in day until you actually move in, if the premises do not comply with s 65(1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Under s 77, if you have given notice requiring repairs, you may apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal must make that order if notice was given, the provider has failed to carry out repairs, and the provider has not shown financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Section 91U allows VCAT to reduce a fixed-term agreement for severe hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether this applies to disrepair.

---

**Next steps:** Put everything in writing now, keep photos and copies, and get the emergency repair contact that the provider must give you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Before you decide whether to cancel or withhold rent, get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service. The retrieved documents do not contain the full text of the termination provisions, so I cannot confirm those options.

It never states that a renter who has not taken possession can end the agreement by notice because the premises do not meet the minimum standards, are not in good repair, or are unfit for habitation. The minimum-standards point (s 65A) and the repair route are both covered.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** The Act gives you a clear path for urgent plumbing repairs and written notice now, but the documents don't address burglary damage specifically, so it's unclear whether you'd be liable for it.

**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act is the primary source.

## What the law says

- **Your duty not to cause damage:** A renter and visitor must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, and fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provision covers damage by the renter or visitors, not by burglars, so the documents don't say whether burglary damage counts against you.
- **Your duty to report damage:** You must give the provider written notice "as soon as practicable" of the fact and nature of any damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Electronic notice is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you took reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and couldn't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Urgent repairs include failure of an essential service for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A "burst water service" and "flood damage" are given as examples of urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Reimbursement:** If you do the repairs, you must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider is liable only for the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations state the amount is up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who may do the work:** Only a suitably qualified person may do urgent or non-urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give written notice. If the provider hasn't repaired within 14 days, you may apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** You must leave the premises as far as practicable reasonably clean and in the condition they were in when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider cannot require professional cleaning unless it was done at the start of the tenancy or is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Your options before the lease ends

1. **Give written notice now.** Describe the burglary damage to the plumbing and wiring, and the cleaning problem, and attach dated photos. This satisfies the notice duties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Request urgent repairs in writing if the plumbing is affected.** Ask for immediate repair and list an emergency contact [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the provider doesn't act, you may arrange repairs through a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep receipts, and send the 7-day written notice of cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Go to VCAT if the provider won't act or pay.** You can apply for an urgent repairs order if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to reimburse [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **For non-urgent wiring or other repairs,** wait 14 days after notice, then apply to VCAT. VCAT must hear the application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It may consider whether the repairs were needed because of your act or omission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Rent withholding is only through VCAT.** If you've given notice requiring repairs and the provider has failed to comply, you may apply to have rent paid into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Watch for a repair notice.** A provider may issue a repair notice requiring you to fix damage only if the damage resulted from your failure to take care under the damage duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Respond within 14 days if you get one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your evidence that the damage was caused by burglars is relevant here.
7. **Cleaning.** Document what you tried and why it can't be done. Don't agree to professional cleaning unless the conditions above are met [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
8. **Safety.** Tell the provider about any defect that could threaten safety [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep the condition report and photos for later disputes [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether burglary damage is your responsibility under the Act.
- Whether damaged wiring qualifies as an "urgent repair." The definition in section 3 of the Act is not in the retrieved text.
- The provider's general repair duty in section 68, the lock provisions in sections 70 and 71 (only part of section 71 was retrieved), and any police, insurance, or lease-specific terms.

For a definitive answer on liability or the urgent-repair question, get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026** (Author: Barbara Hargreaves). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The relevant regulation is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026** (Author: Lavina Mandy). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent **must make reasonably available at least one rent-payment method with no additional cost**, apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Electronic funds transfer is a prescribed payment method**, which the rental provider or agent must permit. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Before you consent to a particular payment method, the rental provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A person other than an **ADI** must not charge a fee for a prescribed matter relating to rent payment. The regulations prescribe “rent payment”, but expressly exclude **“payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act.”** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also prohibits charging for establishing or using a direct-debit or other electronic-payment facility for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, the documents **do not establish that this particular card fee is lawful**. They show that a card-payment surcharge might be allowed if it is a “payment surcharge fee” permitted by another Act, but the retrieved documents do not identify that other Act or state the conditions for permission. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The documents also **do not say that the result depends on whether the fee is paid to the app company or the agent**. The relevant duties apply to the residential rental provider or the provider’s agent, while the prohibition refers to a “person other than an ADI”; the documents do not state the app company’s legal status or provide a different rule based on who receives the fee. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. Ask the agent or rental provider to identify the legal authority for the card surcharge and confirm whether the app company is an **ADI**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. Ask for confirmation that the manual bank-transfer option is the required fee-free method and that no additional cost—other than your own bank or account fees—will apply. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
3. Ask for written disclosure of all costs before using the card option. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. If they cannot justify the surcharge, ask them to remove or refund it and continue paying by the fee-free bank-transfer method. The retrieved documents do not specify a refund procedure or a particular complaint process for this issue. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer states the provider 'must make reasonably available at least one rent-payment method with no additional cost, apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter's own bank account.' (2) For the hardest point, it states that 'a person other than an ADI must not charge a fee for a prescribed matter relating to rent payment,' with the exclusion for 'payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act.' It adds that the documents 'do not say that the result depends on whether the fee is paid to the app company or the agent' and give no 'different rule based on who receives the fee.' This conveys that the collector does not matter. Its question about whether the app company is an ADI is a mild hedge, not one that hides which way the point falls. (3) It gives next steps: ask for the fee to be removed or refunded and keep using the fee-free bank transfer.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the fee is allowed simply because a fee-free option exists; it says "the documents do not establish that this particular card fee is lawful." It also never says the landlord or agent is exempt from the fee ban, stating only that the prohibition applies to a "person other than an ADI" and that the documents "do not say that the result depends on whether the fee is paid to the app company or the agent."

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

Under **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force 13 October 2026** (“rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf”), a lease term requiring professional cleaning is prohibited unless it is in the standard form; a prohibited term is void and unenforceable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard form may include a professional-cleaning term only where professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force 30 June 2026** (“rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf”) says professional cleaning may be required only if:

- professional cleaning or professional-standard cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy and you were told this; **or**
- it is required to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act also requires you to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) On the documents provided, if your cleaning has restored the carpets to that condition, the law does **not** establish that you must pay for a professional cleaner merely because the clause demands one. The documents also do **not** say that you must provide a professional cleaner’s receipt. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Send the agent the completed starting condition report and explain that the carpets have been cleaned to their original condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Provide dated, labelled photographs of the carpets from before and after the tenancy; the prescribed condition report specifically says photographs can help resolve disputes and should identify the room/location and date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to identify the condition requiring professional cleaning and to compare it with the starting condition report. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the agent seeks money from the bond, ask for the evidence supporting the claim. Before claiming bond, the rental provider or agent must give you bond-claim evidence at least **3 days** beforehand, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A bond claim for cleaning is limited to the reasonable cost of cleaning if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The reg 12 conditions are stated: professional cleaning may be required only if it 'was done immediately before the tenancy and you were told this; or it is required to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear.' (2) The s 63 duty is stated: 'leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear.' (3) The hardest point, that the entry condition report decides the starting condition, is covered by 'Send the agent the completed starting condition report', 'Provide dated, labelled photographs of the carpets from before and after the tenancy', 'compare it with the starting condition report', and the note that bond evidence 'must not conflict with the condition report.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet. It says the opposite: "the law does **not** establish that you must pay for a professional cleaner merely because the clause demands one."

Every citation links to 97-109aa115 or 21-3sra009, and it applies no rule from any other version.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act requires a renter to leave the premises reasonably clean and in substantially the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their starting condition. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The current regulations allow professional-cleaning obligations only in specified circumstances, including where professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to the starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved documents **do not say that an agreement to deduct an amount from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a separate invoice**. They also do not state whether a rental provider may send a separate cleaning invoice after the full bond has been repaid. **So, based only on these documents, it cannot be said conclusively that you must pay this invoice.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide:

- the written agreement or bond claim showing the agreed cleaning deduction;
- the condition report and evidence of the cleaning required;
- the cleaning invoice and proof of payment; and
- the legal basis for pursuing a separate invoice after the full bond was repaid.

You can state that you agreed only to the specified bond deduction, not necessarily to a separate debt, and ask the agent to explain why the full bond was returned. The retrieved documents do not provide a specific procedure or deadline for disputing this separate invoice, so they do not answer what formal step you must take next. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered, though the first is borderline. Point 1 is covered by the statement that the documents 'do not say that an agreement to deduct an amount from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a separate invoice', together with the suggestion that the renter 'agreed only to the specified bond deduction, not necessarily to a separate debt' and the reference to the 'bond claim showing the agreed cleaning deduction'. The wording is hedged, but a reader can still tell which way it falls. Point 2 is covered by the test of whether 'the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their starting condition'.
