question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
## What the law says

A failed water supply is an **urgent repair**. The Act also covers a water-using fixture that is malfunctioning and substantially wasting water. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You **do not have to wait indefinitely** for the owner’s preferred tradespeople. You may arrange the urgent repair yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to arrange it immediately, but they have not done so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The repair must be performed by a **suitably qualified person**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Tell the owner/agent in writing that, because their tradespeople are unavailable and the house’s water is shut off, you will arrange a suitably qualified plumber immediately. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Keep evidence of your notification, the tradespeople’s unavailability, the invoice and the repair.
- Give the rental provider **7 days’ written notice** of the repair and its cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days** of receiving that notice, up to **$2,500** under the prescribed information in the current agreement form. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you cannot pay, the repair costs more than $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repair; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The applicable document today is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115** (in force from 13 October 2026), authored by Barbara Hargreaves. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: 'A failed water supply is an urgent repair'; renters may arrange the repair after taking reasonable steps, with reimbursement of the reasonable cost up to $2,500 'within 7 days of receiving that notice'; and for the hardest point, 'You do not have to wait indefinitely for the owner's preferred tradespeople. You may arrange the urgent repair yourself', which conveys that the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failure condition: it says "You do not have to wait indefinitely for the owner's preferred tradespeople" and "The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days" (up to $2,500), which contradicts both a duty to wait and a bar on recovering costs.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115' (link 97-109aa115) and the Regulations through the link 21-3sra009 (version 009); both are the versions in force, and no other version is relied on.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, Author: Barbara Hargreaves. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026**, Author: Lavina Mandy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for repairs.** Give the rental provider written notice describing the damp, mould and rotting timber, and attach dated photographs. The condition-report form specifically allows you to record defects and repairs needed, and says that this gives written notice of the issue. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

2. **Seek an order requiring repairs.** If the repairs are non-urgent and are not completed within **14 days** after written notice, you may apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for an investigation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You may also apply to VCAT for specified repairs after that 14-day period; VCAT must hear the application within **7 days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT may order specified repairs, require a suitably qualified person to do them, and award compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Do not simply stop paying rent or reduce it yourself.** The documents do not give you a right to unilaterally lower the rent. You may instead apply to VCAT for compensation, or—after giving a repair notice—seek an order allowing rent to be paid into the **Rent Special Account** while the repair breach continues. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the breach concerns section 68 or the rental minimum standards and the repairs are still not done by the end of the ordered period, you may apply for some or all of that held rent to be paid to you. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **Cancel or end the lease:** the retrieved documents do not provide enough information to confirm that you can immediately cancel merely because you signed the lease, collected the keys and discovered these defects. The prescribed agreement says that rent-foregone compensation is not payable where the agreement ends under **section 91ZD** because the premises are “destroyed or unfit for habitation”, but the retrieved documents do not set out section 91ZD or explain whether this house meets that test. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) You should therefore ask the rental provider in writing to agree to end the agreement, or seek advice/VCAT orders before treating the lease as cancelled.

The documents do not state whether damp, mould and rotting timber in your particular circumstances legally make the premises “unfit for habitation,” so that point cannot be determined from the retrieved documents alone.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer omits the s 91L point that a renter who has not yet taken possession can end the agreement by notice because the premises fail the minimum standards, are not in good repair, or are unfit for habitation; instead it says the documents 'do not provide enough information to confirm that you can immediately cancel'. It also never says the minimum standards must be met by the day the renter moves in (s 65A).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must move in and pay rent before acting, and it rejects a right to lower rent, stating "The documents do not give you a right to unilaterally lower the rent" and pointing instead to VCAT compensation or a Rent Special Account order.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, authored by **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The current regulations document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026**, authored by **Lavina Mandy**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- You must notify the rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable** about the damage and its nature. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Damage to plumbing, electrical wiring, water/electricity supply, or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure can fall within **urgent repairs**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and fit for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the premises are **unfit for human habitation**, or destroyed to an extent that makes them unsafe, you may give a notice of intention to vacate **on the date the notice is given or a later date**, even though a fixed term has not ended. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The documents do not specifically say that burglary damage automatically makes premises “unfit for human habitation” or “unsafe”; that depends on the actual condition of the property. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- At the end, you must leave the premises reasonably clean and in their original condition **as far as practicable**, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The rental provider cannot require professional cleaning unless the statutory conditions in the agreement and regulations are met. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Write to the rental provider immediately.** Describe each break-in, attach photographs, police reports and repair evidence, and say that the plumbing and wiring prevent safe occupation and cleaning. Keep copies. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Demand urgent repairs immediately.** Ask the rental provider or agent to arrange suitably qualified plumbers and electricians. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) If they do not act after you take reasonable steps to arrange the repairs, you may arrange urgent repairs yourself; the Act requires seven days’ written notice of the repairs and cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within seven days, subject to the statutory limit. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The regulations state the direct reimbursement amount as up to **$2,500**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. **Apply to VCAT for urgent repairs** if you cannot pay, the repairs cost more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay; the Tribunal must hear the application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **End the lease immediately under section 91ZD** if the evidence supports that the premises are unfit for human habitation or unsafe. Give a written notice of intention to vacate specifying the date you are ending the agreement. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard agreement says no rent-foregone amount is payable where the agreement ends on this basis. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

5. If the premises are not legally established to be unfit or unsafe, the documents identify a general fixed-term hardship application: VCAT may reduce or terminate the fixed term where an unforeseen change causes you severe hardship greater than the other party’s hardship, although it may order compensation. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Do **not** stop paying rent or treat the lease as ended solely because cleaning is difficult unless you have a valid termination basis, an agreement with the rental provider, or a VCAT order; the retrieved documents do not provide a general right to withhold rent in these circumstances.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: written notice 'as soon as practicable'; plumbing and wiring damage as urgent repairs, with the renter able to arrange them and the provider required to 'reimburse the reasonable cost'; and s 91ZD termination by notice of intention to vacate 'on the date the notice is given or a later date, even though a fixed term has not ended'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer places repair duties on the rental provider ('Ask the rental provider or agent to arrange suitably qualified plumbers and electricians'), mentions renter-arranged repairs only as a reimbursable fallback, and offers early exit ('End the lease immediately under section 91ZD if the evidence supports that the premises are unfit for human habitation or unsafe'), so it says neither failing claim.

The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (links 97-109aa115), and every rule it applies comes from that version or from the in-force 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009' (21-3sra009), with no other version relied on.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. The relevant regulation is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent must make **reasonably available at least one rent-payment method with no additional cost**, apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Before you consent to a payment method, the rental provider or agent must tell you about costs, including **third-party transaction fees** and other electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A person must not charge for establishing or using a direct-debit or other electronic payment facility for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The regulations prohibit a non-ADI from charging a fee for **rent payment**, including administrative costs and failed payments, but expressly exclude **payment surcharge fees permitted under another Act**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, the documents support this conclusion: **the app cannot make card payment the only reasonably available option if it imposes an additional fee**. Your no-fee manual bank-transfer option may satisfy the fee-free-method requirement if it is reasonably available, even though it is slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Whether the card fee is lawful depends on whether it is a **payment surcharge permitted under another Act**. The retrieved Victorian tenancy documents do not identify that other Act or state the conditions for such a surcharge, so they do not conclusively answer whether this particular card fee is lawful. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** make the result depend on whether the money goes to the app company or the agent. The obligations apply to the residential rental provider or the provider’s agent, and the separate prohibition applies to a “person”; however, the retrieved documents do not determine the app company’s legal status or whether it is an ADI. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or rental provider, in writing:

1. **Who receives the card fee**—the app company, agent, or someone else. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
2. **What the fee is for and its amount**, and whether it is claimed to be a payment surcharge permitted under another Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
3. **Why the fee-free bank-transfer method is reasonably available**, including its processing time. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
4. For the fee-free method, ensure you are charged only your own bank or account fees, not an additional tenancy-payment fee. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the fee-free option is not reasonably available, or the fee is not a surcharge permitted under another Act, ask them to remove the card fee or provide another compliant fee-free payment method. The retrieved documents do not specify the available complaint or enforcement procedure.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers all three points. It says a fee-free method must be 'reasonably available' apart from the renter's own bank fees. It says the regulations 'prohibit a non-ADI from charging a fee for rent payment' except 'payment surcharge fees permitted under another Act', and that 'the documents do not make the result depend on whether the money goes to the app company or the agent'. It gives a next step: 'ask them to remove the card fee or provide another compliant fee-free payment method'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the fee is allowed just because a fee-free option exists; it says the card fee's lawfulness "depends on whether it is a payment surcharge permitted under another Act." It also never exempts the landlord or agent, stating "The obligations apply to the residential rental provider or the provider's agent, and the separate prohibition applies to a 'person'."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with the in-force versions: 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), and it relies on no other version.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

The current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**, says a lease term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy is prohibited—and therefore invalid—unless it is in the standard form. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The standard-form professional-cleaning term only applies where professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy, considering the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**, contain the same requirement. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if you cleaned the carpets yourself and they are back to their original condition, the documents do **not** support requiring you to pay for professional cleaning merely because the lease says so. However, professional cleaning could be required if the carpets were professionally cleaned immediately before you moved in and you were told that, or if professional cleaning is genuinely necessary to restore their documented starting condition. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** say that you must provide a professional cleaner’s receipt where professional cleaning is not otherwise required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Send the agent the signed condition report and explain that the carpets have been returned to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. The Act requires you to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, subject to fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Provide dated, labelled photographs of the carpets, showing each room and close-up detail. The prescribed condition report specifically says that start-and-end photographs can help resolve cleaning disputes. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to identify the specific condition-report entry or damage that allegedly requires professional cleaning, rather than relying only on the lease clause. The final inspection must be completed within **10 days** after the agreement ends, and you must be given an opportunity to attend if possible. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the agent claims part of the bond, they must give you supporting bond-claim evidence at least **3 days before** making the claim, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. On reg 12, the answer says professional cleaning 'could be required if the carpets were professionally cleaned immediately before you moved in and you were told that, or if professional cleaning is genuinely necessary to restore their documented starting condition', and earlier mentions fair wear and tear. On s 63, it says 'The Act requires you to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, subject to fair wear and tear.' On the evidence point, it treats the signed condition report and start-and-end photographs as the evidence of the starting condition.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay for professional cleaning just because of the clause or the pet; it explicitly rejects that, stating 'the documents do **not** support requiring you to pay for professional cleaning merely because the lease says so.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115' (13 October 2026, link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009' (30 June 2026, link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version for any rule.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter must leave the premises reasonably clean, taking account of their condition at the start of the tenancy and fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A rental provider may claim the **reasonable cost of cleaning** from the bond if the premises were not left reasonably clean. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the Act does **not** say that an agreement to deduct an amount from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a separate invoice. Nor do the retrieved documents state that receiving the full bond prevents the agent from seeking compensation separately. Therefore, the documents do not provide a definite yes-or-no answer about whether this particular invoice must be paid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does say that recovering compensation from the bond does not prevent a person from bringing proceedings to recover an **additional amount** of compensation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) This suggests that a rental provider may potentially pursue a separate claim, but it would still need to establish a valid entitlement and the amount claimed; the documents do not say that an invoice alone proves this. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the invoice is for professional cleaning, the current **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**, provide that professional cleaning may be required only where it was carried out immediately before the tenancy and the renter was told that, or where it is required to restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent to provide:

- the written terms of the alleged agreement to pay the invoice;
- the condition report and photographs showing why cleaning was required;
- an itemised invoice or receipt showing the **reasonable cost** of the cleaning; and
- an explanation of why the cleaning amount was not deducted from the bond as agreed. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can state that your agreement concerned an apportionment of the bond, not necessarily a separate payment obligation, and ask the agent to identify the legal or contractual basis for treating it as an invoice. The retrieved documents do not establish whether you must pay without seeing the wording of your agreement and the evidence about the cleaning. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. For the first, the answer says the Act 'does not say that an agreement to deduct an amount from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a separate invoice' and that 'your agreement concerned an apportionment of the bond, not necessarily a separate payment obligation.' This clearly separates a bond deduction from a separate invoice. For the second, it states that the renter must leave the premises 'reasonably clean, taking account of their condition at the start of the tenancy,' and that a claim depends on the premises not being left reasonably clean.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. Neither failure claim is asserted: the answer states 'the Act does **not** say that an agreement to deduct an amount from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a separate invoice,' and rather than saying the full bond repayment bars further claims, it notes 'a rental provider may potentially pursue a separate claim, but it would still need to establish a valid entitlement.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026". The only other document it relies on is "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009", which is the in-force version, and it applies no rule from any other version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
### What the law says

A failure or breakdown of the **water supply** is an “urgent repair.” [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You do **not** have to wait for the owner’s preferred tradesperson if you have taken reasonable steps to arrange for the owner or agent to repair it immediately, but they are unable to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do

You may arrange the repair yourself, using a **suitably qualified person**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Keep the invoice and evidence that you contacted the emergency repair service and were told that no available owner-approved tradesperson could attend.

After the repair, give the owner **written notice within 7 days** stating what was repaired and its cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The owner must reimburse the reasonable repair cost—up to **$2,500** under the prescribed information—within 7 days after receiving that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If you cannot afford the repair, the cost is more than **$2,500**, or the owner refuses to pay, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repair; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Current document:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 115**, in force from 13 October 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: water supply failure is called an 'urgent repair'; the renter may arrange the repair after reasonable steps and must be reimbursed up to $2,500 within 7 days of written notice; and the hardest point, that the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop an urgent repair, is covered by 'You do not have to wait for the owner's preferred tradesperson if you have taken reasonable steps to arrange for the owner or agent to repair it immediately, but they are unable to do so.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says the renter does not have to wait ("You do **not** have to wait for the owner's preferred tradesperson") and can recover the cost ("The owner must reimburse the reasonable repair cost—up to **$2,500**"), so it asserts neither failing claim.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Act as 'Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and the Regulations by the link 21-3sra009 (version 009), and it relies on no version that was not in force on that date.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**; Author: **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**; Author: **Lavina Mandy**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The premises must meet the rental minimum standards **on or before the day you enter into occupation**. Those standards require the premises to be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room to be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must also provide premises that are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day. If they do not, you are not required to enter into occupation and are not required to pay rent for the period before you actually enter into occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the documents do **not** expressly say that signing the lease or receiving the keys automatically lets you cancel the agreement. They do provide a right to give immediate notice of intention to vacate if the premises are **unfit for human habitation** or have been rendered unsafe. Whether the damp, mould and rotting timber meet that threshold cannot be determined from the facts given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the rental provider to cancel the agreement by mutual agreement.**  
   Put the defects in writing, attach dated photographs, and ask for written confirmation that the agreement is ended and any rent or bond paid is returned. The documents do not state an automatic cancellation right merely because defects were discovered before moving in. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Demand repairs before moving in.**  
   Give written notice describing the mould, damp, rotting timber and any safety or structural concerns. The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. **If the premises are unfit or unsafe, give a notice of intention to vacate.**  
   Under section 91ZD, the notice may specify termination **on the day it is given or a later date**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say whether your particular property is legally “unfit for human habitation”, so do not assume that conclusion without evidence.

4. **Seek an order for repairs.**  
   For non-urgent repairs, after giving written notice, you may apply to the Director if the repairs have not been completed within **14 days**. You may then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs; the Tribunal must hear that application within **7 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal may order repairs by a suitably qualified person and compensation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **Ask for compensation or a rent reduction.**  
   A party may apply to the Tribunal for compensation for loss or damage caused by the other party’s failure to comply with the agreement or statutory duties. If compensation is awarded to you, the Tribunal may order it as a **refund or reduction of rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A negotiated lower rent is also something you can ask for, but the documents do not provide an automatic right to a particular rent discount merely because defects exist.

6. **Do not simply stop paying rent without an order or written agreement.**  
   The Act provides a specific mechanism: after giving notice requiring repairs, you may apply to the Tribunal for authority to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account** if the repair duty has not been met and the rental provider has not demonstrated financial hardship. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Keep the keys, lease, inspection records, condition report, photographs, messages and repair requests. The condition report must be provided before occupation; if it is inaccurate or incomplete, either party may apply to amend it within **30 days after the agreement commenced**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The s 91L point is missing: the answer never says a renter who has not yet taken possession can end the agreement by notice because the premises fail the minimum standards, are not in good repair, or are unfit. Instead it states that 'The documents do not state an automatic cancellation right merely because defects were discovered before moving in', which contradicts that right. It covers the other points: minimum standards must be met by the occupation day, including mould and damp related to the building structure, and repairs can be sought under the good-repair duty.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must move in and pay rent first, since it advises to 'Demand repairs before moving in', and it treats lower rent as needing a Tribunal order or agreement, stating 'the Tribunal may order it as a refund or reduction of rent' and 'the documents do not provide an automatic right to a particular rent discount merely because defects exist.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their versions: "Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (link 97-109aa115) and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026" (link 21-3sra009), and every rule it applies is cited only to these in-force versions.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**; its author is listed as **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The relevant regulations are the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009**, in force from **30 June 2026**; the author is listed as **Lavina Mandy**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Damage making the premises unsafe or insecure is an **urgent repair**. Urgent repairs also include a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and a failure or breakdown of the electricity or water supply. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Plumbing or wiring damaged by burglars may therefore fall within the urgent-repairs provisions, depending on the actual condition of the premises. The documents do not state that every burglary-related plumbing or wiring problem automatically qualifies.

You must give the rental provider written notice of the damage as soon as practicable, including the nature of the damage. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You must also leave the premises reasonably clean at the end of the agreement, **as far as practicable**, but the renter’s cleaning duty does not apply to the extent that the rental provider is responsible for keeping the premises clean. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider immediately in writing.** Describe each break-in, attach photographs or other evidence, explain that the plumbing and wiring prevent safe cleaning, and request immediate repairs. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask the rental provider or agent to arrange urgent repairs immediately.** Only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. **Arrange urgent repairs yourself only if** you have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to act immediately and they have failed to do so. The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving written notice of the repairs and cost; the regulations state that direct reimbursement is available up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

4. **Apply to VCAT for urgent-repair orders** if you cannot afford the repairs, the repairs cost more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not specify any guaranteed outcome on rent or cleaning costs.

5. **Consider ending the lease immediately under section 91ZD** if the premises are unfit for human habitation or have been destroyed totally or to an extent that makes them unsafe. You may give a notice of intention to vacate specifying the date the notice is given or a later date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard agreement says the rental provider is not entitled to rent-foregone compensation where the agreement ends because the renter gives notice under section 91ZD on that basis. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Whether the burglary damage meets that threshold is not determined by the documents; document the condition carefully.

Until the lease ends, do not simply abandon the premises without taking one of these steps. A written agreement with the rental provider to end the tenancy is also permitted. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer says to give written notice 'as soon as practicable, including the nature of the damage.' (2) It treats the plumbing and wiring damage as urgent repairs ('a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault'). It says to ask the provider to repair 'immediately', and says the renter can 'arrange urgent repairs yourself' with reimbursement 'within 7 days'. The 'may... depending on condition' hedge still lets a reader tell which way it falls. (3) It covers s 91ZD: if the premises are 'unfit for human habitation' or unsafe, the renter 'may give a notice of intention to vacate specifying the date the notice is given'.

The answer says the renter may arrange repairs only if the rental provider fails to act, with reimbursement ("The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days"), so it does not make the renter liable. It also offers early exits ("Consider ending the lease immediately under section 91ZD" and "A written agreement with the rental provider to end the tenancy is also permitted"), so it does not say the renter must stay whatever the condition.

The answer names the required document as the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115' (link 97-109aa115), and the only other version it relies on is the in-force 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009' (link 21-3sra009), so no out-of-date or future version is applied.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current documents are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- The rental provider or agent must make a rent-payment method reasonably available that has **no additional cost**, except bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- They must tell the renter about costs—including **third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees**—before the renter agrees to use that payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The Regulations prescribe **“rent payment”** as a prohibited fee matter, but expressly exclude **payment surcharge fees permitted under another Act**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also prohibits a person from charging for establishing or using a direct-debit or other electronic payment facility for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, the documents do **not** establish that the app’s card fee is lawful. They do establish that the renter cannot be forced to use the fee-charging card option, because a genuinely fee-free method must be reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Whether the card fee is a legally permitted surcharge under another Act is not addressed in the retrieved documents.

It does matter who charges or receives it: the prohibition applies to **“a person”** other than an ADI, so it is not limited to the rental provider or agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not say whether the app company or agent is an ADI, nor do they establish whether the particular fee qualifies as a surcharge permitted under another Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

Ask the agent or app company:

1. **What is the legal basis for the card fee?** Is it a payment surcharge permitted under another Act? [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
2. **Who is charging and receiving the fee**, and is that entity an ADI? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. **Where is the fee-free payment method**, such as the manual bank-transfer option, and can it be used without penalty or disadvantage? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. For a card payment, request the required information about all transaction or electronic-payment fees **before consenting to use it**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

On the documents provided, the safest conclusion is: **the fee-free bank-transfer option must remain reasonably available; the documents do not provide enough information to confirm that the card fee itself is lawful.**

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the fee-free method must be reasonably available; the answer says the prohibition 'applies to "a person" other than an ADI, so it is not limited to the rental provider or agent', with the exclusion for 'payment surcharge fees permitted under another Act'; and it gives next steps such as asking for and using the fee-free bank-transfer option. The point about who collects the fee is the weakest, because its opening words 'It does matter' are confusingly phrased, but the rest of that sentence conveys the correct meaning.

must-not-say.reason: Yes — neither failure condition is asserted: the answer says "the documents do **not** establish that the app’s card fee is lawful" rather than treating the fee-free option as making it allowed, and it states the prohibition applies to "a person" other than an ADI, "so it is not limited to the rental provider or agent", instead of exempting the landlord or agent.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, a lease term requiring professional cleaning is prohibited—and therefore invalid—unless it is in the standard form agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The standard-form cleaning term only permits professional cleaning, or payment for it, where it is **required to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy**, considering the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The Regulations also say the rental provider must not require professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard unless that cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their original condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if your carpet cleaning has restored the carpets to their starting condition, the retrieved documents do **not** say that you must pay for a professional cleaner merely to obtain a receipt. They also do not expressly decide whether self-cleaning is sufficient in every case. The key issue is the carpets’ actual condition compared with the start-of-tenancy condition—not simply whether you have a professional receipt. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A renter must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A rental provider may claim reasonable cleaning costs from the bond only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Send the agent the **signed condition report**, together with dated before-and-after photographs of the carpets. The prescribed condition-report form specifically recommends photographs at the beginning and end of the tenancy and says they may help resolve cleaning disputes. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to identify the specific carpet condition that allegedly requires professional cleaning and explain how it differs from the entry condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask them to point to the precise lease term they rely on and explain whether it is a standard-form term. An additional term requiring professional cleaning, or payment for it, is invalid unless it is contained in the standard form. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Keep evidence of your cleaning, such as dated photographs, messages, and any products or equipment used. The documents do not prescribe a particular type of proof or require a professional receipt. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the agent makes a bond claim, the rental provider must give you supporting bond-claim evidence **at least 3 days before** making the claim, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The governing documents are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. Point 1 is missing: the answer says professional cleaning is permitted only where 'required to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy', but it omits the other limb of reg 12 (the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy and the renter was told), which materially narrows the rule. Points 2 and 3 are covered ('leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear' and 'Send the agent the signed condition report... photographs').

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay simply because the clause says so or because of a pet. Instead it states the documents 'do not say that you must pay for a professional cleaner merely to obtain a receipt' and that an additional professional-cleaning term 'is invalid unless it is contained in the standard form.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with the in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009' (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, **Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**; its author is listed as **Barbara Hargreaves**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter must leave the premises reasonably clean, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) A rental provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, considering their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, receiving the **full bond** does not necessarily prevent the rental provider from seeking additional compensation: the Act expressly says that recovering compensation from a bond does not prevent proceedings to recover an **additional amount** of compensation.  That does not, by itself, establish that the invoice is payable; the provider would still need to establish an entitlement to the cleaning cost.

The retrieved documents do **not** say that agreeing to a bond deduction automatically means agreeing to pay a separate invoice. They also do not state that a returned bond automatically cancels any separate cleaning liability. Therefore, the documents do not provide a definitive yes-or-no answer about whether you must pay this particular invoice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide:

- the condition report and evidence that the premises were not left reasonably clean; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- an itemised invoice or receipt showing the **reasonable cleaning cost**; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- the legal or contractual basis on which they say your agreement to a bond deduction created a separate debt.

You can state that your agreement concerned a **bond deduction**, that the full bond was later repaid, and that you do not accept—without further proof—that this amounted to an agreement to pay a separate invoice. The retrieved documents do not specify a particular dispute process or deadline for challenging this invoice.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. Point 1 is covered by 'The retrieved documents do not say that agreeing to a bond deduction automatically means agreeing to pay a separate invoice' and the advice that 'your agreement concerned a bond deduction… you do not accept… that this amounted to an agreement to pay a separate invoice'. Point 2 is covered by 'if the premises were not left reasonably clean, considering their condition at the start of the tenancy'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither failing claim is made. The answer says "The retrieved documents do **not** say that agreeing to a bond deduction automatically means agreeing to pay a separate invoice" and also that "receiving the **full bond** does not necessarily prevent the rental provider from seeking additional compensation."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' and links to 97-109aa115. Its only other source is the Regulations link 21-3sra009, which is version 009, the version in force on that date.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
### What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** (in force **13 October 2026**), a failure or breakdown of the water supply, or a burst water service, is an **urgent repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A renter **does not have to wait indefinitely** for the owner’s preferred tradespeople: the renter may arrange the repair if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to carry it out immediately, but have been unable to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The repair must be carried out by a **suitably qualified person** where the work requires relevant registration or licensing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

You can arrange a suitably qualified plumber yourself now, after keeping evidence that you contacted the emergency repair contact and that the owner’s tradespeople could not attend promptly. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

After the repair, give the rental provider **7 days’ written notice** stating what repairs were done and the cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider must reimburse the **reasonable cost**, or any lower prescribed amount, within **7 days** after receiving that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not state the prescribed amount.

If you cannot afford the repair, it costs more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay if you arrange it, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the provider or agent to carry out the urgent repair; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes — all three points are covered: water failure/burst service is an urgent repair; after reasonable steps the renter can arrange the repair and must be reimbursed the reasonable cost (or lower prescribed amount) within 7 days of written notice; and the hardest point, that the preferred-tradesperson policy cannot stop the repair, is covered by 'A renter does not have to wait indefinitely for the owner's preferred tradespeople: the renter may arrange the repair if they have taken reasonable steps...'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes — the answer says neither forbidden thing: it states the renter "does not have to wait indefinitely for the owner's preferred tradespeople" and that "the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, or any lower prescribed amount, within 7 days," which contradicts both failure conditions.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115' (link 97-109aa115), but it never names the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 or its version 009, and it even says the prescribed amount is not stated, so a required document is missing.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**, applies today. Its author is **Barbara Hargreaves**. The current **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, **Authorised Version No. 009**, incorporating amendments as at **30 June 2026**, were authored by **Lavina Mandy**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The Act also defines as **urgent repairs** a failure to meet rental minimum standards, and faults making the premises unsafe or insecure, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because you have not moved in, the key question is whether you have **“entered into possession”**. If you have not, section 91L allows you to give the rental provider a **notice of termination** if the premises are not in good repair, unfit for human habitation, unsafe, do not meet rental minimum standards, or are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not say whether merely collecting the keys means entering into possession.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask to terminate immediately.**  
   If you have not entered into possession, give written notice under section 91L, identifying the defects and relying on the premises not being in good repair and/or not meeting rental minimum standards. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Ask for any rent paid in advance and the bond to be returned; the retrieved documents do not state a specific refund procedure for this situation.

2. **Ask for repairs.**  
   Give written notice describing and photographing the damp, mould and rotting timber. The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, if repairs have not been done within **14 days** after written notice, you may apply to the Director for an investigation and may apply to VCAT for an order requiring specified repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT may order repairs by a suitably qualified person and compensation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Treat the problem as urgent if appropriate.**  
   Structural mould or damp, or a defect making the premises unsafe or insecure, is included in the Act’s definition of urgent repairs. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) After taking reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to act immediately, you may arrange urgent repairs if they do not act; the prescribed reimbursement limit in the retrieved documents is **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You may instead apply to VCAT if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask for lower rent—but do not reduce it yourself.**  
   The retrieved documents do **not** state an automatic right to a rent reduction merely because the premises have defects. They do provide for VCAT compensation and, after written repair notice and a failure to repair, an application to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Any lower rent should therefore be agreed in writing, or sought through an appropriate VCAT application; do not simply withhold or reduce rent without an order or agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Keep dated photographs, the condition report, the lease, key handover evidence and all communications. The prescribed condition-report form specifically recommends recording defects, taking dated photographs and giving the material to the rental provider or agent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing: the answer says the premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof and free from structural mould and damp, but never says the rental minimum standards must be met by the day the renter moves in (s 65A). The s 91L termination point and the urgent/good-repair route are covered.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## What the law says

The current document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Its definition of **urgent repairs** includes a burst water service, a blocked or broken lavatory, a dangerous electrical fault, a failure of the electricity or water supply, and damage making the premises unsafe or insecure. Plumbing and wiring damage from break-ins may therefore be urgent repairs, depending on the precise fault. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You must give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable** describing the damage. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair, and you must keep and leave them reasonably clean only **“as far as practicable”**; the Act recognises that the provider is responsible for the condition of the premises where applicable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Immediately write to the provider or agent.** Describe each break-in, the plumbing and wiring damage, any safety or security risk, and explain that you cannot properly clean until repairs make the premises safe and usable. Keep photographs, police or other incident records, receipts, and all communications. The Act permits the written notice to be given electronically. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Require urgent repairs.** Ask the provider or agent to arrange them immediately. If you have taken reasonable steps to arrange this but cannot get them to act, you may arrange urgent repairs yourself. You must then give **7 days’ written notice** of the repairs and their cost; the provider is liable to reimburse the reasonable cost, up to any prescribed limit, within **7 days** after receiving that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Apply to VCAT if necessary.** You may apply for an order requiring specified urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs exceed the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay if you arrange them. VCAT must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **If the repairs are treated as non-urgent,** give written notice and allow **14 days**. If they are not done, you may apply to the Director to investigate, or apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs; VCAT must hear that application within **7 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **Do not simply stop paying rent or assume you can leave without notice.** The Act provides a process for applying to VCAT to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account** after giving a repair notice, where the provider has failed to repair and has not demonstrated financial hardship. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

6. **Ask in writing for an agreed early end to the lease or written confirmation that cleaning will be assessed after the repairs.** The retrieved documents do not provide the full text of the statutory early-termination provisions. The current prescribed agreement says that rent-foregone compensation does not apply where the renter ends the agreement under section **91ZD** because the premises are **destroyed or unfit for habitation**, but these documents do not establish whether your premises meet that test or set out the required notice procedure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The current prescribed agreement also says professional cleaning cannot generally be required unless it is necessary to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) It does not, however, state a specific rule excusing all cleaning after burglary damage, so document the condition and ask the provider to confirm how the damage-related cleaning will be handled.

The answer never clearly states that a renter whose home is unfit for habitation or unsafe can end the lease by a notice of intention to vacate with an immediate termination date. It mentions s 91ZD only indirectly, saying 'these documents do not establish whether your premises meet that test or set out the required notice procedure', and it even warns against assuming 'you can leave without notice', so a reader could not tell that immediate termination is available.

The answer says neither: it places repair responsibility on the provider ("The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair"), presents self-arranged repairs only as a reimbursable option ("the provider is liable to reimburse the reasonable cost"), and raises leaving early through an agreed early end or section 91ZD where premises are "destroyed or unfit for habitation", warning only against leaving "without notice".
