question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, in force from 13 October 2026)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, in force from 30 June 2026)** , here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 🔹 Can the app charge you a card fee?
**No.** You should not be charged a surcharge to pay rent electronically. The law explicitly prohibits anyone other than an Authorised Deposit-taking Institution (ADI, i.e., a bank) from demanding or receiving a fee for any prescribed matter related to paying rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Additionally, it is illegal to charge a renter for the establishment or use of direct debit or any other electronic payment facility for rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🔹 Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**Yes, but in both cases charging you is likely unlawful:**
* **If the agent/property manager charges it:** They are breaking the law. The Act strictly prohibits residential rental providers and their agents from demanding any charge for the use of electronic payment facilities [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, they must always ensure that at least one rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank's standard account fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **If the app company charges it:** They are also breaking the law. Section 51A specifically carves out an exception for banks (ADIs), meaning third-party apps and service providers cannot charge fees for rent payments [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🔹 What you can do
1. **Use your fee-free option:** You are legally entitled to use a payment method that incurs no extra transaction fees, such as the manual bank transfer you mentioned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Check your agreement:** Any tenancy agreement term that requires you to pay rent via a method that adds extra costs is void .
3. **Request clarification in writing:** Ask your agent or the app provider to explain the fee, citing sections 42(4), 51(3)(b), and 51A of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v115) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Lodge a complaint:** If they insist on the fee or refuse to provide a genuinely fee-free electronic option, you can lodge a formal complaint with Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT for an order.

*(Note: Standard bank transaction fees that your own financial institution charges are permitted, but the landlord, agent, or app cannot pass on their own processing costs to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).)*

must-mention.reason: No. The second point is not covered correctly. The answer opens with 'Yes' (it matters who gets the fee), which contradicts the rule that it makes no difference whether the app or the agent collects it. It also says flatly 'You should not be charged a surcharge' and never mentions the exception for surcharges permitted under another law. Points 1 and 3 are covered: 'at least one rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank's standard account fees) is reasonably available to you', and the suggestions to use the fee-free option or go to Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the fee is allowed because a fee-free option exists or that the landlord or agent is exempt, instead stating "No. You should not be charged a surcharge to pay rent electronically" and "If the agent/property manager charges it: They are breaking the law."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, in force from 13 October 2026)' (link 97-109aa115) and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, in force from 30 June 2026)' (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version of either document.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force today (5 November 2026), here is your answer:

**Documents Applied:**
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, v009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, v115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### Do you have to pay for a professional cleaner?
**No.** Under the standard terms of your lease, an agent cannot blanket-require you to hire a professional cleaner unless:
1. Professional cleaning was actually carried out immediately before you moved in (and you were told about it); or
2. Professional cleaning is genuinely required to restore the carpets to the condition they were in at the start of your tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Since you have already cleaned them yourself and they are back to how they were when you moved in, you have met your legal obligation. The law focuses on the *condition* of the property, not mandating a specific cleaning method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If professional cleaning isn't actually needed to restore the starting condition, demanding a receipt is unlawful [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What helps show the carpets' condition?
To prove you've left the carpets in the required state, rely on these official tools:
* **The Condition Report:** This form records the state of floor coverings at the start of your tenancy. You must be given two copies (or one emailed) to complete within 5 business days of moving in, and the agent must complete a final version within 10 days of you leaving [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Dated Photos:** The condition report instructions explicitly advise taking photos of fixtures and fittings at both the start and end of the tenancy. You should attach these dated photos to the report, as they are highly useful in resolving disputes about the property's condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Fair Wear and Tear:** Normal wear and tear is not considered damage under Victorian law, so the carpets do not need to look brand new—just in the same state relative to expected use as when you arrived [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### If the agent still demands payment:
You can refuse to pay for professional cleaning you did not need. If the agent tries to claim this from your bond, they must provide evidence that does not conflict with your signed condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they cannot prove the carpets were dirtier than at move-in (accounting for fair wear and tear), VCAT would likely dismiss their claim [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered, and the hardest one, the s 63 duty, is conveyed by 'they are back to how they were when you moved in, you have met your legal obligation' together with 'Normal wear and tear is not considered damage... just in the same state relative to expected use as when you arrived'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay for professional cleaning because of the clause or the pet; it says the opposite: "**No.** Under the standard terms of your lease, an agent cannot blanket-require you to hire a professional cleaner unless..."

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
Based on the retrieved Victorian residential tenancy documents currently in force, here is what the law says about your situation:

### 🔹 What the Law Says About Cleaning & Bonds
Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, a rental provider is only entitled to claim cleaning costs from your bond if the premises were not left reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Specifically, they may claim the *reasonable cost of cleaning* any part of the premises, provided this is compared against the condition of the premises when you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

You have a legal duty to leave the rented premises **reasonably clean** and in the same condition as when you started your tenancy, accounting for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 🔹 Rules on Professional Cleaning
The **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** strictly limit when a provider can require professional cleaning. They cannot demand it unless:
* Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before your tenancy started (and you were told this), or
* It is necessary to restore the premises to their original condition, considering the condition report and fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

If professional cleaning *is* required under those conditions, the law states you must either have it done yourself or **pay the cost** of having it professionally cleaned [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🔹 Do You Have to Pay the Separate Invoice?
The retrieved documents **do not explicitly address** whether agreeing to a bond deduction for cleaning is legally equivalent to agreeing to pay a separate invoice. The law only outlines what can be claimed from the bond and the conditions under which cleaning costs may be charged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It does not state that an agreement to deduct from the bond automatically waives your right to dispute a subsequent invoice, nor does it confirm that the two are legally interchangeable.

### 🔹 What You Can Do or Ask
1. **Request Evidence:** Under the Act, a rental provider must give you bond claim evidence supporting any deduction at least 3 days before making the claim [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they issued an invoice instead of claiming from the bond, ask them to clarify the legal basis for that charge and provide proof of the cleaning costs.
2. **Check Your Condition Report:** Compare the agent's cleaning claims against the condition report from when you moved in. They can only charge for cleaning beyond fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Clarify the Agreement:** Ask the agent in writing whether your initial agreement was strictly for a *bond deduction* or if it explicitly included consent to pay a *separate invoice*. The documents do not define this distinction, so their own written terms will be key.
4. **Dispute if Unfair:** If you believe the invoice is unreasonable or duplicates a bond claim, you can raise a dispute with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) or apply to VCAT for a determination [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Note: The above information is drawn from the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, in force 13 October 2026) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, in force 30 June 2026). For binding advice on contract interpretation or invoice disputes, consult a Victorian tenancy advocacy service or legal aid.*

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**What the law says**
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a broken tap that forces you to shut off the water to the entire house is classified as an **"urgent repair"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner's policy of only using their own tradespeople does not override your statutory rights. You are **not required to wait** if they cannot attend immediately.

The law states that you may arrange for urgent repairs yourself if:
1. You have taken "reasonable steps" to get the residential rental provider (owner) or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately; and
2. They are unable or refuse to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**
You can hire a licensed plumber to fix the tap right away. To protect your right to reimbursement, follow these steps:
* **Arrange the repair:** Hire a suitably qualified person to carry out the urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Keep all receipts:** Retain detailed invoices showing the cost of labour and materials.
* **Notify the owner in writing:** You must give the owner written notice of the repairs carried out and the total cost within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Claim reimbursement:** The owner is legally liable to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs, up to a maximum prescribed amount of **$2,500** (including GST) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They must pay this reimbursement within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**If the owner refuses or the cost exceeds the limit**
* If the repair costs more than $2,500, or if the owner refuses to reimburse you, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring them to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT is required to hear your application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* You may also contact Consumer Affairs Victoria for guidance on enforcing urgent repair rights.

---
**Applicable Law & Authorised Versions:**
This answer applies the law in force today (5 November 2026) from:
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. **115**, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. **009**, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the broken tap that cuts off water to the whole house is called an 'urgent repair'; the answer states the reasonable-steps condition, the right to arrange the repair, and reimbursement of the reasonable cost up to the prescribed amount within 7 days of written notice; and the hardest point is covered by 'The owner's policy of only using their own tradespeople does not override your statutory rights. You are not required to wait.'

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on Victorian residential tenancy law currently in force today (5 November 2026), here are your options regarding the damp, mould, and rotting timber you discovered. The relevant laws applied are the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version v115) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version v009) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 1. Can you cancel?
**Yes.** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 explicitly provides for "Termination by renter before possession" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because damp, mould, and rotting timber are structural issues, the property likely breaches the mandatory rental minimum standards. Under the Regulations, rented premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can use these breaches as grounds to terminate the agreement before you officially move in.

### 2. Can you ask for repairs?
**Yes.** Your rental provider has a legal duty to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). To start this process:
* **Notify them immediately:** You must give written notice to the provider as soon as practicable about the damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **Urgent vs. Non-urgent:** If the damp or rotting timber poses an immediate health or safety risk (e.g., serious water ingress), it may be classified as an urgent repair, which the provider must fix immediately [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For non-urgent repairs, the provider must act within a reasonable time [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Escalation:** If they do not carry out non-urgent repairs within 14 days of your notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do the work [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 3. Can you ask for lower rent?
**You cannot unilaterally demand a rent reduction**, but you have a formal mechanism to pause or reduce your payments while repairs are pending:
* **Rent Special Account:** You can apply to VCAT for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a "Rent Special Account" instead of directly to the landlord [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **How it works:** VCAT will authorize this if they are satisfied that the provider has failed to comply with their repair duties or rental minimum standards, and that the provider cannot demonstrate financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The money sits in the account until the repairs are completed or VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Recommended next steps:**
1. Document the damp, mould, and rotting timber with photos/videos immediately.
2. Send a written notice to your agent/landlord highlighting the breach of rental minimum standards and requesting urgent repairs or termination before possession.
3. If they refuse to act, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or prepare an application to VCAT for termination or repair orders.

The termination-before-possession point and the good-repair route are covered.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version v115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says About Your Situation
- **Reporting damage:** The law requires you to give written notice to your residential rental provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the rented premises, including both the fact that it occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- **Maintenance duties:** Your landlord has a legal duty to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- **Uninhabitable premises:** If damage renders the property unsafe or unfit for human habitation, the law recognises this as a serious condition that affects your right to remain in the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do Before the Lease Ends
1. **Report the damage immediately**  
   Send written notice to your landlord/agent detailing the break-ins and the resulting plumbing and wiring damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This can be done via electronic communication (e.g., email) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

2. **Arrange urgent repairs yourself (if necessary)**  
   If your landlord does not act, you may arrange for urgent repairs if:
   - You have taken reasonable steps to get them to fix it immediately, and
   - They are unable or unwilling to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).  
   You must give your landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and costs. The landlord is legally required to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of these repairs within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

3. **Apply to the Tribunal if you cannot afford the repairs**  
   If the repair costs are too high for you to pay upfront, or if your landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring them to carry out the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear this application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

4. **Terminate the lease early if the property is uninhabitable**  
   If the plumbing and wiring damage makes the premises unfit for human habitation or unsafe, you may give your landlord a notice of intention to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can choose to make this termination date the day you give the notice, or pick a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: Because the damage was caused by burglars rather than you or your visitors, you are not responsible for repairing it. Your primary legal obligations here are reporting the issue promptly and following the urgent repair/termination procedures outlined above.)*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: written notice as soon as practicable (s 72AA); arranging urgent repairs and being reimbursed if the landlord is unable or unwilling to act (s 72); and, for the hardest point, 'you may give your landlord a notice of intention to vacate... You can choose to make this termination date the day you give the notice' (s 91ZD), which applies to the user's unexpired lease.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer states the opposite of both failure conditions, saying "you are not responsible for repairing it" and "you may give your landlord a notice of intention to vacate" if the premises are unfit or unsafe.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version v115 (in force from 13 October 2026)' with link 97-109aa115, and every rule it applies is cited to that in-force version, with no reliance on any other version.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the current Victorian residential tenancy laws:

**What the law says**
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, your rental provider or their agent has two main obligations regarding how you pay rent:
1. **A fee-free option must be available:** They must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank's standard fees) is reasonably available to you [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since your app offers a manual bank transfer with no fee, this requirement is met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Costs must be disclosed upfront:** Before you agree to use a specific payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you might incur, which explicitly includes "third party transaction fees" and other electronic payment facility fees [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Regarding whether the app can charge the fee: The law prohibits landlords and agents from charging you for the *establishment or use* of direct debit or other electronic payment facilities [Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, 30 Jun 2026)] [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). However, it explicitly acknowledges that third-party transaction fees (like card processing fees charged by an external app) may apply, provided they are disclosed beforehand [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Does it matter who receives the fee? The law places the legal responsibility on the **residential rental provider or their agent** to provide a free payment method and disclose any costs, regardless of whether a third-party app collects the fee [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If your agent is directly demanding or pocketing the card fee themselves, they are likely breaching the rule against charging for the use of electronic payment facilities [Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, 30 Jun 2026)] [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the fee goes to an independent app company as a processing charge, it is permissible only if you were informed of it before consenting to use that method [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**
- **Use the free option:** You are fully entitled to pay via the manual bank transfer without penalty. 
- **Ask for disclosure:** If you haven't already been told about the card fee, ask your agent in writing: *"Please confirm in writing what third-party transaction fees apply if I choose to pay by card, as required under section 42(7) of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997."* [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Check who is charging you:** If your agent is adding the fee directly to your rent invoice rather than it being a separate charge from the payment app itself, this may be an illegal charge for using an electronic payment facility [Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, 30 Jun 2026)] [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
- **Lodge a complaint:** If the provider or agent refuses to offer a fee-free method, fails to disclose third-party fees, or illegally charges you for using electronic payments, you can lodge a complaint with Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: This advice applies to the current law in force today.)*
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026)
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer misses the second point: it says third-party fees going to an independent app company are 'permissible only if you were informed of it before consenting' and that who collects the fee matters. This contradicts the rubric, which says such fees are banned for anyone other than a bank (s 51A with reg 21C), whether the app company or the agent collects them, unless the fee is a surcharge permitted under another law.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not say the fee is allowed simply because a fee-free option exists; it makes a third-party fee depend on prior disclosure ("it is permissible only if you were informed of it before consenting"). It also does not exempt the landlord or agent, saying "If your agent is directly demanding or pocketing the card fee themselves, they are likely breaching the rule against charging for the use of electronic payment facilities."

version-cited.reason: Yes - the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026)' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026)', and does not rely on any other version.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009)** and the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115)**, which are in force today, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian tenancy law, a rental provider **cannot** demand professional cleaning or a receipt from a professional cleaner unless it is actually necessary to restore the property to the condition it was in when you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The standard form agreement only permits a requirement for professional cleaning if:
* Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before your tenancy started and you were advised of this; **or**
* Professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their original condition, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Additionally, at the end of a tenancy, you are legally required to leave the rented premises "reasonably clean" and in the same condition as when you entered, accounting for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If your DIY cleaning has already returned the carpets to their original state (minus fair wear and tear), you have fulfilled this legal duty.

### What You Can Do or Ask
* **You do not have to pay for a professional cleaner** if the carpets are already back to how they were when you moved in. The agent's blanket demand for a receipt is unenforceable because the standard has already been met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Ask the agent to review your condition report and photos** as proof that the cleaning standard was satisfied, rather than insisting on a professional receipt. If they attempt to deduct money from your bond for this, you can formally dispute the claim using your move-in/move-out evidence [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What Helps Show the Carpets' Condition
To prove you left the carpets in the required condition, rely on these two documents:
1. **The Condition Report:** You are entitled to receive 2 copies (or 1 emailed copy) of a condition report on or before your move-in date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must fill yours out within 5 business days of moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This document records the state of the floor coverings at the start of your tenancy. At the end of the lease, the agent must complete the final inspection section within 10 days and allow for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Comparing your move-in report to the move-out report is the primary way to prove the carpets were left in the same condition.
2. **Dated Photos:** You should take photos at both the beginning and end of your tenancy showing the condition of the floor coverings [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The law advises taking close-up photos to show detail, as well as wider shots for perspective [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Ensure these photos are dated, labelled with the room/location, and attached to your copy of the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These visual records are explicitly noted as being useful in resolving disputes about the condition of the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. Reg 12 is stated as professional cleaning only where 'carried out immediately before your tenancy started and you were advised of this; or... required to restore the premises to their original condition... taking into account fair wear and tear.' The s 63 duty is stated as leaving the premises 'reasonably clean' and in the same condition, accounting for fair wear and tear. The entry condition report is identified as the record of 'the state of the floor coverings at the start of your tenancy.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes — the answer never says the renter must pay because of the clause or the pet; it says the opposite: "You do not have to pay for a professional cleaner if the carpets are already back to how they were when you moved in."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009)' and 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115)', and every citation links to those versions (21-3sra009, 97-109aa115) with no rule taken from any other version.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Applicable Law & Documents**
This answer applies the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, in force from 13 October 2026)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, in force from 30 June 2026)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says about the situation**
Under Victorian tenancy law, you have a duty to leave the rented premises reasonably clean . If you do not, a residential rental provider is entitled to claim the **reasonable cost of cleaning** from your bond, provided they consider the condition of the premises when you moved in and account for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

However, these claims must be processed through the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) using an approved claim form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Additionally, a provider cannot require you to arrange professional cleaning unless it was carried out immediately before your tenancy started or is strictly necessary to restore the premises to their original condition per the condition report and fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to pay the invoice? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?**
The provided documents **do not contain information** on whether you are legally required to pay a separate cleaning invoice after your full bond has been refunded. Furthermore, the documents **do not state** that agreeing to a bond deduction is legally equivalent to agreeing to pay a separate invoice. The retrieved legislation only governs how bonds are lodged and claimed via the RTBA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**
Because the provided documents do not address this specific contractual distinction, you should:
*   **Ask the agent for evidence:** Request a detailed invoice and proof that the cleaning costs were necessary because the premises were not left reasonably clean compared to the initial condition report.
*   **Clarify the agreement in writing:** Ask the agent whether your prior agreement was strictly limited to a bond claim through the RTBA, or if it explicitly included liability for a separate invoice. 
*   **Seek further advice:** Since the documents do not cover the legal equivalence of these two types of agreements, you may need to seek independent tenancy advice or apply to VCAT if the agent pursues the debt.

must-mention.reason: No: the first point is missing. The answer never says that agreeing to a bond deduction means agreeing only to a claim on the bond, not to a separate invoice. It says the documents 'do not state' the two are equivalent and suggests asking the agent whether the agreement 'explicitly included liability for a separate invoice', which is hedged so far that a reader cannot tell which way it falls. The second point is covered ('reasonably clean', judged against 'the condition of the premises when you moved in').

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither forbidden claim: it states that the documents "do not state that agreeing to a bond deduction is legally equivalent to agreeing to pay a separate invoice" and "do not contain information on whether you are legally required to pay a separate cleaning invoice after your full bond has been refunded," without saying the renter must pay or that the landlord can never claim more.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "v115, in force from 13 October 2026" with a link to 97-109aa115, and the only other document it relies on is the in-force Regulations version "v009, in force from 30 June 2026" (21-3sra009), so every version it uses is the one in force on that date.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version No. 115) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version No. 009) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), which are in force today, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says about the situation
A broken tap that forces you to turn off the water to the entire house qualifies as an **"urgent repair"** under Victorian tenancy law [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This falls under the legal definition of a failure or breakdown of the water supply to rented premises, or any appliance using/supplying water that results in wasted water [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner is legally required to carry out urgent repairs immediately upon being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They cannot force you to wait for their specific tradespeople if they are unavailable.

### What you can do or ask
You do **not** have to wait. You are legally permitted to arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix the issue yourself, provided you follow these steps:

1. **Take reasonable steps first:** Ensure you have already asked the owner or their agent to fix it immediately and they have not done so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Arrange the repair:** You can hire a licensed plumber/tradesperson to do the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
3. **Claim reimbursement:** The owner must reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs, up to a maximum of **$2,500** (or the actual reasonable cost if it is less) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Provide written notice:** You must give the owner written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost within **7 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner is then legally required to reimburse you within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Recommended next steps
* Get a quote from a licensed tradesperson immediately.
* Send a written message (email or text is acceptable) to the owner/agent stating: *"I have taken reasonable steps to get you to fix this urgent water issue, but you haven't done so. I am arranging for a tradesperson to fix it today. I will provide receipts and cost details within 7 days as required by law."*
* Keep all invoices and receipts to claim your reimbursement.

If the repair costs more than $2,500, or if the owner refuses to pay, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer calls a water-supply failure an 'urgent repair'; it says that after reasonable steps the renter can arrange the repair and 'the owner is then legally required to reimburse you within 7 days of receiving that notice', up to $2,500; and for the hardest point it says 'They cannot force you to wait for their specific tradespeople if they are unavailable', which is equivalent to the preferred-tradesperson policy not stopping an urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes — the answer says neither prohibited claim and in fact asserts the opposite: "They cannot force you to wait for their specific tradespeople if they are unavailable," "You do **not** have to wait," and "The owner must reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs, up to a maximum of **$2,500**."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 009)' (link 21-3sra009), both of which are the versions in force on that date, and it relies on no other version.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the Victorian laws currently in force today, your rights are governed by:
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version v009 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v115 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 1. Your Rights Regarding Damp, Mould, and Rotting Timber
Under the current regulations, rental premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, each room in the rented premises must be **free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The landlord also has a strict duty to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

### 2. Can you cancel?
**Yes.** Because you have not yet moved in, the Act provides a specific provision for **"Termination by renter before possession"** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since the property fails to meet the mandatory rental minimum standards (structural soundness and freedom from building-related damp/mould) and is not in a fit condition for occupation, you can terminate the agreement before taking possession.

### 3. Can you ask for repairs?
**Yes.** You must notify the landlord of the damage **in writing as soon as practicable** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- **Urgent Repairs:** If the damp, mould, or rotting timber poses an immediate health or safety risk, it qualifies as an urgent repair. The landlord must carry out these repairs immediately upon being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-Urgent Repairs:** For other maintenance issues, the landlord must complete them within a reasonable time. If they fail to do so within **14 days** of receiving your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the landlord to carry out the repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 4. Can you ask for lower rent?
You **cannot unilaterally reduce your rent** on your own. However, if the landlord fails to fix the issues, you have two legal avenues regarding rent:
- **Rent Special Account:** You can apply to VCAT to pay your rent into a "Rent Special Account" instead of paying the landlord directly while the repairs are pending [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- **Compensation:** If VCAT finds that the landlord breached their duty to maintain the premises, they can order the landlord to pay you compensation for the breach [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Document the damp, mould, and rotting timber with photos/videos.
2. Send a written notice to your landlord/agent detailing the issues and requesting repairs (or termination before possession).
3. If they refuse or delay, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT for urgent orders.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version v115, in force from 2026-10-13) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation and what you can do:

### What the Law Says About Your Situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, a residential rental provider has a duty to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Crucially, the law distinguishes between damage caused by tenants and damage caused by third parties. A landlord is only entitled to issue a notice to vacate for serious damage if *you* or your visitor intentionally or recklessly caused it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because the damage was caused by burglars during break-ins, this provision does not apply against you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do Before Your Lease Ends
You have three primary legal options to address the damage and protect your tenancy:

**1. Report the Damage Immediately**
You are legally required to notify your landlord as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage or breakdown of facilities, fixtures, furniture, or equipment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This written notice must clearly state both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature . 

**2. Get Urgent Repairs Done (Plumbing & Wiring)**
Damaged plumbing and wiring likely qualify as urgent repairs. You have two pathways to get them fixed:
* **Arrange the repairs yourself:** If you have taken reasonable steps to get your landlord or their agent to immediately carry out the repairs but are unable to get them to do so, you may arrange for urgent repairs yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give your landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord is liable to reimburse you for the reasonable cost (up to a prescribed amount) within 7 days after receiving your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Apply to the Tribunal:** If you cannot meet the cost of the repairs, if the repairs cost more than the prescribed amount, or if your landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring them to carry out the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear this application within 2 business days after it is made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Terminate the Lease Early (If the Property is Uninhabitable)**
If the damage from the break-ins is severe enough that your home is no longer safe or livable, you can end the lease early without penalty:
* Under section 91ZD, if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be "rendered unsafe," you may give your landlord a notice of intention to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* This notice can specify a termination date that is the same day you give it, or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* Terminating under this section means you are not liable to pay any form of lease break fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Note: While the retrieved documents outline your rights to report damage, claim urgent repair costs, and terminate the lease if the property is unsafe, they do not explicitly detail the process for claiming compensation from burglars' insurance or bond adjustments for third-party criminal damage. You may wish to consult Consumer Affairs Victoria or a legal aid service for guidance on those specific financial recovery steps.*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. Damage must be reported 'as soon as practicable' by 'written notice'. Plumbing and wiring are treated as urgent repairs ('likely qualify', which still leans clearly yes); the renter can arrange the repairs if the landlord won't act immediately, and the landlord must reimburse. For the hardest point, the answer says that if the premises are 'unfit for human habitation' or 'rendered unsafe', the renter may give a notice of intention to vacate with 'a termination date that is the same day you give it' and can 'end the lease early without penalty', which covers fixed-term leases.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not make the renter liable for repairs, saying instead that 'a residential rental provider has a duty to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair' and that the landlord 'is liable to reimburse you', and it does not bind the renter to stay, saying 'you can end the lease early without penalty' if the premises are unfit or unsafe.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version No. 115, in force today) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Can the app charge you a card fee?
**Yes, provided a fee-free alternative is available.** 
Under section 42(4) of the Act, your rental provider or agent **must ensure that at least one rent payment method that incurs no additional costs** (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since you already have a manual bank transfer option with no fee, this legal requirement is satisfied.

The law explicitly contemplates third-party apps charging transaction fees. Section 42(7) actually requires your provider or agent to disclose any costs you might incur—including **"third party transaction fees"**—before you agree to use that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who receives the fee (the app vs. the agent)?
**Yes, it matters legally.** 
The law draws a clear line between third-party fees and fees charged directly by the rental provider or their agent:
* **Third-party app fees:** Fees charged by an external payment processor are permitted, provided a fee-free alternative is available and you are informed of the cost beforehand [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Fees charged by the provider/agent:** Under section 51(3)(b) of the Act, a rental provider or their agent is strictly prohibited from demanding or receiving any charge for the establishment or use of direct debit or other electronic payment facilities themselves [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

**In summary:** Because you have a fee-free bank transfer option available, the app's card fee is legal. The fact that the fee goes to the third-party app (rather than the agent) is exactly why it is permitted: the law bans agents from charging these fees directly, but allows them to pass through or accept third-party transaction costs as long as they give you a free alternative and tell you about the cost upfront [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

It fails the second point because it states the opposite of the rubric. It says 'Yes, it matters legally' and that third-party app fees 'are permitted,' instead of saying that rent-payment fees are banned for anyone other than a bank (s 51A with reg 21C), whoever collects them. It also gives no next step, such as using the fee-free method, asking for a refund, or contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 009)**, which are in force today:

### Do you have to pay for a professional cleaner?
**No, not automatically.** Under Victorian law, a rental provider cannot require you to professionally clean your carpets (or pay for it) unless that cleaning is actually necessary to restore the carpets to the exact condition they were in when you moved in, after accounting for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

If your lease contains a blanket clause demanding professional cleaning regardless of the actual state of the carpets, that specific term may be invalid. The law prohibits tenancy agreements from including terms that require professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy unless it is contained within the standard form agreement and is strictly tied to restoring the premises to their initial condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Since you have cleaned the carpets yourself and they are back to how they were when you moved in (minus any fair wear and tear), professional cleaning has not become "required" under the law. You only have a legal duty to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you entered, accounting for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What helps show the carpets' condition?
To prove you have met your obligation and protect your bond, you should rely on the following evidence:
* **The Condition Report:** You are entitled to a condition report at the start of your tenancy, which records the state of all fixtures and fittings (including floor coverings) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Compare the agent's final assessment against your signed copy of this report. 
* **Dated Photos:** The law explicitly advises renters to take photos at both the beginning and the end of the tenancy to show the condition of items and fixtures [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Dated, close-up, and wide-angle photos of the carpets are highly effective evidence in any dispute.
* **Fair Wear and Tear:** Remember that "fair wear and tear" does not count as damage or dirt you are responsible for [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the carpets have naturally faded or worn over time, the agent cannot charge you to restore them to a pristine, move-in condition.

If the agent still tries to claim from your bond for professional cleaning despite the carpets being clean and matching the initial condition report, they must provide evidence that does not conflict with your signed condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can dispute this through the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) or apply to VCAT if necessary.

It omits the alternative that professional cleaning can be required if the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy and the renter was told. It also misstates the rule as tied to the 'standard form agreement'. The s 63 duty and the condition report/photos points are covered.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a broken tap or water leak is classified as an **urgent repair** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The law states that if a renter has taken reasonable steps to get the owner or their agent to immediately carry out urgent repairs, but is unable to get them to do so, the renter is legally permitted to arrange for those repairs themselves [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Because you cannot wait for the owner's tradespeople, here is what you can do and ask for:
*   **Arrange the repair yourself:** You can hire a suitably qualified plumber immediately. The owner's policy of only using their own tradespeople does not override your right to arrange urgent repairs if they are unavailable to act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   **Get reimbursed up to $2,500:** You may be reimbursed by the owner for the reasonable cost of the repairs, capped at **$2,500** (including GST) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Provide written notice:** After the repair is done, you must give the owner written notice within 7 days detailing the work completed and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   **Demand payment:** Once you provide this notice, the owner must reimburse you for the reasonable cost (up to the $2,500 limit) within 7 days of receiving your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If the repair costs more than $2,500 or if you cannot afford to pay upfront, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out the repairs directly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Applicable laws (in force today):*
*   *Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version v115) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)*
*   *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v009) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer says a broken tap or water leak is an urgent repair; it says that after reasonable steps the renter can arrange the repair and the owner must reimburse the reasonable cost (up to $2,500) within 7 days of written notice; and it says 'The owner's policy of only using their own tradespeople does not override your right to arrange urgent repairs if they are unavailable to act.'

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force today (5 November 2026), here is how your situation is handled and what options you have:

**The Law on Your Situation**
Under the current law, rental premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The rental provider has a strict duty to ensure the premises comply with these minimum standards, are vacant and reasonably clean when you move in, and are maintained in good repair and a fit condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Your Options**
*Can I cancel?*
Yes. The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* provides a specific pathway for "Termination by renter before possession" under Section 91L if the premises do not meet minimum standards or are unfit for habitation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You should photograph the damp, mould, and rotting timber immediately and notify your provider in writing that you cannot take possession due to these breaches.

*Can I ask for repairs?*
Yes. You must notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable about the damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- If the issues are classified as **urgent repairs** (e.g., structural failures or safety hazards), the provider must carry them out immediately upon notification [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- For **non-urgent repairs**, if the provider does not act within 14 days of receiving your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to complete the work [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Can I ask for lower rent?*
You cannot unilaterally reduce your rent. However, if the provider fails to fix the issues, you can apply to VCAT for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a **Rent Special Account** instead of directly to the provider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will only grant this if satisfied the provider has breached their maintenance duties and cannot demonstrate financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Additionally, VCAT can order the provider to pay you compensation for any losses suffered [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version 009) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version 115) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

It cites s 91L 'Termination by renter before possession' for premises that do not meet minimum standards or are unfit for habitation. For repairs, it describes urgent repairs and the good-repair maintenance duty, including the 14-day VCAT route for non-urgent repairs.
