The Act is given as "Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026" (link 97-109aa115). The Regulations are given as "version 009, in force from 30 June 2026" (file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, link 21-3sra009). Every rule it applies is sourced only from these versions.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Document used:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I found no later version in the documents retrieved.

## What the law says

- **Your duty:** At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning and the bond:** A residential rental provider can claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean". The test is the condition of the premises when the tenancy started [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider includes its agent for bond purposes [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Claiming beyond the bond:** A person who has recovered compensation from a bond can still take proceedings under Part 5 to recover an additional amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Part 5 proceedings are applications to the Tribunal (VCAT). The Tribunal can order compensation if it is satisfied that compensation should be paid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Money already recovered:** When it hears these applications, the Tribunal may consider whether money has already been paid or recovered, including from the bond [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Do you have to pay the invoice?

The Act has no provision making an agent's invoice payable on its own. The documents don't say that an agreement to a bond deduction is also an agreement to pay a separate invoice. The Act treats the two as separate routes:

- A bond claim is made to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority on an approved form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Anything beyond the bond is a compensation claim, and the Tribunal decides it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Your agreement was to a deduction from the bond. The full bond was returned, so nothing was actually taken for cleaning. Whether you owe anything depends on whether the premises weren't left reasonably clean and what the reasonable cost is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't tell that from the documents.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the evidence.** Before a bond claim, the provider or agent must give you "bond claim evidence" at least 3 days earlier. That means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph or other prescribed evidence, and it must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the condition report.** Compare the cleaning charge with the condition report. A report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition on the day it specifies, with some exceptions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check for a professional-cleaning term.** A term requiring you to pay for professional cleaning is prohibited unless it is in the standard form. The standard form allows it only where professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Dispute it.** Either party can apply to the Tribunal where there is a dispute under the agreement or a breach of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal's general monetary limit is $40,000 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Gaps in the documents

- They don't say whether your agreement to the deduction is binding as a contract or can be relied on to support the invoice.
- I didn't find a time limit for the agent to bring a cleaning compensation claim.
- Check the agent's claim against your agreement and the condition report, and consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT before paying.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the first, the answer says 'The Act treats the two as separate routes' and 'Your agreement was to a deduction from the bond', which separates a bond claim from a separate invoice. On the second, it says 'Whether you owe anything depends on whether the premises weren't left reasonably clean' and 'The test is the condition of the premises when the tenancy started'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not say the renter must pay because they agreed to a deduction, and it does not say the full bond return bars any further claim. Instead it says "Whether you owe anything depends on whether the premises weren't left reasonably clean and what the reasonable cost is" and that "Anything beyond the bond is a compensation claim, and the Tribunal decides it."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), and every rule it applies is cited to that in-force version, with no reliance on any other version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely. The Act lets a renter arrange urgent repairs once the rental provider hasn't acted. You must first make reasonable efforts to get them done, and the details below matter.

I relied on two documents:
- **rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf** is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997. Its file name and metadata label it version 115, in force from 13 October 2026. This is the latest version in the documents. I couldn't see the words "Authorised Version" in the extracts, so I'm quoting the version number as labelled. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf** is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What the law says

- **Is it "urgent"?** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes a burst water service. It also includes a failure or breakdown of the water supply to rented premises. It also covers a water-using appliance, fitting or fixture that is malfunctioning in a way that wastes a substantial amount of water. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A broken tap that forced you to shut off water to the whole house plausibly fits one of these, but the documents don't say whether a broken tap alone qualifies.
- **When you can arrange the repair yourself.** You may do so if you have (a) taken reasonable steps to have the rental provider or their agent carry out the repairs immediately, and (b) been unable to get them to do it (s 72(1)). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Owner's own tradespeople.** The documents don't say a rental provider can insist on using only their own tradespeople. The test in s 72(1) is whether the provider or agent actually gets the repair done. If their tradespeople can't come, you've reported it, and the water stays off, you appear to meet that test. This is my reading of the text, not an express rule in the documents.
- **Who does the work.** The standard rental agreement says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or not. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The Act defines "suitably qualified person" to include a tradesperson registered or licensed for the work, where the work requires it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) So use a licensed plumber rather than doing it yourself.

## What you can do

1. **Report it and ask for an immediate fix.** Contact the emergency contact named in your agreement. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Keep a record, such as email or text, of your attempts and their answers. The Act also requires written notice of damage or breakdown as soon as practicable (s 72AA). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. **If they can't fix it promptly, arrange a licensed plumber.**
3. **Give written notice.** Tell the provider about the repairs and the cost, with 7 days' written notice (s 72(2)(a)). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. **Get reimbursed.** The provider is liable for the reasonable cost of the repairs, or the prescribed amount if that is greater, whichever is less. They must pay within 7 days of receiving written notice of the repairs and the cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard-form summary says reimbursement is for reasonable costs up to $2500. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) I haven't seen the regulation that sets the prescribed amount, so treat $2500 as the figure stated in the form.
5. **If they don't pay or you can't afford it:**
   - You can apply to VCAT for an order that the provider carry out urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is above the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear that application within 2 business days (s 73). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
   - If you've paid and haven't been reimbursed within 7 days of giving notice, you can apply to VCAT for a compensation or compliance order (s 209AAB). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Limit:** The urgent-repairs right doesn't apply to fixtures, furniture or equipment that you supplied yourself (s 72(4)). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Not covered:** The documents don't tell me whether your tap breakage meets the definition on its facts, or what any clause in your own agreement says about repairers. For those, check your agreement or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: Yes (pass). The answer covers all three points. It states that burst water services and water supply failure are urgent repairs. It sets out s 72(1)'s reasonable-steps test and reimbursement of reasonable costs, capped at the prescribed amount, within 7 days of written notice. For the hardest point, it says the policy cannot block the repair: 'If their tradespeople can't come, you've reported it, and the water stays off, you appear to meet that test.' That is hedged and does not cite reg 11(e), but a reader can still tell which way it falls.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither: it tells the renter "You don't have to wait indefinitely" and "The documents don't say a rental provider can insist on using only their own tradespeople", and on cost it says "The provider is liable for the reasonable cost of the repairs" and explains how to seek reimbursement, including through VCAT.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' ('version 115, in force from 13 October 2026', link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf' ('version 009', link 21-3sra009), and every rule it applies is sourced only from these in-force versions.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Document relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf") [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is the version in force today (6 November 2026). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The regulations excerpt doesn't print an "Authorised Version" number, so 009 comes from the file's metadata.

## What the law says

- **Damp, mould and structure are covered by the rental minimum standards.** Premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The provider must meet those standards by move-in.** A rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the prescribed standards on or before the day the renter enters occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The general repair duty applies too.** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. This applies even if the renter knew of the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Some of this counts as "urgent repairs".** The definition includes a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards. It also includes a fault that makes the premises unsafe, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your options

**1. Cancel the agreement**
- If you haven't entered into possession, the agreement terminates once you give the provider a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or do not meet any rental minimum standards [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The documents don't say whether collecting the keys counts as "entering into possession". Check that point before relying on this route.
- If you are treated as already in possession, you can give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation. The termination date can be the day you give the notice or later [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Whether mould and rotting timber make a particular house "unfit for human habitation" is not defined in the retrieved text.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- You can issue a request for urgent repairs to bring the premises up to the standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If the provider doesn't act:** you may arrange urgent repairs yourself once you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and couldn't. Give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The reimbursement is capped at the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less. The agreement form states the figure as $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **VCAT (the Tribunal) for urgent repairs:** apply if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear it within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** give written notice. If nothing is done within 14 days, you can ask the Director to investigate or apply to the Tribunal, which must hear the application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal orders:** it can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, plus compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent Special Account:** after giving a repair notice, you can ask the Tribunal to let you pay rent into this account if the provider hasn't done the repairs. It must grant this unless the provider shows financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Record the defects:** the provider must give you a condition report before you move in. If you weren't given one, you can complete your own within 5 business days after entering occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A condition report given to the provider counts as notice of the defects listed in it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Lower rent**
- The retrieved Act doesn't give a right to unilaterally cut your rent for these defects.
- **The rent-free right doesn't fit your facts.** The provision that stops rent running before you move in applies only where the premises are not vacant or not reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't mention damp or mould.
- **Compensation route:** you can give a breach of duty notice. If it isn't complied with, you can apply to the Tribunal for a compensation or compliance order [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A compensation order may take the form of a refund or reduction of rent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal can also consider whether any rent reduction or refund has already been made [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered:** the retrieved text doesn't give the "required time" for a breach of duty notice, so I haven't stated one. This is a summary of the documents, not legal advice.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer says each room must be 'free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure' and that the provider must meet the standards 'on or before the day the renter enters occupation'. (2) It says 'If you haven't entered into possession, the agreement terminates once you give the provider a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or do not meet any rental minimum standards'. The note that the documents don't say whether collecting the keys counts as possession only concerns how the rule applies to these facts, so it does not hedge the rule itself. (3) It says 'You can issue a request for urgent repairs to bring the premises up to the standards' and also states the good-repair duty.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must move in and pay rent first, and on rent it states "The retrieved Act doesn't give a right to unilaterally cut your rent for these defects", mentioning a reduction only as a possible form of a Tribunal "compensation order", which the rubric allows.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' and the Regulations as 'rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf', version 009, and every citation links to an in-force version (97-109aa115 or 21-3sra009), with no rule drawn from any other version.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
## Source used
I used the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file title "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026. Its metadata gives the version as **115**. I also used the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file title "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026, version **009**. The metadata doesn't use the phrase "Authorised Version", so I'm giving the version numbers as they appear.

## What the law says

- **Reporting damage:** A renter must give the rental provider written notice of damage as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** At the end of the agreement the renter must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable", and in the same condition as at move-in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because the test is "as far as practicable", damaged plumbing and wiring are relevant to what you can reasonably do.
- **Damage you cause:** A renter and their visitors must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say who is responsible for damage done by third-party burglars. I can't answer that from them.
- **Repairs:** The provider must keep the premises in good repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). "Urgent repairs" include a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, failure of the gas, electricity or water supply, and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Damage from a break-in could fit these categories, depending on the facts.

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Notify the provider or agent in writing now**, describing the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Include the break-ins and the plumbing and wiring damage.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** If you've taken reasonable steps to get the provider or agent to act immediately and they don't, you may arrange the urgent repairs yourselves [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The regulations' form of agreement states the direct reimbursement limit as $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT (the Tribunal) for urgent repairs** if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount ($2,500 per the form), or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **For non-urgent repairs:** Give written notice. If the provider hasn't acted within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate or to the Tribunal for an order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear a non-urgent repairs application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can also order rent to be paid into the Rent Special Account if repairs aren't done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Consider ending the lease early.** A renter may give a written, signed notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation or have been destroyed totally or to an extent that makes them unsafe [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The termination date can be the day you give the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Without this ground, a notice under the general 28-day provision is of no effect on a fixed-term agreement if its termination date is before the end of the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - For fixed-term agreements of more than 5 years, the standard form says no "rent foregone" is payable when the renter ends the agreement on this ground [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - The documents don't define "unfit for human habitation". I can't say whether your premises meet that test.
6. **Agree an early end with the provider.** The agreement can be terminated by agreement of both parties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Not covered
The documents don't say who is liable for the burglars' damage, how it affects your bond, or any insurance or police-report steps. I haven't answered those.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: written notice of damage as soon as practicable; urgent repairs (burst water service, dangerous electrical fault) that the renter may arrange and have reimbursed within 7 days if the provider doesn't act immediately; and early termination for unfit or unsafe premises, where 'the termination date can be the day you give the notice or later' and the answer contrasts this with the general 28-day rule for fixed terms. The hardest point is the urgent-repairs one, hedged as 'could fit these categories, depending on the facts', but it is still clear because the answer directly advises asking for urgent repairs.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer does not make the renter liable for the burglary damage, saying "The documents don't say who is responsible for damage done by third-party burglars," and it does not bind the renter to stay, noting "A renter may give a written, signed notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115" (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", links 97-109aa115), and the only other document it relies on is the in-force Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 "version 009" (links 21-3sra009), with no rules drawn from any other version.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Documents used:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, dated 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions I retrieved, and both are dated before today (6 November 2026). I can't confirm from the documents that no later version exists.

## What the law says

- **Card fee:** The Act says "a person, other than an ADI" must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent (s 51A). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Prescribed matters:** The Regulations prescribe "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" and "failed payments". This has applied since 31 March 2026 (reg 21C) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Electronic payment facilities:** A separate rule says a person must not demand or receive a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" (s 51(3)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Free option:** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than the renter's own bank or account fees, is reasonably available (s 42(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The free bank transfer helps the agent meet that duty. However, the documents don't say that having a free option makes a card fee lawful. Section 51A is a separate prohibition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Disclosure:** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs, including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees, before you consent to a payment method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

On the text, not much. Sections 51(3) and 51A apply to "a person", not just the agent or rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So a fee going to the app company is not automatically outside them.

Two things could change the outcome:
- **Who receives it:** Section 51A excludes an "ADI" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't define that term, so I can't say whether the app company or a payment processor qualifies.
- **Surcharge exception:** The regulation excepts "payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't name that Act or say whether your app's card fee qualifies.

So the documents don't settle whether your app's fee is lawful. The general rule points towards it being prohibited, subject to those two exceptions.

## What you can do

- **Use the free bank transfer.** The documents say nothing that makes you pay a fee for the faster option.
- **Ask the agent or provider in writing** for the fee amount, who receives it, and the legal basis for charging it. They must disclose rent payment costs before you consent (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cite ss 51(3)(b) and 51A and reg 21C** if you want the fee removed or refunded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your rental agreement.** The standard form notes that the provider "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say how to make a complaint or claim a refund, so I can't give those steps.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer states the provider or agent must make reasonably available a rent payment method with no additional costs other than the renter's own bank fees (s 42(4)). (2) For the hardest point, it says ss 51(3) and 51A apply to "a person", not just the agent, so the app company is not outside them, and that "the general rule points towards it being prohibited, subject to those two exceptions" (the ADI exclusion and permitted surcharges under reg 21C). Its uncertainty about the term ADI does not leave the direction unclear. (3) It gives next steps: use the free bank transfer, and cite ss 51(3)(b), 51A and reg 21C to have the fee removed or refunded.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer rejects the free-option justification ('the documents don't say that having a free option makes a card fee lawful') and does not exempt the landlord or agent, saying ss 51(3) and 51A 'apply to "a person", not just the agent or rental provider.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 009, dated 30 June 2026" (link 21-3sra009), and every rule it applies (s 42(4), s 42(7), s 51(3)(b), s 51A and reg 21C) comes from those in-force versions.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions in the retrieved set, so I've applied them as the law today (6 November 2026). The files give version numbers but I didn't see an "Authorised Version No." label in the text I retrieved. I haven't seen your lease, so this assumes your pet clause is an extra term added to the standard form.

## What the law says

- **Extra professional-cleaning terms are prohibited.** A rental agreement must not include a term requiring the premises to be professionally cleaned at the end of the tenancy, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard-form rule is narrower.** The rental provider must not require professional cleaning unless one of two things applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  - (a) Professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy started, and you were told so.
  - (b) Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to the same condition as at the start, having regard to the condition report and allowing for fair wear and tear.
- **You only have to pay if cleaning is actually needed.** You must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if cleaning becomes required to restore them to their starting condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The general duty is about condition, not receipts.** At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

So an automatic "professional clean" pet clause is likely void [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Even under the standard-form rule, you wouldn't have to pay for a professional clean if the carpets are already back to their starting condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent to point to the legal basis.** Ask whether professional cleaning was done before you moved in and you were told, or whether the condition report shows the carpets need it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved don't say a receipt is required where a renter has cleaned themselves.
2. **Use the condition report.** A condition report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition on the day it states. This doesn't apply to statements where you wrote a disagreement on your copy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The report lists floor coverings and records whether each item is clean and undamaged [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Get the final inspection done properly.** The agent must complete the end-of-tenancy condition report within 10 days after the tenancy ends. They must do it in your presence or give you a reasonable chance to attend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Take photos.** The prescribed condition report form says photos should be taken at the start and end of the tenancy. They should be dated and labelled, with close-ups and wider shots, and should show the room or location [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Compare them with any photos attached to your move-in report.
5. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** A renter can ask the Tribunal to declare a term invalid or vary it. The Tribunal can do this if the term is harsh or unconscionable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act also notes that the Tribunal can declare terms invalid under sections 28 and 472 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover how bond disputes are handled in practice, so I can't say more on that.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers all three points: reg 12's two conditions ('Professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy started, and you were told so' or 'needed to restore the premises to the same condition as at the start... allowing for fair wear and tear'), the s 63 duty to 'leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear', and the condition report as evidence ('A condition report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition on the day it states')

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay simply because of the clause or the pet. It says the opposite: an automatic "professional clean" pet clause is "likely void", and "you wouldn't have to pay for a professional clean if the carpets are already back to their starting condition."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009' (link 21-3sra009). Every rule it applies is cited only to these versions.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Source:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the latest version in the documents I retrieved, so I treated it as the version in force today (6 November 2026).

## What the law says

- **Cleaning duty.** At the end of the agreement, a renter must leave the premises reasonably clean, as far as practicable. They must also leave them in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claims.** A provider can claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean", judged against the condition at the start of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence.** A provider claiming the bond must give the renter "bond claim evidence" at least 3 days before the claim is made. That evidence can include an invoice, receipt, quote or photograph, and it must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claims don't cap the provider.** Someone who has recovered compensation from a bond can still bring proceedings under the same Part for an additional amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The Tribunal decides disputes.** If compensation is claimed, the Tribunal can order it paid. It considers, among other things, whether money has already been recovered from the bond and whether the claimant tried to limit the loss [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning terms.** An agreement must not require the renter to pay for professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless that term is in the standard form. Any such term is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?

The documents don't say. I found nothing in the Act that treats agreeing to a deduction from the bond as agreeing to pay a separate invoice. I also found nothing saying it isn't. The Act deals with agreed bond claims only through the bond claim form. The provider must not get your signature on a claim form that doesn't state the amount of bond to be refunded and how it is apportioned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether what you agreed amounts to a binding promise to pay more is not answered in the retrieved text.

## Do you have to pay the invoice?

The documents don't give a yes or no. Nothing I found makes the invoice automatically payable. Your liability depends on whether the cleaning cost is reasonable and whether the premises really weren't left reasonably clean compared with the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Ask for evidence.** Request the invoice, photos and the condition report. Compare them with the condition at move-in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your agreement.** If it makes you pay for professional cleaning and isn't a term in the standard form, that term is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check what you signed.** Look at what you agreed to and whether it named an amount. The claim form must state the amount of bond to be refunded and the apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Dispute it in writing** if you think the cleaning wasn't needed or the cost is unreasonable. If the agent pursues it, the Tribunal decides any compensation claim [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't state a time limit for the agent to bring a compensation claim for cleaning. They also don't say whether a verbal or written deduction agreement changes your position. For those points, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer misses the first point. It hedges on whether agreeing to a bond deduction is agreeing to pay an invoice, saying "The documents don't say... I also found nothing saying it isn't" and "Whether what you agreed amounts to a binding promise to pay more is not answered," so a reader cannot tell that it is agreement to a bond claim only. The second point, the reasonably-clean test judged against the start-of-tenancy condition, is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must pay because they agreed to a deduction ("Nothing I found makes the invoice automatically payable"), and it never says full bond repayment bars further claims, instead noting "Someone who has recovered compensation from a bond can still bring proceedings under the same Part for an additional amount."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on that date, and every rule it applies comes from that version.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Version relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026. The file name and metadata give it as version 115 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The excerpts I retrieved don't contain the words "Authorised Version". The version number comes from the file name and metadata only.

## What the law says

- **Urgent repairs:** The Act's definition includes a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply to the premises, and a water-using fitting or fixture provided by the rental provider that is malfunctioning so that a substantial amount of water is wasted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether your tap falls within these depends on the facts. The documents don't address a broken tap specifically.
- **You don't have to wait indefinitely.** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if both of these are true [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  1. You have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately.
  2. You are unable to get them to do it.
- **The owner's preference for their own tradespeople doesn't change this.** The test in the Act is whether you could get the provider or agent to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how long you must wait before the test is met. If the contact says nobody can come yet, that is a strong basis for saying you were unable to get the repairs done. Keep a record of what you were told.
- **Who may do the work:** The standard-form agreement says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or not [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says a suitably qualified person includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So hire a licensed plumber rather than fixing it yourself.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify in writing now.** Give written notice of the damage or breakdown as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can take it into account if you don't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Document your attempts.** Record when you contacted the emergency contact, what they said, and that no one could attend.
3. **Arrange a licensed plumber** if the provider's tradespeople still can't come [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Claim reimbursement.** The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if that is greater, whichever is less. This includes GST. Payment is due within 7 days of receiving your written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard-form agreement summary states the figure as up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I haven't seen the regulation that sets the prescribed amount, so check your own agreement.
6. **If they don't pay or you can't afford it:**
   - You can apply to VCAT for an order that the provider carry out the urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - If the provider hasn't reimbursed you within 7 days of your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

I haven't found anything in the documents on your obligations to the plumber beyond the points above. For a specific dispute, the Consumer Affairs Victoria urgent repairs guidance is the usual next step, but it isn't in the documents I retrieved.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer says the urgent-repair definition includes "a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply to the premises". It explains that after reasonable steps the renter may arrange a licensed plumber and must be reimbursed the reasonable cost, capped at the prescribed amount ("up to $2500"), within 7 days of written notice. The hardest point is covered by "The owner's preference for their own tradespeople doesn't change this. The test in the Act is whether you could get the provider or agent to carry out the repairs."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states "You don't have to wait indefinitely" and "The owner's preference for their own tradespeople doesn't change this," and it says "The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost," so it affirms the renter can arrange the repair and recover the cost.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Sources:** The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The excerpts I retrieved don't print an "Authorised Version No." for the Regulations, so I can only give the version from the file metadata.

## What the law says

- **Condition of the premises.** The provider must ensure the premises are "provided and maintained" in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. This applies even if the renter knew of the disrepair before moving in (s 68(1), (1A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum standards.** The premises must meet the rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter (s 65A(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Those standards require the premises to be "structurally sound and weatherproof". They also require each room to be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Vacant and clean.** The provider must also ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed day. If they aren't, you aren't required to enter, and you don't pay rent from the agreed day until you actually enter (s 65(1)–(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This only covers vacancy and cleanliness, so it doesn't clearly cover damp, mould or rot.

## Your options

**1. Cancel before moving in.** An agreement ends if the renter has not entered into possession and gives notice of termination on the ground that the premises are:
- not in good repair;
- unfit for human habitation;
- not meeting any rental minimum standards; or
- for any other reason unavailable for occupation (s 91L) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved text doesn't say whether collecting the keys counts as "entering into possession". Check that point before relying on s 91L.

**2. Cancel after moving in.** You can give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or destroyed or unsafe. The termination date can be the date of the notice or later (s 91ZD) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Otherwise, a general notice must give at least 28 days (s 91Z), and on a fixed-term agreement it has no effect if the termination date is before the end of the term (s 91ZA(1)(b)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for repairs.**
- **Urgent repairs.** These include "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure", any fault making the premises unsafe, and any failure to comply with rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the premises don't comply on or just after the day you enter, you can request urgent repairs (s 65A(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Doing the repairs yourself.** If you've taken reasonable steps to get the provider to act and can't, you may arrange urgent repairs. You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the provider must reimburse you within 7 days (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Form 1 standard agreement states reimbursement of up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **VCAT for urgent repairs.** You can apply if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear it within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs.** Give written notice (s 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) or to VCAT (s 75). VCAT must hear a s 75 application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **VCAT orders.** VCAT can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, within a set time, plus compensation under s 212(2) (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The text of s 212 wasn't retrieved, so I can't say how compensation works.

**4. Lower rent.** The retrieved provisions give no right to demand a reduced rent because of defects at the start of a residential rental agreement. The closest options are:
- You don't pay rent until you enter if the premises aren't vacant and reasonably clean (s 65(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- After you give repair notice and the provider fails to repair, VCAT must order your rent paid into the Rent Special Account unless the provider shows financial hardship (s 77(2)). If the breach is of s 68 or the minimum standards and the repairs still aren't done by the end of that period, you can apply for that rent to be paid to you (s 77(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Compensation may be ordered under s 76(1)(c) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Practical steps

- **Record the defects.** Photograph them, and note them on the condition report. The provider must give you the report before you move in, and you can complete your own (s 35). A condition report given to the provider counts as notice of the defects (s 36(1A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Correct the report if needed.** You can apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate condition report within 30 days after the agreement commences (s 35A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the disclosures.** Before the agreement, the provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the minimum standards, and any repair notice about structural mould or damp in the last 3 years (reg 16(2)(b)–(c)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is a summary of the retrieved legislation, not legal advice. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre can help with your specific facts.

All three points are covered: the answer says the minimum standards, including being 'free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure', must be met 'on or before the day you enter (s 65A(1))'; it says an agreement ends if 'the renter has not entered into possession and gives notice of termination' because the premises are not in good repair, unfit for human habitation or not meeting minimum standards (s 91L); and it says 'you can request urgent repairs (s 65A(2))', alongside the s 68 good-repair duty and the non-urgent repair route.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
# Burglary damage to plumbing and wiring during a Victorian tenancy

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf". Its metadata gives version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). No later version came up in my search. The documents don't use the words "Authorised Version No.", so the version numbers above come from their metadata.

## What the law says

- **Urgent repairs:** The Act's definition includes a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglary damage to plumbing and wiring may fall within these, depending on the actual damage.
- **Your duty to report:** You must give the rental provider written notice of damage as soon as practicable after becoming aware of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the damage stops you cleaning, this wording helps you, but the documents don't say how a Tribunal would apply it to your situation.
- **Fault for the damage:** You must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider can only give a repair notice if the damage came from your failure to take care [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider can claim on the bond for damage caused by the renter or a renter's visitor [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A visitor means someone on the premises with the renter's permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and burglars wouldn't be that.
- **Lease-ending provisions:** A renter may give notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe". The termination date can be the date of the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing now.** Describe the damage and ask for urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **If they don't act, arrange the repairs yourselves.** You can do this if you've taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to the prescribed amount, within 7 days of the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The standard-form agreement summary gives that amount as $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve the operative regulation setting it.
3. **Apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order.** You can do this if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear it within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Leave early if the premises are unfit or unsafe.** Give a notice of intention to vacate under s 91ZD [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - Whether the damage meets that threshold is a factual question the documents don't answer.
   - For a fixed-term agreement of more than 5 years, the standard form says the provider can't claim lost rent if you leave on this ground [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say the same for shorter agreements.
   - The ordinary notice-of-intention-to-vacate rule requires at least 28 days' notice. For fixed terms it has no effect if the termination date falls before the end of the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Raise the repeated break-ins and locks.** The standard agreement requires the provider to ensure window locks and deadlocks that meet the rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the provider unreasonably withholds consent to a lock change, you can apply to VCAT for a determination that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

They don't address who bears the cost of burglary damage, insurance, or reporting to police. For your specific fixed term and any lease-break consequences, check your own agreement and consider advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers written notice as soon as practicable, and urgent repairs with renter-arranged repairs and reimbursement. It misses that a s 91ZD notice works whether or not the lease is a fixed term. It says the termination date 'can be the date of the notice or later' but never states this applies to fixed terms, and it muddies the point by noting the ordinary notice 'has no effect if the termination date falls before the end of the term' and that the documents 'don't say the same for shorter agreements', so a renter mid-lease cannot tell whether immediate termination is available to them.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never makes the renter liable for the burglary damage: it says a provider can give a repair notice only if the damage came from "your failure to take care", and that the provider "must reimburse the reasonable cost" of urgent repairs. It also does not bind the renter to stay, since it offers the option to "Leave early if the premises are unfit or unsafe" under s 91ZD.
